There are some spoilers here so beware.

This was truly a phenomenal game that brought back what I loved about Resident Evil. To start off, the environments were great. I loved the aesthetics of this game. From the prison area in the beginning, the village later in the game, and lab more towards the end, I loved the classic RE feel this game had. Inventory management was brought back, thought not the same as it was originally, it's handled better than most Resident Evil games that did away with the idea (RE5 for example). The music was beautiful and gave me vibes from the first game. Seeing more traditional zombies again was great and is always welcomed. The puzzles in this game were genuinely so great and I'm glad they decided to bring them back as I felt 3, 4, Revelations 1 and 5 all lacked good puzzles, but this game really brought them back and they were very enjoyable. Some puzzles had me actually having to think which can't be said about the previous games. The story was fine. It wasn't anything that stands out to me personally, but I like what was done with Natalia and the Burtons. Speaking of, seeing Barry again after the first game was awesome. I'm glad this game was able to reintroduce classic characters in a more modern setting, including Claire who I also loved in this game (besides one thing that I will get back to). The episodic nature was fun, though it felt short despite the game's runtime. Maybe it was just because you switch between Claire's and Barry's campaigns so quick (often 30 minutes each) and only having 4 episodes makes it feel shorter, but it does pick up in length towards the end (except for one part, which again, I'll get into). The side characters were fine in this game. They weren't anything noteworthy but I enjoyed their presence. Yuri Lowenthal being in this game was unexpected but I loved his performance. The character switching was a fun concept, but I did feel like it was a little off since it felt more optimized for two players but this game isn't online so you're having to take care of two characters at once. It made for some fun puzzles though. The gameplay was very fun with the gunplay, dodge mechanic, flashlight, and Natalia's abilities. The mansion segment at the end of the game was great, but that could be me being a little biased since RE1 is still my favorite. Short hair Claire is not something I thought I needed but man, I loved seeing her at the end with that new makeover. She looks great with shorter hair, but I am saying this as a Jill fan so again, I could be biased. And finally, the second phase of the final boss was pretty unique. It was easy for the most part, but it was something different that makes the boss fights not feel so redundant. 

Now, for my issues with the game. There were many times where I would get stunlocked and would be unable to do anything against the enemies attacking me. It was very annoying. I didn't like how common the big enemies were as it didn't feel as special to see them later on. They were scary at first because "oh no, a big guy that'll eat my ammo, I really have to be wise about how I go about this" but as you progress, you see more and more of them so it became more of a nuisance than an actual challenge. The lockpicking mechanic sucked. Genuinely the worse iteration of lockpicking in any game ever. Now, the issue I mentioned I had with Claire was: How come she couldn't comfort Natalia? I understand that Claire was looking for Neal and was set on finding him, but the game makes it out as if Moira is the one that's good with kids despite Claire helping Sherry throughout RE2 and I'd assume helped to raise her after? So you would think she would be the one that would be good with talking to kids but apparently not. I also didn't enjoy the fact that any time I would play as Natalia with zombies around, Barry just couldn't defend himself. This was annoying for one specific puzzle later in the game but it wasn't that big of a deal, just something that annoyed me in the moment. Another thing I referenced earlier was how the game picks up in length in the later half of the game, except for Claire's episode 4 segment which only lasted 18 minutes for me, and that was with me being stuck at one part. Meaning that had I not gotten stuck, I possibly could have done it in 15, making it by far the shortest segment in the game even though its Claire's last one. I hated how much health the recurring boss that attacks Barry has. I don't mind the boss reappearing at times, I like that, in fact. However, the amount of ammo and bottles it took to defeat the boss each time was just so annoying. Some enemies also love to hit through walls. Nothing much else to say because it's obvious as to why that'd be annoying. Also, the bug guys. They. Suck. And finally, the first phase of the final boss was only annoying because the segment before it has you unload all of your ammo into a hoard of enemies so you go into the final boss with nothing, making the final boss difficult not out of a design trait from the boss, but from a lack of resources from the player.

Overall, this game was a great experience. I enjoyed just about every minute of this game, and was even a little sad when it ended since I wanted more. But, it was a good time and I'm sure it would be even better if you had a friend to play with. I highly recommend.

After getting some struggles with remoteplay to behave I honestly found myself really enjoying this game and for all that it's worth. I'm not sure why it's called Revelations 2 as if it's a direct sequel to 1 when in all honesty there's only a brief mention of a location in 1 called Terragrigia and an organization called the FBC while the rest of the game is more or less its' own standalone narrative aside returning characters.

The story was great but also weird, and I feel like it's due to the archaic design of being episodic; pacing was very great until randomly getting awkward for a very obvious cliffhanger as each episode wasn't a full part of a character pair's story, you always play as [spoiler]Claire and Moira, or Barry and Natalia[/spoiler] and every episode has to continue everyone's story - so while you have very solid tension, and emotional depth, character development that ends up leading to extremely satisfying closure, you also have moments where the peak of the interesting parts start to get going it gives you a big cut to black "NEXT TIME ON REVELATIONS" moment and then the pacing soft restarts. I still loved the end product by the end of the day, but I can't deny it left me wondering how much better it would have felt in design if this were just a full content drop day 1 title.

Gameplay is Rev1 but polished up and better in just about every single way; gun customization came back with the same stat amp and pick-and-choose buildcrafting in a sense, local co-op for the main story where P1 is your sort of combat specialist, while P2 is your gimmick character that can do unique helpful interactions/and majority solves the brunt of the puzzles, and lots more off the beaten path content than the first game.

Soundscape and OST got a glow up, not necessarily much better, but I think there's a few tracks that actually stand out here as opposed to how disappointingly monotonous the first game was.

Raid mode is hilariously silly and fun, an RPG-like minimode to break away from mercenaries during the peak of exhaustion due to 5, 6 and Mercenaries 3D all existing really close to eachother. It allows you to play through static repeatable levels to get gear, to then challenge the harder levels with new tilesets, to then get gear and repeat until you've maxed everything out and make hilarious heatseeking angry beehive guns with negative recoil.



All in all, it's a solid recommend from me [b]Only[/b] if you get the Deluxe edition for all 6 episodes at the cheapest value, otherwise with only ep1 and the sliver of content that gives you it's a hard skip from me as it does nothing amazing on its' own without the rest of the majority content.

Resident Evil: Revelations была очень неожиданным, но очень приятным глотком свежего воздуха в серии, чья экшеновая направленность уже на момент 2012 года близилась к своему апогею в виде Resident Evil 6 и Operation Raccoon City. Пока многие негодовали, Capcom тихонечко выпустили спин-офф, который рассказывал о событиях, произошедшиях с Джилл Валентайн и Крисом Редфилдом между четвёртой и пятой частями сериала, которая была по духу близка к началу серии. Игрокам такой эксперимент пришёлся по вкусу, а Capcom заприметила себе на будущее новое денежное направление - спин-оффы с практически забытыми в основной линейке персонажами серии, направленные, в основном, на более консервативную аудиторию. 
В 2015 году свет видит первый эпизод сиквела "откровений", двойка в которой указывает не на сюжетное продолжение оригинала, но на развитие идей, заложенных в нём же. Получилось ли у разработчиков так же клёво, как было в прошлый раз? На мой скромный взгляд - вовсе нет.

Сиквел повествует о Барри Бёртоне и Клэр Редфилд, которых не было видно ещё со времён первой Resident Evil и Code Veronica - 1996 и 2000 годов соответственно, а посему задел на интригующую историю - состоялся. Эпизодический формат подливал масло в огонь, предлагая нам следить за завязкой и развязкой на протяжении четырёх недель - с одним эпизодом на неделю. В целом, идея была интересной, и интрига какая-никакая присутствовала, но... ребят, это же Resident Evil. Здесь сюжет всегда на заднем плане, посему о нём и говорить смысла нет - все те же тропы и сюжетные повороты, ничего интересного. 
Что уж точно всегда было на первом плане, так это геймплей. И здесь он, мягко скажем, вторичный. Если первые "откровения" радовали нас интересным кораблём, который хоть и был более коридорен, чем условный особняк из самого первого резидента, но всё же был обустроен довольно красиво и с интересными деталями, то вторая часть предлагает нам солянку из разных, но прямых как труба локаций, в которых и исследовать-то толком нечего. И каждый раз нам подсовывают классическую проблему: для открытия двери вперёд нужен ключ, который лежит буквально в следующей комнате. Это ну уж очень удручает. 
Экшен здесь несильно изменился, но в этом-то и проблема: если первой части это было простительно ввиду направленности игры на портативную платформу, а всеобщая клаустрофобность отчасти компенсировала эту проблему, то здесь мы имеем всё тех же неповоротливых монстряков с огромным опухолем на довольно открытых локациях. Патронов вроде бы и мало, но их всегда хватает в виду того, что врагов мало и они не очень-то и смертоносны. 
Ощущается также и всеобщая вторичность. Я уже даже не хочу говорить про текстуры низкого разрешения - оставим это всяким Ваномасам и ко., речь про бесконечно повторяющиеся геймплейные ситуации (вроде тех же поисков ключей); непонятно зачем добавленный стелс, который накорню ломает сурвайвал-составляющую игры своей летальностью (одного нападения со спины достаточно, чтобы уничтожить любого суппостата); реюз ассетов от пятой, шестой части и первых "откровений" - в общем, видно, как кэпком пытались сделать солянку из, что называется, производственных остатков. Это слегка раздражает, ведь это был первый резидент в восьмом поколении консолей, а на деле кроме неплохих моделей персонажей никакой технологичности особо и не ощущается.
Вспомогательный режим "Рейд", представленный ещё в первой части, стал ещё более разнообразным, но как по мне, излишне акцентированным на циферках, чего я не припомню в предшественнице. Да и режим мне, в принципе, кажется довольно спорной заменой уже традиционных "Наёмников", однако, кому как.

Так или иначе, игра безусловно может найти своих любителей - в ней есть потенциал, и интересные идеи, но всё же это вторичный, одноразовый продукт, который вряд ли сможет удивить так же, как и первая часть. Рекомендую брать только со скидкой и не ожидать ничего сверхординарного.

RE:R2 is a very underrated game. It improves upon the first game in nearly every way. Gameplay wise, RE:R2 introduces some of the best enemy design in the entire franchise, and also brings back the duo protagonist feature from RE0, which I was a fan of. The puzzles are pretty cool and fun to solve, and the atmosphere is some of the best in the franchise. The story is actually pretty good and compelling. The characters, both new and old, are interesting, well written and easy to get attached to. The only major issue I have with the game is a choice you have to make about halfway through, which determines which ending you get. At first, I thought the ending made no sense and I thought they were just leaving it on a cliffhanger for a potential third part. After doing some research, I found out that the game has two endings, and I got the bad one. That's when I found out that in the third episode, you actually have to make a choice which determines the ending you get. The fact that you even have to make a choice in the first place is so poorly communicated, that I didn't even realise there was an option, which therefore resulted in me getting the bad ending, which on it's own made no sence. I did check out the good ending on YouTube, and it's clear that this is the 'canon' ending, as it actually makes sense. Apart from that, I only have a few nitpicks. The shooting still feels clunky, and the level design could be a little too simple at times, making the game feel like The Last of Us from Temu. Despite its flaws, RE:R2 is by far my favourite RE game from that era, and seeing it get such hate genuinely makes me a little frustrated, as there was clearly a lot of love and passion put into this project.

By far the worst RE game i've played including Operation Raccoon City.
The PC port really does feel like a mobile game, it feels significantly worse than both the 3DS and PS Vita port.

The game offers two gamemodes, a chapter based Campaign and Raid mode. First part of the review will go over campaign, 2nd raid mode.

The first chapter's is really cool, the SAW esque atmosphere is awesome and the new enemy designs are swag... There really is no issue with the first chapter at all, but as soon as chapter 2 starts the game falls apart and progressively gets worse both gameplay and atmosphere wise. The lack of headshot or body staggering makes combat tedious and often requires you to dump 3-4 shots in the head of a normal enemy before they get staggered.

The game was made with co-op in mind just like RE5 and RE6 but somehow handles it even worse than both of them. Resident Evil 5 released 6 years prior to this mess and is widely known for having a mentally handicapped AI that plays as sheva whenever you play solo, yet that game has superior AI to this game. You do have the option to "Partner swap" a function that returns from Resident Evil 0, This time however it works.
I honestly wish it didn't work, and that is because the two characters you can swap to are incredibly boring to play as and can't use any guns. 

Playing this in couch co-op feels like you are either punishing your friend who was to play as the character without guns or as some form of humiliation ritual if you yourself play this mess for 15 ish hours without a weapon, being only able to either aim a flashlight at dark corners to find collectibles or stun enemies (lame)

The weapon upgrade system sucks and requires you to find weapon upgrade parts in different containers that you can then apply to your weapon using a workbench. It almost feels like the same system Dead Space 3 used 2 years earlier (that went super well...)

The story is bad even for Resident Evil standards with the story split up between two duos and lets you play as Claire Redfield (shawty from RE2, Chris Redfield's sister) and Moira Burton (Daughter of the fat dumbass cop from RE1) The other duo consists of said dumbass Barry Burton and Natalia, a hungarian child that can throw bricks.

 Long story short Claire and Moira get kidnapped by terrorists and placed in a prison "The penal colony... (I will ♥♥♥♥ on this later). Barry tracks down his daughter and accidentally runs into Natalia the brick thrower, a mysterious orphan child. The whole game consists of Barry and Natalia trying to find Claire and Moira who tries to find a way off the island and kill their kidnapper Alex Wesker, 1 of 12 siblings of Albert wesker.

Arguably the worst part of the whole campaign is the fact that Dai Satō has filled it with Franz Kafka references (Larp Larp Larp) Each of the campaign chapters are named after Kafka literature.
Episode 1: Penal Colony (In der Strafkolonie)
Episode 2: Contemplation (Betrachtung)
Episode 3: Judgment (Das Urteil)
Episode 4: Metamorphosis (Die Verwandlung)
Extra Episode: The Struggle  (Beschreibung eines Kampfes)
Extra Episode: Little Miss (Eine kleine frau)

Even collectibles in the game are pages from his books... The main antagonist even reads the funny cockroach book and writes a reddit tier review about it (One of said collectibles mentioned earlier) You can also find 5 of Kafka's sketches throughout the game by using Moira's flashlight.

Part 2: Raid Mode. With the release of Resident Evil Revelations 2 the awesome raid mode from Resident Evil Revelations 1 returns.

 This time it is much better for casual players but a let down for RER 1 veterans. The core gameplay in itself is better due to the fact that movement and shooting is better, On the other side it does get very repetetive due to how short the levels are and how many times you need to replay them to get better skills.  
RER1's raid mode was significantly harder and required you to be somewhat mindful of resource managment when using herbs, RER2 however alot of the time offer no challenge as long as you are not completely underleveled and somewhat sapient (optional tbh)

Raid mode has been expanded a ton with around 200 ish missions to complete either solo or co-op. 
This time it features levels and characters from prior Resident Evil games (RE6 and RER 1) which is really cool.
Skill trees and leveling has been expanded, This time leveling is based on which character you choose and not tied to your account in general. 

From my casual perspective I belive that raid mode is almost a direct upgrade in this game, The difficulty might be a bit too easy and as someone who had only played raid mode once or twice on the PS4 in 2017 I feel like the game should be harder as I have next to no experience lol.

LIGHT SPOILERS AHEAD! 

Never before an ending managed to ruin and undo an otherwise good game for me quite like the one to Resident Evil Revelations 2. An improvement over the first Revelations game in every way, throughout its solid 15-hour campaign, it was slowly, but surely, marching into my personal survival horror Hall of Fame, along with titles like System Shock 2, Dead Space and The Evil Within Dilogy.

But then the ending happened... spoilers - for those "in the know", I got the "bad" ending, just because somewhere after the middle point of the game I made a split-second decision that looked to be either rather insignificant or at least not important enough to warrant much thought. The choice at the time made perfect sense, as the alternative was quite counterintuitive and contradicted a major plot point about one of the main characters. So off I was with that choice. However, not only that decision resulted in one of the main characters DYING soon thereafter - even though I honestly couldn't really see any direct, causal connection with the choice made -  but that split-second decision also locked in a thoroughly depressing, AWFUL final ending that just spits in the player's face and can't be changed or altered in any way. And that terrible ending was still HOURS away.

I want make this crystal clear - I'm not a fan of multiple choice endings just before the grand finale, when one can just load the last save file and see all possible endings no matter what happened throughout the story (think Singularity or to a lesser extent, Deus Ex: Human Revolution). But again - the choice in the middle must be communicated clearly. Not necessarily through words, but at least implicitly, via notes, foreshadowing, well, with SOMETHING. Just having a random minor choice at roughly 70% of the game's runtime triggering  a nonsensical "bad" ending and the death of TWO main characters you've got attached to is not a hidden genius move, its abysmal game design and writing. 

And no, it's not Bioshock situation either, where harvesting even one Little Sister also locked in the bad ending (justifiably so). Believe me when I say, that the choice determining an OK ending (for a survival horror game) and a dark, depressingly hollow bad one is truly, truly MINOR and shouldn't have the consequences it has. And if, for some odd reason, that's what the game designers wanted to do, they should have - again - communicated this clearly. It could have been a suggestive line of dialogue, an expression on character's face, just something, give us something! You can't just pull out a seemingly meaningless "choice" out of nowhere in the penultimate chapter and then force the player to trudge all the way to the ending, which mockingly negates everything he tried to accomplish throughout the game. It stops being survival horror and instead becomes just pessimistic, depressing mess trying to "subvert the expectations" Ryan Johnson-style.

Bringing back some old faces to face against new terrors, Revelations 2 manages to strike a decent balance between action horror and survival horror during a somewhat turbulent time in the franchise's history.

Resident Evil: Revelations 2 (2015) is the sequel to Revelations, though tangentially related in story, as well as a canon installment in the series (as are all spinoffs, but this one is obviously connected to the main timeline more significantly). You once again are fitted into familiar shoes, this time into longtime absentees Claire Redfield, sister of Chris Redfield and a counterterrorism veteran in her own right, and Barry Burton, a family man who hoped he could get away from a life of evil corporations and genetically engineered monsters in favor of spending his days with his loved ones, as they're tangled in the newest plot by Wesker, although not the one they'd imagined. Claire and Moira Burton, Barry's estranged teenage daughter, are attending a welcome party at Terrasave, one of many anti-bioterrorism organizations, when they're ambushed by an armed militia and abducted to a mysterious island, fitted with strange wristbands. All the while, Barry Burton is on a mad hunt to find his missing daughter, no matter the cost. 

Resident Evil Revelations 2 is a game wracked with the unfortunate position of riding the coattails of one of the most controversial games in the series, Resident Evil 6 (although one I'm not that harsh on, I think it's a bit overhated if you ask me), and so it has a lot to prove itself on. I think it does a fairly good job given that it's the final game before the series marks a transitioning period, but you might be surprised to know that it's not as different from some newer entries. The game is split into four main 'episodes', with two subchapters in each, each being fairly lengthy (I averaged over an hour in each chapter, sometimes more due to confusing level design and just being scatterbrained). The Revelations formula of switching back and forth between characters returns, now letting you freely swap at will between the different pairs of characters you play as, which is a very welcome change. Every other chapter you will swap between Claire and Moira, and Barry and the little girl he finds on his journey, Natalia, and you can swap between those two characters at will during the campaign, each character in a pair having a different role in gameplay. Claire and Barry are your normal RE protagonists, fitted with all the guns and combat tools you would expect, while Moira and Natalia are more supporters, having tools unique to them that aid in puzzle solving and cooperation. A mechanic similar to the scanner from Revelations 1 makes its way into the game, but changed into a flashlight for Moira and a pointing finger for Natalia, helping you find hidden loot around the map. This game could be considered a prototype for several mechanics seen in the future RE engine games, especially the remakes, as it features the cross-bar/wheel style weapon select from 2R-3R-4R, a dodge ability not unlike the one in 3R but without the bullet-time and auto-aim, and finally a stealth kill system reminiscent of the one from 4R, though you have no knife durability to worry about. A mechanic similar to the item exchange from RE0 also shows up, letting you stash any overflowing items in your other character and pass it to them whenever you wish if in range, serving as a second inventory. Nearly all of the mechanics from the action trilogy are here as well (4-5-6), with the "coup de grace"/melee finisher you can trigger by staggering enemies, the ever-coveted infinite hitsun knife that you can use anytime by just pressing the attack button when not aiming, and an end-of-chapter tally and perk system similar from the one from 6, giving you useful perks such as faster healing time and higher support item damage. Enemy variety here is not the best, but what few are there are very well designed visually, being some of the most disgusting enemies in the series, right alongside its sister game Revelations 1. Crafting is reintroduced for the first time in over a decade since RE3: Nemesis (1999), letting you craft healing items and throwables. The new fear-induced mutations of the T-Phobos virus developed on the island results in some of the gnarliest designs I've seen, as well as providing the game with some decent mechanical variety to watch out for. My favorite are the Revenants, which are basically the Rasklapanje from 6 or the Dividers from Dead Space, though if their limbs were like a game of whack-a-mole instead of runaway body parts. I did not like the invisible insect enemies, though. To tie the game off in a bow, you get two additional DLC mini-campaigns, one for Moira and Natalia each, with Moira having one particularly annoying stealth section, but otherwise being fun, and Natalia just having stealth as an entire campaign. You can opt to not play these, but I'd suggest at least doing Moira's, as it does actually provide some nice character development for her, and makes you appreciate her a little more as a character. The final addition being the second iteration of Raid mode, it itself being a bit of a Mercenaries mode type deal. It has decent side content for a spinoff.

The story is about what you'd expect from Resident Evil. Moira's welcome party at Terrasave is crashed by insurgents and she and Claire are abducted to Sein Island (localized as Zabytij in the English version of the game for some reason, the original name is a nod to Franz Kafka whose writings are frequently mentioned in this game), trying to escape, but eventually getting split up. Barry's sections take place chronologically six months after Claire and Moira's, leading to a narrative back-and-forth in an almost detective mystery of what exactly happened in that time gap. Some very interesting revelations (heh) are made during the story, as well as research into the transfer of human consciousness into a new vessel, which definitely doesn't get mentioned again in one of the newest games in the series.. no sir..

My only gripes are mostly just Moira cussing a fair bit, but compared to RE3 Remake Jill, she's a teenager, and teenagers are generally annoying, so I give her a pass, compared to a full grown adult and police officer acting like they just lost a match in Valorant. Moira also gets better over time, unlike Not-Jill. That and Revelations 2 initially being sold piecemeal, though now you can get all of the episodes via Deluxe Edition.

Presentation wise, being an actual console title, unlike the first Revelations which was intended for handheld (but later ported), visuals here are pretty decent. The MT Framework engine is really being pushed to its limits here, in probably its last outing before Capcom released their new proprietary engine, with some fairly nice character and environmental models, though maybe a little outdated for the year. The BOW designs here are definitely the nastiest I'd seen apart from maybe some of the old tank control games' ones, with the delapidated industrial zones and overgrown forests of the island providing a rather vibrant playground for the player to get lost in. On the technical side, the game comes with the same host of quality of life features as Rev1, with unlocked framerate options, higher resolutions, window options, etc. 

For a sideline title, Revelations 2 offers some interesting lore tidbits, intuitive controls for the series, and overall a pleasant and entertaining experience. If you just want more action Resident Evil, this'll do the job. Minor gripes like borderless mode being a bit buggy and the game initially being released on a per-episode basis over time aside, I had a fun time. I would purchase the Deluxe Edition of this game on sale, as it contains all of the main campaign episodes. Do not buy just the base game, you will not get the entire story mode if you do, you've been warned.

I ended up enjoying Revelations 2. It feels much closer to what a Resident Evil game is, but does feel a bit unpolished and rough around the edges, but has a good core. I actually enjoyed the story quite a bit, and the atmosphere/tone is very consistent and builds on itself very well. That's probably this games strongest parts, is the atmosphere and story. Combat was interesting and a bit different. Claire's campaign had probably the most bland combat, but I really enjoyed Barry's part of the game, having to switch characters to kill enemies efficiently and save ammo. If you don't try to play optimally, you'll be starved of ammo the whole game.

Bosses are also pretty good. However, at times, the game can feel like a slog, particularly in the middle. Environment design is generally spooky, some areas felt a lot like Half Life 2, and one section felt like Rust from MW2 . However, for most of the game, I felt is was generally pretty uninspiring, looking like it was just straight ripped out of a horror movie. Not necessarily a bad thing, but there are very few areas that stand out. 

This game did feel very unpolished. There's a lack of enemy variety, and I ended up using the same 4 weapons generally for each character most of the game because they were just better. Sometimes, puzzles felt unclear. However, the story and characters outweighed then negatives from this.

Resident Evil: Revelations 2 is an episodic survival-horror game following Claire Redfield and Moira Burton, who are abducted by a mysterious "Overseer" and imprisoned on a monster-infested island. The story, set between RE5 and RE6, splits into two, featuring Claire/Moira's escape attempt and Barry Burton's search for his daughter six months later, revealing a plot involving the T-Phobos virus and mysterious character with ties to the original Resident Evil. 

Gameplay, as mentioned is split between Claire and the legendary Barry, both of which control fantastically and will feel familiar to those who've played action resi. Both characters have a unique companion that whilst the inclusion of another companion is annoying they are at least more thematic in their inclusion and offer unique gameplay and you can switch to them at will. Barry's sections do feel a bit the last of us lite but ultimately this is just a fun game to play. 

The other big thing on offer is Raid mode, massively upgraded and just a fun to play as it was in Rev 1. This time it has it's own narrative with more fleshed out system and plenty of characters, weapons and skills to unlock. 

So not a perfect game, definitely not the best in the series but a good game if you're a fan but are sick of the silliness. It's crazy how much DNA this game shares with some of the more modern 3rd person resi games. Really I'm just happy Barry got his chance to shine.

First off, the game performs poorly on my machine. That could be my fault, but I'm not sure.
But secondly, and this is arguably worse: the game is episodic via installments, and if you are like me, you only have episode 1. You have to buy the other 3 episodes.
To be clear, I bought this because I finished the first Revelations. So my expectations were built on that experience. But so far they are really not the same kind of game. 
Immediately the theming of the game is not as stylized or unique; the first mission is just kind of a horror-house prison, with hanging bodies and very ridiculous looking zombie models. (They look like they got stung by bees.)
The AI companion (Moira/Natalie) has been improved considerably on a mechanical level (over Parker); but also weakened functionally, as they are not combatants like Parker was in the first game. You may 'swap' between the characters as well, which allows the player to correct or enforce behavior. So, I have mixed feelings about the AI; more advanced, but also asymmetric. Berry and Natalie complement each other better than Claire and Moira.
Another major issue is Moira herself. Any time she talks, it is just a lot of exclamations and cursing. She says weird things too. Her noisy behavior drowns out the player's emotional response to events, and makes me think she was intended for a younger, perhaps more casual target audience; which clashes with the difficulty of the game, since it is actually a bit hard out the get-go. I honestly died a lot near the end of mission 1 because I didn't realize you can turn the flaming head machine to burn the oncoming horde of zombies. As soon as you enter that room, they are already on top of you and you don't have time to properly assess and solve the situation. Nor have you encountered such a flaming head before, thus, not mechanically literate of what it can do.
I will say, mission 2 was a lot better. I like Berry and Natalia way more, they have more clear roles in their game loop, and they get a fairly unnerving jaunt through a dark forest with tough enemies. But even mission 2 reuses much of mission 1's prison map. It was a little underwhelming. But then again, Revelations 1 had a lot of looping through old areas as well (they just looked better).

Do I recommend it? Ah.... not really, no.

Building on the formula introduced in Resident Evil Revelations, Resident Evil Revelations 2 makes some small but meaningful improvements.

One of the biggest additions is the weapon selection system, which feels much closer to what we see in the more modern Resident Evil titles. It’s smoother, more intuitive, and makes combat flow better than in the first Revelations.

Unlike the previous game, Revelations 2 also handles unlockables much better. You can unlock infinite ammo for all weapons, and there are far more special weapons to earn overall. For completionists and replay-focused players, that’s a huge improvement.

Raid Mode returns as well, largely unchanged from the first game. That’s not necessarily a bad thing — it was already a solid side mode — but don’t expect major innovation there.

Overall, this feels like a refinement rather than a reinvention. It doesn’t dramatically change the formula, but it improves enough of the rough edges to make it the stronger of the two Revelations titles.

I think Resident Evil Revelations 2 is a fine game, it's nothing special and it has some flaws but for fans of the series it does enough to garner a recommendation by me. For one, much like its predecessor, it feels like a horror focused game, unlike 4 and 5, which are more action focused in my opinion. It also allows for the toggling between partners, for better and for worse. Each of the main characters has a partner you can play as, these partners don't use guns so their combat potential is limited but they can be used for puzzles and finding hidden items. I think this addition is good in theory but poorly implemented. Since they can't use guns, you will never want to use them for combat, so instead you end up just switching to them in every room to see if there's a hidden item and then going back to the other stronger character. One of these partners, Moira, is also extremely annoying and I hated listening to her speak, mostly due to how she's written. 

Gameplay wise, the gunplay is pretty good. There's the usual variety of weapons, and the throwables are genuinely fun to use. The enemy variety is lackluster though, and a lot of the enemies are just downright annoying. The developers thought an invisible enemy that one shots you would be a fun addition and it just isn't. Your partner is supposed to be able to guide you to where to shoot but this is far too slow to be a viable strategy, especially when there's other enemies coming at you too. There's also enemies that can cover your screen with disgusting gunk that makes you blind, which is always fun to deal with in the cramped spaces the game takes place in. 

So with all this criticism why do I recommend it still? Well mostly for Barry's story arc. His half of the campaign is FAR better than the Claire, Moira part of the campaign because Barry is just written really well. Him having to protect Natalia and the way it fits into his broken relationship with his daughter, Moira, is just really well done. The gunplay is also pretty solid as I said and the atmosphere and horror part of the game is pretty well done. If you're a fan of Resident Evil give this game a shot. It's far from perfect but there's great moments scattered throughout the game and it fleshes out the world of Resident Evil after 5 pretty well. When I reviewed Revelations 1 I mentioned how the shambling unhuman masses that were the enemies of the game gave it a strong Silent Hill-esque vibe, here they decided to up the ante by tossing you a Pyramids Head every five minutes and the result is actually a pretty good game. 

Jokes aside while I think the enemies in Barry’s campaign maintained that same creepy horrifying vibe the oozes build on the first Revelations game, the enemies on Claire’s campaigned felt short on that promise, as they were just more agile versions of regular zombies and they lost much of the fear factor they build up on the prison as soon as you ended that first chapter and got yourself more firepower. I will say though that I’m glad that enemies no longer require a battalion’s worth of ammunition to take down.

The episodic story structure of the game with its whole previously on and up next trailer-like cutscenes actually make sense this time around as this game originally came out episodically though I’m kind of mixed on it. Every chapter seemed to end on a cliff hanger that was instantly resolved by the first cutscene of the next episode, so I t did fell kind of pointless when playing them continuously. There were still plenty of plot twist here, what would a revelations game be without them right? Although I thought they serve their purpose better here as they weren’t as unintentionally hilarious as in the first one. The game was also much better in keeping the tone and tension going throughout the story.

Having Claire back of course was a treat as a diehard Claire-fan but I did feel this game didn’t give her much to do in terms of her character which in the end ended up working in it’s favor as having her in a more background role did give time to the other characters both new and old that really needed it. I don’t know the general consensus of the fanbase of Moira, but I feel like she probably was a divisive inclusion. I mean her character seem like the result of Chloe Price from Life is Strange suddenly stumbling in a zombie Outbreak, she ended up being my favorite character here, but it was definitively out of the ordinary for this franchise. I never would have thought that I would want to have Barry back to be honest with how much the cast of the mainline series became stacked over time, but boy I’m sure glad he had a bit more time to shine and kick some Wesker ass. I don’t have much to comment about Natalia as she felt more like a plot element then a full character but she was fine enough in that role.

I will say I’m a bit disappointed with the main villainess of the story, as I expected more from how much she was hyped as Albert’s equal, but she just didn’t have that presence. Don’t get me wrong I wasn’t expecting here to we dancing around bullets all the time while saying she only has 7 minutes to play with me, but I was expecting more twirling mustache evil moments from her especially with how much she was involved in provoking agony in her victims, in her final confrontation with Moira and Claire it genuinely felt like she didn’t ultimately care about all the horrible things she did. You just can’t compare that to Albert which sure he always prioritized his goals first and foremost, but he always made a point to mock you every step of the way and his hatred for Chris in particular was always palpable.

Touching on gameplay for a bit I feel like this game absolutely nailed the forced cooperation with a companion on a horror game approach. While 5 and 6 could feel a bit lackluster in that respect on single player, that’s mainly due to those games being designed first and foremost with 2 player co-op in mind. Revelations 1 approach was absolutely tack-ed on with any regards to fun gameplay dynamics as they can barely be useful for drawing aggro for a while and 0 while it did try something similar at the time it just didn’t make Billy and Rebecca different enough were as the felt like two characters with totally different skill sets. This game fixes all those issues from a single-player perspective, each character is useful in it’s own way, each contribute both in combat, exploration and puzzle-solving in it’s own way, and their pairing is actually necessary given that both campaigns have a non-combatant on the team.

I whole heartly recommend this for at least one playthrough as outside of the original trilogy and 4 this has so far been the most fun I had with an RE game and definitively the best game overall in it’s action-era.

Resident Evil Revelations 2 is a direct continuation of the first Revelations and also connects to Resident Evil 5 and 6. During gameplay, it’s obvious that the game had a lower budget, with more dated graphics and stiffer gameplay, but it’s still a solid action game with survival horror elements. The biggest negative points of the game, in my view, are some goofy dialogues involving Claire and the guy from Terragrigia. Even though these moments are short, the main issue is the game’s pacing.

The game is episodic, which is fine, but the early episodes are much faster than the later ones—especially Claire’s section in Episode 3 and Barry’s in Episode 4. These parts really hurt the pacing, making the final stretch of the game feel dragged out.

Overall, I recommend the game. Resident Evil is always fun, it’s short, and it’s worth playing to follow the story, but it does have pacing issues that could have been handled better.

[h1]Apparently We’re Mad at Good Resident Evil Now[/h1]

I literally told myself, out loud, like a responsible adult, that I was going to avoid Resident Evil 6. I said it with confidence. Authority. Wisdom. Then the very next day it showed up on my store for $3.75 and my brain immediately folded like a lawn chair. I bought it, played the Chris campaign, and had to stop because it felt like chugging diarrhea syrup on top of a poop-flavored ice cream cone. I needed a palate cleanser. A reset. Something to remind me that this franchise didn’t actively hate me.

That detour led me here.

I came in for exactly two reasons and zero optimism: Claire Redfield finally existing again after Code Veronica, and Barry Burton—an actual playable Barry Burton instead of a polite cameo and a mustache. That’s it. I fully expected a throwaway spin-off I’d forget faster than a bad sneeze. Instead, this thing got me by the balls.

First of all, why are people trashing this game? This is why we don’t deserve nice things. This game actually has tension. Like, real tension. I was creeping around with my ass clenched, jumped at multiple very obvious jump scares, and yes, I yelled. Like a little ♥♥♥♥♥. Backtracking is here, but done like an adult—small, logical spaces, no map-induced aneurysms, and progression that doesn’t feel like punishment. Resource management matters again, time doesn’t stop when you open your inventory, crafting is useful, evasion exists, molotovs don’t suck, and stealth kills are so satisfying I started actively hunting for them like a psychopath.

The two-character system actually works because the second character isn’t just “gun, but worse.” Natalia in particular is fantastic, especially if you’re chasing secrets. Moira grows on you too—eventually. She’s basically that try-hard edgy kid we all knew at ten, swearing nonstop because they thought profanity was a personality and maturity came with a four-letter word quota.

The Burtons are the heart of the story, and it’s about damn time. Barry is everything you want him to be and never drops the ball. Moira starts rough but earns her development. Claire, sadly, is just sort of… there. Which hurts—but the dialogue at least sells shared history and chemistry.

And then the game just keeps going. Raid Mode alone is fun, and the amount of content makes me a differently abled to call this a short experience.

This game mixes classic and modern Resident Evil better than mainline entries, takes risks, and actually sticks the landing. It deserves more respect, and honestly, it deserves a third entry. Play it. Stop whining.

Resident Evil Revelations 2 stands as my favorite Resident Evil title to date. The story is engaging and easy to follow, and for once, you can genuinely feel for the main characters and the world of Resident Evil as a whole.

I started playing the first chapter solo, but after buying the remaining episodes, I played Episode 2 and 3 of both Claire’s and Barry’s campaigns with a friend. I didn’t even realize the game had multiplayer support until we looked it up — and honestly, that’s a real issue with this game. On top of that, I didn’t know there were two endings, which caused me to replay Chapter 1 of Episode 3 and the final mission twice.

My Breakdown
Story – 22/30

Revelations 2 focuses on two main characters who, prior to this game, hadn’t received much spotlight. Claire may have had Code: Veronica, but this truly feels like her game.
The story revolves around fear and loss. Claire’s campaign is fun but deeply unsettling when you really think about it, while Barry’s campaign focuses on grief and coming to terms with that loss. Both narratives complement each other extremely well.

Gameplay – 23/30

The gameplay feels like a refined version of the RE4/5/6 formula. From combining items in your inventory to stunning enemies with a flashlight, everything feels intentional.
I loved that one character has a gun while the other doesn’t — this design choice forces teamwork and encourages strategic thinking. The gun upgrade mechanics allow meaningful customization, and the skill tree is fantastic. The overall layout of the systems is clean and satisfying.

Audio – 5/10

The audio design is extremely well crafted. Gunshots feel loud and close, healing sounds are impactful, and actions like knifing or lunging feel weighty.
That said, I do wish the audio were better synced at times, as it can slightly break immersion.

Visuals – 7/10

The game is visually striking, often feeling like you’re trapped inside a Saw scenario. Blood, rust, and decay dominate the environments, making it easy to get lost in the world.
Even when you leave enclosed areas, the forest environments breathe with light and air. A remake or remaster would only enhance what already feels like a near-perfect setting. However, the heavy screen grain — especially in pre-rendered cutscenes — looks noticeably different from the in-game effects and made screenshots hard to take.

Voice Acting – 10/10

The voice acting genuinely made me cry multiple times. Barry and Moira’s relationship is incredibly well performed. You can hear the pain when Barry believes Moira has died — and the pure joy when he learns she’s alive.
Barry alone elevates this game to a 10/10.

Music – 4/10

The weakest part of the game. While there are a few standout tracks, most of the music didn’t leave a lasting impression outside of emotional scenes.

Final Thoughts

Despite a few issues, Resident Evil Revelations 2 delivers one of the most emotionally resonant experiences in the franchise. Strong characters, excellent gameplay, and a powerful story make it unforgettable.

Overall Score: 71/100

This is one of those games where the individual pieces are decent, but they just don’t fit well together.

I respect the developers—there’s obvious talent here. Enemy animations are great, the atmosphere has moments, and the co-op mechanics are genuinely interesting. But despite all that, the game isn’t really scary. It tries to be eerie, but when the narrative doesn’t land, the atmosphere ends up feeling kind of empty.

I came into this expecting that I could just understand the story on its own terms, because this isn’t a mainline entry. But the truth is: if you haven’t played Resident Evil 1 through 6, a lot of this won’t make sense. I tried for hours to get invested in the narrative, but the more I played, the more confused and bored I became. The pacing swings wildly—sometimes things happen too fast, sometimes nothing happens for hours, and by the time the plot finally tries to go somewhere, I was completely checked out.

Gameplay-wise, it’s fine. Shooting feels decent, and there’s a good idea buried in the partner-switching system. Ammo exists, but it’s too limited for how action-focused the game is. If the intention was to make gunplay feel meaningful because ammo is scarce, okay—but melee (especially for Barry) is borderline useless, and there’s no real crafting system to support that style of design. Combine that with only a handful of enemy types and the combat gets stale way faster than it should.

I played solo, and I’ll give the game credit: switching between characters actually works smoothly. It’s not a chore. But it’s also very clear this game was designed for co‑op first and single-player second.

The bigger picture is this: from about 2012 to 2016, Capcom didn’t seem to know what Resident Evil was supposed to be anymore. Resident Evil 6 and Revelations 1 were stuck between action-heavy set pieces and survival horror, and neither side felt fully realized. The dev teams were being asked to do too much, which meant every individual idea was stretched thin.

Revelations 2 feels like it came from that same confused era. Since the first Revelations released in 2012 and Resident Evil 7 wasn’t arriving until 2017, Capcom clearly needed something to fill the gap. Whether the team wanted to make this or not, they had to make something—and this is what it turned into: a game full of individually good ingredients that never truly come together.

My honest take: I don’t hate it. I don’t love it. I finished it because I wanted it off my steam backlog. It’s not terrible, but it’s not good enough for me to recommend unless you’re already a committed Resident Evil fan. At best, it’s an interesting relic from a messy period in the series’ history.

This is a great Resident Evil game. Since the early days of the franchise we always had some spin-off games releasing between the numbered ones and, while the success of the remake era we are now in is trully great for the IP, I personally think Revelations 1 and 2 were the best those in-between-mainline-titles have ever been simply for the fact both are complete new games (not remakes) with gameplay as good as the main games of their time. Revelations 2 feels as good if not better than Resident Evil 5.

The game is set in 2011 (about two years after RE5 and two years before RE6) and it features Claire Redfield and Barry Burton as the main characters, along with Moira (Barry's daughter) and Natalia as support characters (you can also control them to find hidden items and solve puzzles, although they're weak in combat). You'll always be controlling a pair of characters (or Claire and Moira, or Barry and Natalia) but unfortunately there's no online coop in this one. As for a single player campaign experience though, I think the way the support characters behave in Revelations 2 and the fact you can alternate the character you're playing with at any time make this one funnier than playing through Resident Evil 5 or 6 (if you're playing alone).

Capcom tried a different approach with Revelations 2 and although the game was already complete from the start, it was released in an episodic format similar to Telltale games. In Rev2's case you "only" had to wait one week between each episode, being 4 episodes in total, and in every single one of them you start playing a section as Claire and Moira and them you play as Barry and Natalia six months later. I've just finished playing Resident Evil Revelations 2 a survival horror game developed and published by CAPCOM Co., Ltd. both the main campaign as well as the two extra missions can be easily completed in 10~15 hours.

Lil' Bobby Capcom managed to sneak his way into the office again on bring your kid to work day. After the mixed reception from the first game, Lil' Bobby read his first full length novel, written by Franz Kafka, and was overflowing with inspiration when he once again climbed up into the writers chair, to type up a riveting sequel. Or... at least, that's what one might have expected, but I'm yet again looking through the credits on this game and seeing that it was written by a group of paid adults.

Resident Evil Revelations 2 takes place in the months following the Terragrigia incident, as Claire Redfield and Moira Burton are washed ashore on a non-descript soviet island. Claire, a hardened agent at this point, is immediately thrust into the protector role for Moira Burton, a charity worker and daughter of Barry Burton, as the two must find a way off the island. In typical Resident Evil fashion, it's not long before the island reveals itself to be a testing grounds of sorts for a new bioweapon, T-Phobus, which has seemingly decimated the entire population. However in the midst of the nightmare, Claire and Moira come across a young girl, Natalia, who lost her parents in the Terragrigia incident, and was brought to the island like many others.

Everyone on the island, including Claire, Moira, and Natalia have been injected with the T-Phobus virus, and given a bracelet to monitor their "fear levels." As they soon learn, T-Phobus has been modified in such a way that the virus is dormant until the subject reaches a certain threshold of fear, triggering a violent biological mutation. Whether or not Claire or Moira escape the island is exactly the question which brings Barry Burton to the island six months later. Upon arriving, Barry also meets Natialia, who's largely lost her memories of her time spent with Moira and Claire, forcing the two of them to retrace Claire and Moira's journey across the island.

The story is conveyed as "episodes" with the same ridiculous "next time on Resident Evil Revelations" outros, and "previously on..." intros bookending each chapter like watching Criminal Minds in 2001. In addition to badly dating the game, these also are wholly unnecessary cutscenes as there are only eight chapters total, and none of them are longer than an hour or two. Unfortunately, much like Resident Evil Revelations, the writing veers more towards bad, than bad funny. With characters saying lines so unbelievably dumb, like "It's a butchery. For killing livestock." as if there's any other type of butchery... or reading a note that explicitly lays out the antagonist's plan and immediately going "Strange... I wonder what all this could mean?" 

When the cast is not dropping horrible lines like "Oversee this!" they're fighting their way through levels in what is clearly intended to be a coop style gameplay experience. For Claire and Moira, Claire serves as a traditional Resident Evil fighter, with an arsenal of guns, knives and throwable weapons. Like the first Revelations, she can modify these guns with mod kits discovered along the journey. Moira on the other hand is equipped with a flashlight, which can blind enemies, as well as reveal hidden items. However, unlike Claire, she can only use a crowbar, due to a trauma from her past, which is also the source of her strained relationship with Barry. Six months in the future, Barry plays like a much stronger Claire, whose guns deal far more damage. Natalia on the other hand is a sneaky character, who cannot attack enemies, but can spot hidden foes, and traverse small space. 

In the first two missions, the single player trying to juggle a clearly coop intend game is badly balanced. The AI is atrociously bad when not actively controlling your partner, making them more than happy to stand around getting hit. Were companion deaths not also triggers for game over, this would not be as frustrating, but since they are, it feels like constantly baby sitting the AI companion, while trying to also progress the mission. After about the halfway mark, the game does a better job of splitting up the characters, making encounters feel more reasonable. There are various hidden items, such as gems, which can contribute towards BP, a point system to upgrade skills between missions.

There are a lot of things that missed with this entry in the Resident Evil franchise, particularly when there is such an abundance of good survival horror, it's hard to recommend this entry to most. There are elements to its narrative which could make it important for future games; however, considering it hasn't been touched on in over a decade, perhaps it is a thread Capcom will choose not to pull. It's not a bad game, and there were times where I felt myself enjoying the experience; however, it's certainly among the weakest entries for Resident Evil.

[h1]Revelations 2: A Return to Survival Horror[/h1]

[i]RE Revelations 2 continues the series acclaimed essential survival horror experience, while uncovering startling truths.[/i]

[h2]Story[/h2]
The story takes place in 2011, between the events of Resident Evil 5 and 6. Claire Redfield and her TerraSave colleagues, including Barry Burton’s daughter Moira, are abducted during a company party and taken to a remote island in the Baltic Sea.

[h2]Gameplay[/h2]
Resident Evil Revelations 2 is a third-person episodic survival horror game. To progress, you have to complete objectives like solving puzzles, defeating bosses, finding keys, and reaching specific points. You can carry up to four firearms, four bombs, and a knife. Materials can be found to craft different kinds of items, like firebombs, disinfectants, and more. Weapons include handguns, shotguns, SMGs, and rifles. Gameplay is primarily third-person but switches to first-person when using sniper rifles. You can also dodge enemies’ attacks and it’s much smoother than the first game.

The game features four episodes with two chapters each. The first chapter in every episode you play as Claire Redfield and Moira Burton, and the second chapter you play as Barry Burton and Natalia Korda. This game has no Genesis scanner like the first game. However, you can see flashing glimpses in certain places in the environment, meaning there is an item there. To obtain it, you need to shine on it with Moira’s flashlight or point at it with Natalia’s supernatural abilities to make it spawn, similar to the scanner from the first game.

Claire and Barry use firearms, while Moira and Natalia use melee weapons such as a crowbar, flashlight, bricks, and throwable bombs. Moira’s flashlight can stun enemies, while Natalia’s supernatural senses can see enemies through walls and locate their weak spots. You can switch between characters whenever you want, and certain situations and puzzles require you to do so. Every character has their own inventory, and you can pass items between the two characters you are playing. These features will be familiar if you have played Resident Evil Zero.

Battle Points (BP) can be used to buy Skills that improve your abilities or unlock new various extras, such as weapons, costumes, screen settings, secret files, concept art, figurines, and infinite ammo.

[b][u]Raid Mode[/u][/b]
Raid Mode returns with more missions, features, and playable characters—around 200 missions and 15 characters spanning the entire series. It includes new scenarios and enemy types from Resident Evil 5, Resident Evil 6, and the first Revelations. You can upgrade and customize skills and weapons, purchase new gear, and face special enemy variants with enhanced speed, strength, and other abilities. Raid Mode can be played solo or online.

[h2]Enemies & Bosses[/h2]
The Afflicted are the most frequent enemies you encounter during Claire and Moira's scenarios. They attack by lunging themselves at you, and cause damage either with their hands, or with various implements they come armed with.

The Rotten are the most frequent enemies you encounter during Barry and Natalia's scenarios. These are the zombies of the game. They have no weapons, so they attack using their hands and attempt to throttle and swipe you to death.

Other common enemies, like the Revenant, have a weak central core that exposes itself once you have destroyed enough of its body parts. Natalia can help locate these hidden weak spots with her senses.

There are a few boss encounters throughout the game, most of which rely on shooting exposed weak points while dodging large, telegraphed attacks.

[h2]Environment & Scares[/h2]
The game takes place on a remote island. You go through a run-down prison, lumber mill, fishing village, factory, slaughterhouse, sewers, and more. The level design is linear and somewhat interconnected with very little backtracking and a few shortcuts unlocks later that are not really needed. The game rewards exploration. Like in RE5, treasures make a return. This time they give you BP to spend. Navigation is assisted by a minimap in the top-right corner.

The atmosphere is slightly darker and more unsettling than in the first Revelations, with enemies that feel noticeably more intimidating, though it still falls short compared to true heavyweight horror titles.

[h2]Visual Design & Sound Design[/h2]
The Rotten resemble classic zombies: decayed flesh, tattered clothing, and empty, hollow eye sockets that give them a lifeless, unsettling stare. Revenant's look like severely mutated humans, often appearing with multiple body parts crudely stitched together. Some Revenant's also have crude weaponry embedded onto their limbs, such as knives and serrated blades. 

Weapons feature punchy, responsive sound design that enhances the feel of combat, giving each shot a satisfying sense of power and feedback. Enemies also benefit from distinct audio cues, helping you anticipate incoming threats and react accordingly. Sound is also used cleverly when playing as Barry and you’re up against an invisible enemy, as only Natalia can see invisible enemies she will then tell you to aim more to the left, right, up, or down and when to shoot.

[h2]Constructive Criticism[/h2]
The first chapter in Episode 4 when playing as Claire and Moira was a bit disappointing, as it was very short with very little action.

My biggest gripe with this game is how limited the gameplay mechanics are for Moira and Natalia. They can’t really do much in combat scenarios. They are mostly there for some puzzles and finding items. I usually played as Moira or Natalia to be able to find the “hidden” items, and as soon as the action started I switched to Claire or Barry. I don’t think this game would be very fun in co-op for the player playing as Moira and Natalia.

[h2]The Verdict[/h2]
Resident Evil Revelations 2 delivers a compelling follow-up with a tightly paced narrative, memorable characters, and a solid return to the franchise’s survival horror roots. It improves on its predecessor’s mechanics with smoother combat and more rewarding exploration, even if the invisible item system still feels like an unnecessary holdover.

The combat stands out as fast, responsive, and satisfying, supported by impactful weapon feedback. Finding weapon upgrades add a satisfying sense of progression, though the system is fairly basic in execution. The game has a diverse roster of enemies and bosses that are fun enough to fight. The episodic structure keeps the story moving, and switching between each duo adds variety in both gameplay and atmosphere.

Not everything lands perfectly. Moira and Natalia’s limited combat roles can make them feel less engaging to play, especially in co-op where one player may end up doing far less during action-heavy moments. A few sections, like the brief opening of Episode 4, also miss the mark in pacing and excitement.

Still, the strengths outweigh the shortcomings. With its unsettling environments, strong enemy design, and plenty of extra content in Raid Mode, Revelations 2 proves to be an enjoyable and worthy entry in the series.

Resident Evil: Revelations 2 — Reviewed by Albert Wesker

Ah… Revelations 2.
A sequel not merely in number, but in hubris. The title alone amused me — Revelations in the plural. As if Capcom thought the world could handle more than one.

But this one… this one is personal. Because it features a Wesker.

Unfortunately… not me.

Let us begin with Alex Wesker.
My “sister” in name alone — a byproduct of the Wesker Project’s genetic scattershot. Alex fancies herself my intellectual equal, perhaps even my successor. She experiments with fear as a vector for evolution, prattling on about despair and transcendence.
It’s almost adorable.

She isolates an island, kidnaps test subjects, injects them with the T-Phobos virus, and monitors their emotional states to determine who “overcomes fear.” A commendable theory — fear as a catalyst for survival — but she misunderstands the core principle.
Evolution is not guided by emotion. It eradicates it.

The moment Alex begins quoting philosophy at her prisoners, I can almost hear Spencer’s ghost laughing. She claims to seek godhood, yet trembles before her own mortality. She conducts experiments to escape death… and ends up becoming a monster of it. A tragic irony — one I almost respect. Almost.

Now, to the “heroes.”

Claire Redfield.
The other Redfield. Tireless, stubborn, unkillable — a human cockroach with perfect hair. She spends most of the story shooting mutants and rescuing children, all while moralizing about corporate evil. If I had a dollar for every self-righteous speech she’s made, I could buy back Umbrella twice over.

Moira Burton.
Ah, the daughter of Barry. Foul-mouthed, impulsive, and afraid of firearms. I will never understand humanity’s obsession with irony. Watching her swing a crowbar while shouting obscenities at the undead is… strangely entertaining. Like watching a raccoon threaten a bear.

Barry Burton himself returns, of course. Older, slower, drenched in guilt. Still quoting scripture as if God’s listening to him. But even I must admit — his paternal determination is impressive. Few men face an island of abominations armed with both a magnum and dad jokes.

And then there’s Natalia Korda.
The child — quiet, observant, unnervingly perceptive.
A vessel for Alex’s consciousness, a potential new Wesker. She fascinates me. There’s something in her stillness — the calm of an apex predator before it learns to pounce. If she ever matures into what Alex intended… she might actually be worth studying.

The T-Phobos virus itself intrigues me. A bioweapon triggered by cortisol response — fear. When the host succumbs, mutation ensues. When the host overcomes fear, control is maintained. Ingenious in theory, though ultimately fragile.
Emotion is volatile. Science demands constancy. I would have designed something far more… inevitable.

Gameplay and atmosphere:
Claustrophobic environments. Dual-character mechanics. Limited ammunition. For all its flaws, Revelations 2 remembers something the mainline series forgot — vulnerability. It forces cooperation, tension, and resource management. It flirts with survival horror, even as it occasionally succumbs to action.

However, the episodic structure undermines it. Fragmented pacing, uneven tone, inconsistent challenge. It feels less like a revelation and more like a serialized experiment that ran out of funding halfway through.

Still… I must commend the ending. Watching Alex lose her composure — her arrogance crumbling as she mutates into a shrieking, deformed nightmare — was poetic. Imitation always collapses under the weight of authenticity.

Final Assessment:
A flawed but fascinating glimpse into the Wesker legacy — diluted, distorted, and deliciously self-destructive.
Claire and company stumble through the wreckage of another failed god, while evolution continues without them.

7 out of 10.
A brave attempt at ascension, dragged down by human weakness.
Alex wanted to surpass me… and instead proved why I remain unmatched.

Reviewing (mostly) every game (or DLC) in my library, part 367:

⭐️⭐️⭐️⭐️⭐️⭐️⭐️⭐️☆☆ (8/10)

Wow. I wasn’t expecting to be this impressed, but [i]Revelations 2 [/i]really hit the mark for me. The pacing is tight and tense—you never get bored, and every encounter feels purposeful. The enemies are genuinely terrifying because they run at you. No slow zombies here; it keeps you constantly on edge. I also really enjoyed the stealth sections, which were well-executed and added variety to the combat. The levels are creepy, atmospheric, and consistently engaging, and the AI partner mechanic is surprisingly fun! It actually makes you think strategically about positioning and teamwork. The mixed reviews confuse me, because for me this is one of the stronger RE entries in recent memory. Definitely recommend if you like suspenseful, character-driven survival horror.

👁️‍🗨️[b] Pros:[/b]
[list]
[*] Terrifying enemies and great pacing. The monsters in this game are genuinely scary because they are fast, aggressive, and relentless. Unlike later RE titles that rely on slow, lumbering zombies to build tension, these monstrosities force you to constantly be aware of your surroundings, plan your movement carefully, and react quickly. Even a simple grunt enemy can attack you. The pacing of the game balances intense action sequences with quieter, suspenseful exploration, which prevents fatigue.

[*]Clever stealth mechanics. As Barry and Natalia, you'll have to sense an enemy, crouch, and sneak up behind it. While not groundbreaking, the stealth segments are well-integrated into the game’s overall flow and provide a refreshing change of pace from the combat-heavy sections. It’s a shame the series hasn’t returned to this mechanic in later installments, because it adds a unique tactical layer that balances the traditional RE combat. 

[*]Creepy, atmospheric levels. The environmental design in [i]Revelations 2[/i] is consistently impressive. From abandoned labs and dilapidated complexes to shadowy corridors and eerie outdoor spaces, the game creates a sense of dread without relying on cheap scares. Lighting, sound design, and environmental storytelling all work together to keep you on edge. Get ready for a [i] lot[/i] of tight hallways.

[*]AI partner system. The AI-controlled partner is surprisingly fun and functional. Your partner feels like a real teammate, rather than a disposable sidekick, with behaviors that encourage you to strategize and coordinate. You need to consider their positioning, support abilities, and sometimes rely on them to access areas or distract enemies, which adds tactical depth to encounters. While the AI isn’t perfect and occasionally makes mistakes, it’s rarely game-breaking, and it adds to the feeling of teamwork in a survival situation, which was new to me.

[*]Fantastic characters and writing. The cast is a real highlight, with each character feeling distinct and engaging. Barry’s old-man kindness is heartwarming; Claire’s badass attitude is consistently entertaining; Natalia’s cute curiosity adds charm without being saccharine; and Moira’s panicked-yet-competent personality keeps her from becoming annoying. Their dialogue is natural and often humorous, adding levity without undercutting the tension. This combination of strong characters and dialogue makes you actually care about what happens to them, which is rare in survival horror games.

[*]Gameplay and puzzles. Combat is fluid, responsive, and satisfying, while puzzles are thoughtfully designed to challenge without frustrating. Guns are punchy, while puzzles lead to great loot. There's quite a lot of emphasis on puzzle-solving and resource management, even in later levels. 
[/list]

🧿[b] Cons:[/b]
[list]
[*]2015 graphics. The visuals show their age, with textures and models that don’t quite meet modern standards. Textures can sometime be washed out, and some levels look similar to each other.

[*]Occasional AI dumbness. The AI partner, while fun, sometimes behaves erratically, gets stuck, or makes questionable decisions. A lot of the times the partner would just run away without shooting.

[*]Episodic format. While I played the game as a full, continuous story, I wouldn't enjoy waiting for each episode to drop. It loses the tension that way.
[/list]

It still has flaws and more of a B grade game but despite that, the positives far outweigh the negatives. Besides, not every game you play has to be a 10/10 masterpiece.

This game is peak mediocrity, riddled with design decisions that ultimately make it impossible to recommend. Forcing the player to replay certain levels and marketing it as a feature was a brilliant move by Capcom though. The visuals are unappealing, the game reeks of budget cuts, and at times it looks worse than Resident Evil 4, a freaking 10-year-old GameCube game at this point.

It also features a clumsy, Far Cry-style skill tree with some of the most baffling bonuses imaginable: increased firepower while crouching; increased firepower on the first shot after swapping weapons; and a 10% boost to all attacks for five seconds after switching characters. I wish I were making that last one up.

The Genesis System from Revelations 1 also returns, allowing players to find hidden items—though at least this time it doesn’t require switching to a clumsy first-person mode. It still sucks and should’ve been cut from both titles, but at least this crappy idea saw minor improvement.

The game was marketed as catering to the horror-centric portion of the fanbase, yet it doesn’t lean far enough in that direction. Nor does it embrace the action-oriented style of RE4 and RE5, resulting in a gross mishmash of the worst elements from both approaches that ultimately appeals to no one. The fact that this is the only game with a campaign focused on Barry is the most disappointing aspect of this game.

Straight up, this one’s an 8.5/10 for me. Easily one of the best games in the franchise. It manages to strike that rare balance of being fun to play while still atmospheric, without going off the rails like RE5 and RE6 did.

Gameplay
This is where Revelations 2 really shines. Compared to the previous entry, it’s way smoother, more action-packed, and honestly just more fun. Melee attacks are finally worth a damn here — you can actually pull off some satisfying combos instead of treating them like a panic button. The enemy variety is solid too; each type has its own quirks and weaknesses, so you’re not just spamming one weapon for the whole game.

The real kicker though is the character-switching mechanic. You’re not just swapping because one person can hold a shotgun and the other can’t -each character actually plays differently, with their own skills and tools. It adds a cool puzzle-solving layer and forces you to rethink your approach in combat. Bonus points: the second character is support-focused, so you’re spared the frustration of a braindead AI partner wasting ammo.

Story & Atmosphere
Look, writing has never exactly been Resident Evil’s strongest suit. And yeah, this one doesn’t reinvent the wheel -but it’s still tighter and better put together than most. The environments tell their own story, and the level design plus soundtrack do a lot of heavy lifting in pulling you into the setting. It has that classic RE atmosphere, and it works.

Conclusion
Revelations 2 is proof that Capcom can blend the best of both RE worlds: the tension and atmosphere of the older titles with the punchy, action-heavy gameplay of the post-RE4 era. It’s a horror/action mix that doesn’t just sound good on paper - it’s genuinely fun to play. Shame it didn’t blow up in sales when it launched, because it deserved way more love.

For me, this is easily top 3 Resident Evil material. If you’re a fan of the series, don’t sleep on it.
