Oh Revelations 2, you're hard to judge. Originally I'd barely recommend it as the full content gold edition is $5 with a good sale. The enjoyable Barry chapters and strong raid mode made up for the painful bits of RE5/6 era design that soured Claire chapters. Sure, the monster design was cool but they're cheeaapp and the game sure assumed a second player when I played solo. By the end I was swayed by the sheer energy of the finale and in hindsight see there's a lot to like, though Rev 2 is very firmly for RE superfans. If you're still quoting RE1 lines to this day then you'll be happy here. Rev 2 allows a full playthrough co-op, locally or by the magic of steam remote play. The game becomes far easier but also far funnier with a friend and the brutal extras like invisible mode really demand the help.

No other REs are necessary for the story, with light references to Rev 1 and being a fan of RE1/2 making the protagonists, Claire "Mama Bear" Redfield and Barry "Magnum Dong" Burton, more fun to see again. Rev 2 opens with amoral mercs kidnapping Claire in metaphorical broad daylight to deliver to a comically evil prison island. Barry rides to the rescue and meets a strange girl, Natalia, a mature child who uses second sight. Claire awakens in superjail and must escape with the implied help of Moira Burton, a childish adult. Bioterror ensues! Rev 2 is dumb even for RE plots with a forgettable narrative carried entirely by the campiness of the characters and a few emotional deliveries, the villain being so stupid and overdone they warp back around to enjoyable ham that sets up hype for our heroes.

Rev 2 plays like your action REs with clear DNA from 6. Monsters are fun and chunky to fight, responding with tight tuning to head shots and staggers for follow up melees, leg shots to drop them or various cyst monsters playing hide the weak spot. Explore for resources, soak in the ambiance between tense ambushes and fights in bombastic set pieces. It's been done well since RE4, no surprises here. The big change is partner use. Claire and Barry are default RE runners and gunners. Natalia can throw surprisingly weighty bricks and point out invisible death bugs and weak spot cysts. The hiccup is that Moira is a goofball with an action flashlight which can stun and set up melee finishers but it's awkward to do all the swaps solo and AI partners aren't up to doing anything half the time.

It's assumed that Moira is played and saving you a lot of ammo and enemy focus, at least for the first half of the campaign. Solo you can swap back and forth freely, making Barry sections silky smooth with simple memory. This doesn't go so well with Claire, as Moira usually gets all aggro in the room trying to blind. The only saving grace is that partners are immortal if they get time to regen between hits, making them ridiculous looking tanks. This sucks the other way around though, damage on Claire/Barry is permanent and reinforces the pain of solo play. You really benefit from playing with a friend, giggling with glee as they run point, soak hits with that immortality and setup ruthless zombie curb stomps. It's a lot less frustrating when all the cheap shots can be repaid with cheese of your own. It's also hilarious to witness the power of Natalia's tossed bricks which may as well be magnum rounds. Rev 2 is a silly game but done right it's a highly entertaining one.

Otherwise quality is all over the place. Chapter 1 is mostly competent aside from silent sucker punch spawns. Claire's sections done solo have ammo stretched thin(until you memorize levels and freebies), damage constant and help nonexistent with chapter 2 being grating. By contrast Barry glides through his series of set pieces, finishing with more ammo than he started, enjoying back and forth with Natalia for support and being a breakout personality. I love this big brave dork's endless supply of dad jokes and superior firepower. Claire's experience improves with a better chapter 3 but the devs honestly get bored of making levels for her with a super short chapter 4. Barry emerges as the true star for the final stretch, though some time padding puzzles make things drag. On replay Claire is more enjoyable but that first blind run had me seething.

We wrap up with the ideal raid/mercenaries mode, a shooting gallery against scaling sets of monsters with quirky modifiers challenging you to just one more run to get all the medals. Rev 2 is a fond farewell to the bloated action of mid 2010s REs, a prelude to the current golden age. It's sour with forced co-op partners, some uninspired fights and sections(waiter, more dull brown levels from RE5, please!), the RE movie-tier bad writing... but there's the sweet with standout environment and monster design, when fights are good, the unintentional comedy and unironically good fanservice. Rev 2 is the game for die-hard fans or co-op pairs returning after their RE5 tour of duty. Get the gold version on sale if you've got any doubts, try one chapter if truly skittish and hit up a friend to really juice your enjoyment.

Resident Evil: Revelations 2 doesn’t aim to reinvent the franchise—it aims to refocus it. After the bloated chaos of Resident Evil 6, this follow-up to the first Revelations installment dials things back to what survival horror does best: tight corridors, limited resources, creeping dread, and a lingering sense of unease. It’s not perfect, but it’s a confident and compelling chapter that captures the spirit of classic RE with a modern twist.

The game is structured episodically (four main episodes, plus two bonus chapters), with the narrative split between two pairs: Claire Redfield and Moira Burton, and Barry Burton and Natalia, a mysterious young girl. Claire and Moira’s timeline shows their immediate struggle to survive on a grim island facility, while Barry arrives six months later to unravel what happened.

The storytelling is effective, even if it leans a bit into B-movie territory. Themes of trauma, trust, and transformation run throughout, and the dual timeline structure keeps the suspense alive. Moira and Natalia, new additions to the cast, offer fresh dynamics—and Barry’s return is a treat for long-time fans.

At its core, Revelations 2 blends traditional RE tension with modernized, over-the-shoulder gunplay. Inventory management, crafting, and puzzle-solving make a welcome return, and resource scarcity means every bullet counts—especially in higher difficulties.

What sets this game apart is its partner system. Whether you’re playing solo (with AI) or in split-screen co-op, each character has unique abilities:

-Moira uses a flashlight to find hidden items and a crowbar to open doors or finish off enemies.

-Natalia can sense monsters through walls and point out weak spots.

This asymmetry adds tactical depth and makes co-op more than just “two people with guns.” While AI companions aren’t flawless, they rarely ruin the experience.

Combat feels weighty and responsive, with a mix of stealth, panic, and strategic planning—particularly during boss fights and tense ambushes.

Visually, Revelations 2 trades glossy production for grungy, grounded environments. Think rusty prisons, shadowy labs, and rotting woods. The lighting is intentionally sparse, adding to the tension without relying too heavily on jump scares. The monster designs are grotesque, even if they don’t reach the iconic status of past enemies like Lickers or Hunters.

The sound design does a lot of heavy lifting—creaks in the distance, growling in the dark, and unsettling whispers help build unease. The music stays minimal, letting silence and ambient sounds create suspense.

Beyond the main story, Revelations 2 includes Raid Mode, a fast-paced, arcade-style shooter with unlockable characters, levels, and loot. It’s surprisingly addictive and offers tons of replayability. Whether solo or online, it feels like a fun reward for players who want to keep engaging after the main campaign ends.

Multiple endings based on player choices also incentivize replaying certain chapters, and bonus episodes add extra lore and character insight.

Resident Evil: Revelations 2 doesn’t try to be a blockbuster—it tries to be smart. And it mostly succeeds. Its tighter focus, clever co-op mechanics, and return to horror fundamentals make it one of the stronger entries in the modern RE lineup. It’s not as flashy as Resident Evil 7 or as iconic as RE4, but it’s a solid, moody ride that reminds you what made this series a legend in the first place.

A gritty, suspenseful survival horror with great pacing, memorable characters, and smart co-op mechanics. It may not be the scariest or most polished entry, but it earns its place in the RE canon.

[h2]Experience:[/h2]

I don’t know how long people usually need to finish this game, but for me, it took 10 months. I guess I played a little too much [i]Resident Evil[/i] and got burned out for a while.

That said, [i]Revelations 2[/i] really stood out to me in terms of gore. The dismemberment is impressively realistic — shoot a zombie’s leg, and it comes clean off. I was honestly shocked (in a funny way) at how detailed and visceral the visuals are.

I also liked how Moira’s flashlight tracks your line of sight when playing as Claire — it’s a small touch, but it adds a lot to the atmosphere and gameplay.

The game has two possible endings: a good one and a bad one. I asked ChatGPT for a hint on how to get the good ending without major spoilers and got just enough to nudge me in the right direction. I didn’t realize how much of a twist it would be — I was genuinely surprised when Moira reappeared at the end. I fully expected her to die in the tower collapse.

Also, personal note: the final boss is probably the most disgusting one in the series (in a good way) — it was gross, intense, and very well done.

First playthrough review time.

Resident Evil Revelations 2 is a survival horror game that takes place between Resident Evil 5 and Resident Evil 6. Like the first Revelations, which occurs between Resident Evil 4 and Resident Evil 5, this game places more attention on the story than some of the other titles. It is divided into episodes, and each one ends with a short recap similar to how it is done in The Walking Dead game. The dark and dangerous setting is nice, and the game creates a strong sense of suspense in some parts.

A new part of this game is the ability to switch between two characters during gameplay. Each one has different skills and their equipment, so changing between them is important to continue through the levels. There are also systems to upgrade weapons, improve character skills, and make useful tools. These features give more variety and require some planning and teamwork. The game also has two extra DLC episodes, The Struggle and Little Miss. While they provide some extra background about the characters, they don’t add much to the main story. The gameplay is mostly about survival.

In conclusion, this game brings a distinct style to the series while maintaining its survival horror roots. It is more suitable for those who have played earlier games, since many parts of the story are connected. This can help with understanding the story connections and the background, as a few parts in this game are linked to earlier events in the series.

Big improvement over the original Revelations and a fun departure from the main RE main story. If you played and enjoyed the original RE Revelations then you are in for a treat. If you didn't like the original Revelations, then maybe you might still enjoy this one too. You don't really need to play the original to enjoy this game though there are a few plot references that might require you to look up a wiki. Either way, the game is fun and stands on its own.

With the Revelations games Capcom tried to go in a different direction. The game is set in 4 episodic chapters that is paced longer than the original. They each stand on their own well and gives you a recap intro and always ends in a cliffhanger. Not only do you switch between characters, but also timelines where you approach the story from the beginning and the end simultaneously to meet somewhere in the middle to understand the full story. 

You play either as the Claire/Moira Team A or the Barry/Natalia Team B. It's unique that in each team, one character is the gun tank and the other is the support/item storage locker. The secondary characters have unique abilities that keep them useful like being able to open locks, find hidden items, spot enemies, and access special areas. The ability of Natalia being able to spot invisible enemies that only she can see is a unique and very well through-out gameplay mechanic. It forces you to switch quickly between Natalia and Barry to spot the enemy and actually kill a moving thing and creates some fun panicky moments.

The story itself is good but predictable if you've played other RE games. There's always some new virus or bio agent. There's some lab that devised it and of course some accident happens and unexpected complications and mutations are the result and you're the one that's got to deal with it. And of course, there's a mansion in there and a rocket launcher!

While Revelations 1 was more of lite game, this one is a bit more complicated and involved. The graphics are much better in the PS3 Xbox360 era with better facial assets and textures but everything still looks rather flat in some areas. The gameplay and story distracts you from the graphics woes though. I played this on a Steam Deck and it was a full 90fps on max settings. It's great for a pick-up and put-down Steam Deck experience.

Resident Evil Revelations 2 - Forgotten Treasure or Missed Potential? (Steam Review)

Resident Evil Revelations 2 is an episodic game that was released in 2015 and offered players two intertwined stories with different gameplay focuses. Despite a mixed start, the game gradually won the love of fans thanks to its atmosphere, characters, and cooperative mode. But did Revelations 2 manage to maintain the quality standard of Resident Evil? Let's find out.

What I Liked:

•   Two Intertwined Stories: The game offers two different scenarios that gradually intertwine, creating a captivating overall picture. Playing as Claire Redfield and Moira Burton is more action-oriented, while the story of Barry Burton and Natalia Korda is more tense and stealth-based.
•   Interesting Characters: The return of Claire and Barry pleases fans, and new characters like Moira and Natalia add freshness. Each character has their own unique abilities, which affects the gameplay.
•   Cooperative Mode: Playing the game cooperatively with a friend is a great way to experience the horrors of Revelations 2. The different abilities of the characters require teamwork and tactical planning.
•   Atmosphere: Even though the game isn't as scary as RE7 or the remakes, Revelations 2 still creates a tense atmosphere of an abandoned island full of monsters.
•   Raid Mode: This arcade mode offers many hours of gameplay, character progression, and weapon unlocks.

What You Might Not Like:

•   Episodic Structure: The release of episodes with breaks can annoy those who prefer to play games in their entirety.
•   Graphics: The game looks outdated by modern standards, especially the textures and character models.
•   Story: Despite an interesting concept, the story suffers from clichés and predictability.
•   AI: The artificial intelligence of companions sometimes behaves illogically, which can be annoying.

Conclusion:

Resident Evil Revelations 2 is a decent game that offers a good survival horror experience with interesting characters, two intertwined stories, and a cooperative mode. Despite some shortcomings, such as outdated graphics and a clichéd story, the game can still captivate fans of the series and lovers of the genre.

Is it worth buying? If you're looking for a cooperative Resident Evil experience with the atmosphere of an abandoned island and are willing to overlook outdated graphics, then you'll enjoy Revelations 2.

Highly recommended!

+- While music is mostly fine, I occasionally found it adding little to the overall atmosphere (except for some scenes)
+- Puzzles aren't overdone, but a few more (or a bit harder ones) wouldn't hurt
+- The game starts interesting, but I found myself losing some interest after the first chapter. Chapters 2-3 feel somewhat bland and could've advanced the plot more. Only in the final chapter things started to get interesting again.
+- Controls are generally fine, but sometimes feel a bit "clunky" (especially camera movement while sprinting)
+- While the plot has several similarities to earlier games, at least the protagonists' role in the plot gives the old plot structure a new perspective
+- There's some variety in enemies, but a few different types more wouldn't hurt
+- In a way it's nice to see Barry's perspective of things as he goes through some places where Claire and Moira have already been, but the environments could've also used more rework for Barry's story, because many times it just felt like I was running through the same old areas as Barry, and there was nothing new to add to the experience - the same levels are reused too much. On the flipside, there's also some new areas in Barry's story, so it definitely doesn't constantly feel like replaying everything.

Cons:
- Some side characters could've used more exposition/screen time. Their roles in the story felt downplayed
- While interact/pick up/action can be set to a single keybind, this makes climbing on top of movable boxes impossible, because trying to do so will only trigger the "pick up" action. Not even secondary keybinds helped with this, so I ended up having to use two different keybinds for separate pick up/interact/action purposes, which was a bit annoying. Alternatively, switching keybinds whenever there's a need to move boxes wouldn't be neat either.
- There's a plot hole considering the armbands. It's also not explained how the surviving characters were cured
- Terra Save's role in the plot could've used more work, and the reason why Claire and Moira (and other members) got tangled in the plot feels a bit far-fetched (whereas Barry has a good and obvious reason to be part of the plot)
- The antagonist feels rather surface-level, in a way "your typical RE villain". She could've used a bit more work

The DLCs are decent - The Struggle offers a survival challenge, and Little Miss is an okay'ish short collection of (simple) puzzles. DLCs also shed light on events that no-doubt deserved explaining.

A rather mediocre entry into the franchise.

It came after the near-complete disaster that was Resident Evil 6 (which somehow recovered in sales with a bang), and at a time when the franchise was suffering from an identity crisis.

At the time, the tone of conversations surrounding the franchise was that it was basically over and that Capcom didn't know what to do with it anymore.

Revelations 1 was a very timid and clumsy attempt at a "return to origins", trying to rescue some of the horror that had been completely turned to dust by the explosions and oneliners of the main franchise.

It was a moderate success despite the game's inconsistency in what it wanted to be, but was enough to give rise to this even stranger experiment: 

An episodic Resident Evil, in the style of the late Tell Tale and a return to the duo concept featured in Resident Evil 0.

You always control a pair of characters with distinct abilities that complement each other in solving the problems and simple puzzles that you encounter along the way, and you follow a narrative that uses the function as an excuse to offer multiple perspectives.

Doubling down on horror and action mechanics, the game is relatively solid, despite failing to conjure an engaging atmosphere even with all the horrific details of the setting in which the game takes place.

Level design and exploration are incredibly limited, but a handful of memorable moments in the form of setpieces and encounters with relatively interesting enemies are able to shake up the sluggish and incredibly brainless pace of this experience enough to make it enjoyable.

The game could pass for an alternative Evil Within, with its distorted enemies and grotesque setting, but it barely manages to make me register the experience in an immersive way. But at least it doesn't fail too much as an action game. The core mechanics of Resident Evil 4, although a bit watered down, still shine through the cracks and combined with a bit of resource management, you can actually have a good time.

It's not a very long game either. 2 hours or so per episode, plus a few extras.

In addition to the rankings, you also have a medal system and a progression curve with skills, and NG+ modes to encourage repeat runs.

But don't expect to be surprised by anything. 

Especially today, with the game becoming irrelevant after Capcom reinvented the franchise and then literally returned to its origins and started cannibalizing old games because no one wants to make anything new anymore.

I don't doubt that you'll feel like there's a lot of redundant stuff or things implemented in ways that aren't elegant. And just like its predecessor, this one also lacks focus, standing out in a canned, limited and inefficient way, despite the expanded mechanics.

It's not a particularly well-made or polished and it doesn't have enough personality to be another gem in the franchise that you'll want to play over and over again. But it's good enough that if you're in need and have already played everything else to exhaustion, the idea won't seem so bad.

Not amazing. Just okay.

P.S: Play Raid Mode. It's a arcade mode with a HUGE progression, with hundreds of missions, multiple characters, skill builds and so on. 

I've seen a lot of people commenting that this game is worth it just for this mode, so I recommend it if you don't like the campaign (or if you like it and want more).

P.S.2: One really bad thing about the game is that it doesn't let you start a new game, from scratch, without anything unlocked. 

To do this, you need to manually delete your save from your PC and disable Steam's cloud save functions for the game. 

If you, like me, bought the first episode first just to dip your toe in the water and see what the game was like, and then bought the rest and thought about starting the game again from the beginning, you are forced to play as if you were in a new game+, with your skills, healing items, weapons and the like unlocked. And although some things can be mitigated, leaving your weapons in the bench, certain items simply won't appear in the game twice and you can put yourself in unpleasant (and very unbalanced) situations if you try to self-handicap (Things that wouldn't happen if you could simply play the game normally with the planned difficulty curve). 

And worst of all, if you delete your save, you lose your progress in other areas, including Raid mode. 

Simply brilliant.

RE Revelations 2, while a huge step up in quality when it comes to gameplay, is sadly a step down in Story when comparing it to Revelations 1.

I did not get invested in the story whatsoever. I find it boring, and trudging through the mostly grey areas in this game and completing "Puzzles" that serve as little more than filler that keep you from the actual meat of the game: The gunplay and enemies.

The gameplay, just like Revelations 1, is phenomenal and has seen a huge upgrade compared to its predecessor. Guns feel weighty, Movement and Dodging have improved, and there is enough enemy variety this time around that it can actually get a bit tricky to juggle them all in combat sometimes, the gameplay by far is the best thing in this game, and it kept me going throughout the weird and contrived story that ends up just shoehorning in a villain with little to no motivation that is understandable. Also making said villain related to another one from the previous games made it feel even worse and I just felt dumb...

But yeah, this is my second playthrough as I have played it before on the Switch and let me just say something: You buy this game for Raid Mode.

Yes. Raid Mode is BACK BAYBEE. And it is so much better than Revelations 1 in every way and it will allow for you to make bonkers builds, kit out weapons in the craziest ways to laser down enemies that even dare come near your peripheral vision, and allow you to dodge and weave in ways that you could only dream of in Rev1. The Campaign is just a small primer that lets you unlock stuff for the -REAL- meat of the game!

Episodic games were once a trend, allowing smaller studios to finance projects that would otherwise be impossible. Typically, these games focus on storytelling rather than gameplay. However, Capcom has taken a different approach with Resident Evil Revelations 2, balancing story and gameplay in an engaging way.

Originally exclusive to the Nintendo 3DS in 2012, Resident Evil Revelations aimed to blend classic and modern elements of the franchise. Revelations 2 continues this trend, offering a mix of action, exploration, and horror. The game is structured into four main episodes, each split into two parts, along with two additional episodes introducing new mechanics.

The narrative follows two duos: Claire Redfield and Moira Burton, who are kidnapped and imprisoned, and Barry Burton, who searches for his daughter with the help of Natalia Korda, a mysterious girl with special abilities. The story, set between Resident Evil 5 and Resident Evil 6, is well-paced, offering surprises and classic horror moments.

Gameplay encourages cooperation, either through AI or local co-op, with one character focused on combat and the other on support. While not overly action-packed, the game requires strategic shooting and resource management. Some environments enhance the horror experience, with tense encounters and invisible enemies adding suspense.

Beyond the main campaign, the Raid Mode provides an action-focused experience with RPG-like progression, multiple characters, and online co-op. Though it includes microtransactions, they are not essential. The game also offers collectibles, unlockables, and multiple endings, increasing replayability.

Visually, the game is reminiscent of old console games from the PS4 and Xbox One era. But it there are advantages to this - it running very well on Steam Deck and weak PC. Lighting and effects help mask its graphical limitations. Voice acting is decent - the eerie soundtrack and unsettling sound effects further amplify the tension, with sudden noises and distant screams keeping players on edge.

Overall, Revelations 2 is a strong blend of classic and modern approaches. With an 8-hour campaign, co-op, Raid Mode, plenty of unlockables, and multiple playthrough options, it stands as a worthy addition to the series. This game reaffirms that Capcom was once heading in the right direction.

Resident Evil Revelations 2 is a much stronger entry than its predecessor, addressing many of the issues that plagued the first game. The gameplay, while still clunky in movement and animations, feels more refined and enjoyable. The enemy variety is a major highlight, with a clever evolution in design between Claire and Moira’s campaign versus Barry and Natalia’s, showing the passage of time through decayed, skeletal foes. Combat also introduces interesting mechanics, like Natalia revealing enemy weak spots and detecting invisible threats, adding a layer of strategy.

The tedious scanning system from the first game is gone, replaced by Moira’s flashlight and Natalia’s sensing abilities, making item discovery feel more natural and optional rather than a forced chore. However, puzzles remain underwhelming, with only a few standout moments, like the eerie graveyard puzzle as an example. Unfortunately, the user interface is still a mess, feeling just as clunky and outdated as before. While not perfect, Revelations 2 is a far better experience than the first, with enough improvements to make it worth playing for Resident Evil fans.

[h1]Review[/h1] 
If you try to take a look at the reviews most people don’t tell why they dislike it. The only thing that is hated is that its split in episodes. Yeah, playing the package and seeing a “last time on lost” esque recap is just idiotic. But being able to buy now the whole package: what does the game offer now?

[u]Gameplay[/u]
First the biggest difference to revelations 1 is that the npc who follows you is now someone you can actively change to at any time. There is also the possibility to play the game in split screen which is somewhat the optimal way. Its one of the most unique coop games as its a story that is meant to be played for two people. You constantly split up and have to do tasks that help the other person to advance.

In combat only one person uses weapons while the other has two options. If you play as moira you have solely a flashlight and a melee weapon. Both being useful support weapons for setting up follow attacks. If you play as the kid in barry episodes you are basically useless. You can only throw bricks which are break easily, dont do any damage and are hard to set up. Your task is solely to point at invisible enemies if they appear. 

This creates a somewhat of a asymmetric coop shooter that is more horror focused than resident evil 5 while also being relatively fun in combat, if you aren’t playing the kid in barry´s episode. Instead of upgrading weapons through a shop, you can find upgrades in secret chests that the support character can open. There is also a skill system adding some abilities which is okay.

There is also high replay value with various different modes or the mercenaries mode that is a bit more easier than the first revelations and less grindy.

[u]Story[/u]
You are trapped on an island, starting in a prison and going further to explore what this island is about. If you play barry´s episode, its set in a different time uncovering more. Those two storylines collide and end up in a satisfying finale that is a bit more memorable than the first revelations, although having not much in common story wise aside a few mentions.

[u]Sound[/u]
Maybe one of the weaker resident evil soundtracks while still being decent. Voice acting is available in more than just English, also neat.

[u]Graphics[/u]
Originally programmed for being a download title, its available even on the PS vita. But this is not that noticeable on the pc port. It has a decent grunge look to it and feels more like a silent hill game. Neat.

[u]Conclusion/TL;DR[/u]
I think its a decent resident evil spin-off. The unique coop aspects is what made the game really fun for me. It stands out from the rest due to this, although having its downsides. Combat is decent but absolutely boring for people who have to play the child. There should have been more aspects to the support character gameplay. Although its still fun playing this coop horror shooter.
I just don't think this is a very good RE game. There are so many others that I would recommend over Revelations 2.

This was the first Resident Evil title I ever played. 

While I had heard of the series and seen clips of game play of popular RE titles growing up, I had never actually tried playing any until this one first released in it's entirety on the then new Xbox One in 2015. Having replayed it years later on PC and having played through other RE titles since I feel I can actually now give it a proper recommendation.

To briefly summarize the premise: Claire Redfield and Moira Burton (Barry Burton's now adult daughter) are captured by an unknown group and stranded on a dangerous seemingly abandoned island. Barry's story follows some time later where he arrives to the island to rescue his daughter with the help of a mysterious young girl named Natalia he finds immediately arriving there. The story is told episodically, meaning each level typically ends on a cliff hanger or truth bomb before moving on to the next episode (ie. level) and switches between Claire's parties perspective at the end of their episode's story to Barry's parties perspective. 

Regarding Claire and Moira's story sections, Claire uses firearms and a knife and can melee kick certain enemies to the ground while Moira uses a flashlight to stun enemies and a melee weapon she can swing and can perform finishes on enemies that Claire kicks down. For Barry and Natalia, Barry is well armed and performs nearly all the combat since Natalia is a little girl, however only she can see certain enemies and enemy weak points that Barry can't and she can point them out. She can also throw objects to stun or distract enemies and can reach places where Barry can't as Natalia is smaller. 

The game play is third person with over the shoulder aiming (yes, you can move while aiming) with only Claire and Barry being the only ones to use firearms. Companion ai and health bars work similarly to how they did in RE 4 (2005) and 5 except now they are playable and can be switched instantly between each other with a button in game or can be played by another player in coop. 

Unfortunately, the companion ai much like previous titles is rather poor. Simple commands like "wait" and "follow" can be given to them, they do automatically fight or crouch depending on what the player controlled character does and inventories can be swapped and shared. When playing with Claire and Moira I almost always found myself controlling Moira as she was far more vulnerable when enemies closed in, usually I would stun enemies with the flashlight, quickly switch to Claire to have her give a round house kick to knock down the stunned enemy and then quickly switch back to Moira to perform a finisher. While this was probably the game play loop the developers had in mind when making the game, it can take away from the fun as I like playing Claire more but feel out of necessity not to do so.

Playing Between Barry and Natalia is better as expectations for Natalia in combat are different as you know she can't really fight. When playing as them I found that quickly swapping to Natalia to get a look at an enemies vulnerable spot and then back to Barry to shoot it was generally most effective. Some enemies that can one hit you are invisible and it becomes critical to see where they are. While not very reliable, even as an ai, Natalia can warn Barry verbally about them and can even point to where they are. Switching to Natalia to throw objects and distract enemies and just let ai Barry take them out is not a bad strategy either.

The bigger story as a whole is probably the games weakest aspect to me with only hardcore RE fans probably appreciating it the most. The contained parts of the story are a little better, with the idea of Barry coming to rescue his daughter being my favorite element. Series mains such as Claire and Barry are good to see as an RE fan and were even my favorite characters when I first played the game not realizing they had been much bigger parts of previous mainline games. I don't mind Moira, but her character's backstory to not touching firearms a bit cliche and feels more like it was used to justify the companion style flashlight/melee game play more than anything. Natalia feels the most out of place even though her presence in the story (and the RE canon timeline if your into that) is justified. It's pretty obvious she is something of a proxy daughter going with Barry as he goes to find his now lost adult daughter. It works though.

Graphically, the character models look fantastic, with the environments just being okay.  Dull is a word that comes to mind. What it does well is give an appearance of dreariness and isolation so thematically they get the job done but with more love it could be a lot better. To me the flaws are more noticeable during Claire/Moira levels but that's probably more due to the fact that it's not as dark as Barry/Natalia's.

This title was created after the explosive action packed Michael Bay-esk RE:6, something I played later, and showed that this game was a good step back toward the survival horror the series had been slipping away from at the time. It's atmosphere and setting allows you to feel isolated right away, ammo and healing supplies are scarce and enemies feel dangerous and spooky. Over all, it feels like a horror game with action which is what I've come to believe what Resident Evil should be.

If you are a long time fan of the series then you probably already own this. If you're casual fan of the series and don't feel this is appealing, you're probably safe to steer clear as it doesn't add a whole lot to the series. If you're looking to dip you're toe into the RE universe or just the survival horror genre and don't want to try the excellent remakes that have been coming out then this might be next best thing as it doesn't really ruin or spoil the stories of any of the titles that came before it and while it might have some game play frustrations *cough* (companion ai) *cough cough*, it's still pretty mechanically solid and I think chilling enough to test your nerve which is not too shabby for a ten year old game. 

If you do pick it up I recommend you get all the episodes not just the one. If price is an issue it does go on sale often and you can pick up the entire game for around $5.

While Revelations 2 takes a bit from every Resident Evil formula, it fails to feel like a unique entry and instead an action game with some memories from the horror setting that made the franchise one of a kind. Still, there's fun to be had in this episodic entry. 

With 4 episodes to play with different characters and game mechanics the game keeps it fresh between having a full killing spree and puzzles with exploration for you to figure it out. Each episode will take around 2 hours with one of them being a little longer than the others. After these, two extra episodes will also be ready for you if you want more Revelations 2. The balance of one of your characters being the stronger and the other the support role works well. Guns are satisfying enough, enemies are not huge bullet sponges if you know where to hit them and where to aim (you know those yellow and oranges blobs or the classic one shot with melee combo). Enemy variety is somewhat limited but it helps that the game has decent pacing, meaning that sometimes you'll be more focusing on killing and other times it will be more about exploring, finding keys or security key cards. 

While I feel some enemies design can become like a cheap gaming design choice, in this case it works well. I'm talking about certain enemies that will make teamwork a solid experience. If you can't see an enemy but your partner can, it can provide an interesting and tense moment. Raid Mode is also back and it is what you can expect from a mode that is not new in these entries, however, I have spent little to no time in those modes. At around the 10 hour mark you will have everything the game has to offer campaign wise, unless you fancy more modes with an increase in difficulty. For those who enjoy unlocking achievements those were a little light on the campaign, meaning there's a majority of them to unlock via higher difficulty or by killing a bigger number of enemies. When possible I avoided combat, something I always tried to do in the original Resident Evil games. It feels better to play this way but it's no surprise that such thing changed in the latest and modern resident evil games. On a final note, I found much more fun and enjoyment in the first RE Revelations, the setting and levels are much more creative and the story is more enjoyable, still, RE Revelations 2 was a solid experience with no performance issues despite limited graphical settings.

Revelations 2 is one of the worse RE games before the Winters saga. It has terrible writing, not in the way nerds say, "Buh-well Resident Evil never had good stories!" but to the point that it becomes irksome. Moira Burton is not a character, she is a millennial anger archetype and a conduit for Barry to have his development channelled through. 

Claire Redfield has lost everything in this game, most notably a personality. She talks like she's been lobotomized. Remember when she spent the entirety of RE2 taking care of Sherry? ... Yeah, suddenly this game establishes that Claire isn't good with kids, in order to give Moira exactly one trait.

The odd thing is that even in this game's awful storyline, there are moments of brilliance such as the plot of the Struggle DLC and the true ending. Speaking of true endings, this game has possibly the worst and most arbitrary case of being locked into a bad ending for reasons you could not have foreseen.

As for gameplay. This game has it. The episodic nature did its structure no favours, but there is a lot of clever recycling of locations. I'm pretty sure a few models, animations and sound effects were recycled from RE4 on the PS2 as well; that's fine by me though. The stealth mechanic is completely scuffed and broken, which makes focusing the Little Miss DLC on it a stupid decision. Otherwise however, the third person combat is still pretty fun even in this low-rent state.

The game is buggy and has low production values. It came out in 2015, yet the graphics resemble those of a PS2 game. Even the first Revelations game looked better... on the 3DS. It would make some small sliver of sense if this game was designed with the PS Vita in mind (even though we know the Vita is capable of better) but it clearly wasn't. I've played through the PS Vita port in its entirety, including the DLC, because I am a masochist. It verges on unplayable, with frequent stutters and graphical downgrades that make it look like a pre-alpha version.

The PC version looks so low-end yet demands high system requirements for the visual fidelity on offer. Even on my gaming laptop, it never felt like it was running 100% perfectly, because it's simply built in a very spotty way. 

So why am I giving this game a Recommended despite all those criticisms? Because it's still fun enough to play through. It's like frozen pizza: you know there's far better out there, but this will do in a pinch. Be sure to buy it on a massive discount. And I cannot stress this enough: be sure to buy Claire's Rodeo Outfit and Moira's Urban Ninja DLCs along with it. They are sexy as hell and make the game a whole lot more fun to play through.

Resident Evil Revelations 2 attempts to build on the foundation of its predecessor, but instead of a tense and engaging survival horror experience, it delivers a frustrating mix of uninspired design, underwhelming storytelling, and awkward gameplay mechanics. 
While it has a few redeeming moments, the game ultimately feels like a misstep for the franchise.
One of the biggest issues is the episodic format...
While this structure might have worked as a marketing experiment, it undermines the pacing of the game. 
The cliffhanger endings and constant interruptions make it hard to stay immersed in the story. 
Speaking of which, the narrative is a convoluted mess that fails to engage. 
The idea of two parallel campaigns with Barry Burton and Claire Redfield might seem intriguing, but the execution leaves much to be desired. 
The dialogue is often cheesy, the stakes feel artificial, and the villains are forgettable at best!
Gameplay is another weak point. 
The dual-character system, forcing players to switch between a combat-focused character and a support character, sounds innovative but quickly becomes tedious. 
The support characters often feel like a burden, their abilities either too situational or simply unfun to use. 
While Barry and Claire bring some nostalgic appeal, their counterparts, Natalia and Moira, feel shoehorned into the gameplay, disrupting the flow of tense combat and exploration.
The environments are uninspired, lacking the atmospheric depth that the franchise is known for. 
Most areas feel generic and repetitive, with little to distinguish one location from the next. 
Gone are the eerie, memorable settings of the Spencer Mansion or the Queen Zenobia. 
Instead, players are treated to drab, linear levels that fail to evoke the tension and fear expected from a Resident Evil game!
The enemy design is another letdown... 
While the series has always been known for its grotesque and imaginative creatures, the enemies here feel derivative and uninspired. 
Fighting the same few enemy types repeatedly grows stale, and the lack of variety saps the game of its potential to surprise or terrify.
Technically, Revelations 2 feels like a budget title, with dated visuals and inconsistent voice acting. 
The controls, while serviceable, are not as polished as they should be, and the gunplay lacks the satisfying impact that other entries in the series have managed to deliver.
While there are moments where the game shows glimpses of potential, it never capitalizes on these strengths.
Instead, Resident Evil Revelations 2 feels like a game caught between trying to please fans of classic survival horror and chasing the more action-oriented approach of recent entries, ultimately satisfying neither.
In the end, Resident Evil Revelations 2 is a disappointing and forgettable entry that fails to capture the magic of the series... 
It’s a game that might appeal to die-hard fans for its characters and callbacks, but for most players, it’s a frustrating and uninspired experience better left in the shadows!

A marked improvement over the first game, both visually and mechanically, but not without it's flaws. 

RE: Revelations 2, while being a bit of a spin-off title, could stand it's ground against pretty much all other RE titles. My reasoning? 

1) They have almost perfected survival horror with this one. You will always have just enough to get by with, but you'll never feel overpowered (unless you save all of your magnum ammo). 

2) You never feel helpless in any given situation, but you may dread them. 

3) The audio design is enough to sent shivers down your spine because you just know something has seen you, but you haven't seen IT yet. 

4) Support characters will be separated from you at times (though you can control both through character switching) forcing you to not only focus on the objective, but also forcing you to keep them alive while they do it. 

5) The visual design, while drab at times, also gives way to some really awesome environments. 

The flaws? 

1) The DLC isn't great. I didn't really need a DLC where I'm basically playing an arena shooter through the eyes of a supporting character who never used a gun in the main game with a weird hunting mechanic to earn extra "lives." I haven't gotten to touch the second DLC yet, but hopefully it's better than the first one. 

2) Beyond Chapter 2, I kept getting these weird freezes, where the game would be stuck in a perpetual loading state. In the game, this would also manifest as Barry standing at doorways that you have to pass through to get to the next area. However, this only happened during Barry's chapters. I don't know what caused it, and doing a fresh install + verifying files didn't fix the problem. 

3) While there are only 4 chapters (6, if you count the two DLCs), some of them feel like they absolutely drag on for no reason. It's not entirely a bad thing, but it's also one of those things that just made me scratch my head. Each chapter has two sections, one where you play as Jill and Moira, then a second part where you play as Barry and Natalia, but there were definitely some pacing issues in my opinion. 

5) While the enemy designs are awesome, some of them are just absolute bullet sponges. Yes, weak points help, but some enemies don't have weak points, and you may be low on ammo and NEED to kill them to progress. This does play a positive note, by never letting you feel overpowered (unless you save all of your magnum ammo) but it also is one of those things where I don't want to be trapped in an arena and be forced to backtrack to TRY to find ammo. Especially since this isn't like modern RE games where your map shows you if you've found everything or not. 

6) I'm not a fan of the fact that you can pick up a map, but that map can't be viewed (unless I've missed something). In the first Revelations game, you could pull up your PDA and look at the map whenever you wanted. It gave you all of the information on the doors you could and couldn't open on the whole ship and the locations of all of the weapon boxes. It would make exploring just a little bit more manageable, because there are some open areas where you can poke around to find things. However, with Revelations 2, it seems fairly linear compared to Revelations. But, if I can't view the map, might as well have not included it, in my opinion. Especially since the mini-map gives so little information.

[b]TL; DR[/b] I do not like this quite as much as its predecessor, but it is still a great game, and fun for a couple of playthroughs. This is due in part to the partner system, the way that each character complements their friend, and have unique mechanics, but also the quite stellar enemy design, and worthwhile story. 
I crave spinoff titles for my favourite IPs.

[b]Note[/b] that this takes place in-between the fifth and sixth games.

[h1] Story [/h1]
Moira did not follow in Barry Burton’s footsteps, instead of joining the BSAA like everyone else she joined Terra Save to work alongside Claire Redfield. They are a real up-and-coming organisation, and soon they might even compete in the big leagues, so things are going well, and they are all happily celebrating their successes. Surely, nothing, will go wrong, surely, they will not get attacked and kidnapped.
Terra Save! Because “Terr” doesn’t have to end with “rist.”

[i]Revelations 2[/i] is a short title told in an episodic format, but while its predecessor felt more like a TV-series this is more like a mini-series with fewer instalments but with a similar total length.
This works well to tell a more self-contained story and is a great opportunity to catchup with Barry and Claire as well as exploring certain ideas introduced in previous games, so, yeah, this is proper territory for a spinoff title.
If you wish you can even play the Extra Episodes, they do a good job of bridging narrative gaps, as well as explaining some mysteries left behind after the completing the campaign. [i]The Struggle[/i] is the most entertaining of the two, but I cannot talk about them since that would spoil the entire game.

However, there is one issue I have with [i]Revelations 2[/i], the supporting cast is just sort of bad? In [i]Revelations 1[/i] we met some ridiculous characters but at least they were entertaining, and had some depth, here, they are just not that good, nor is there more than one or two notes to them, yet that is not much of a problem…
Since the game focuses on Claire, Moira, Barry, and Natalia, their interactions are great and are the vast majority of the dialogue. Barry and Natalia, is peak dad-game writing, as was the style at the time, while Moira feels like one of the most normal people in the entire series. Yeah, she is still ridiculous, but at least she knows how ridiculous this is. Maybe it is not normal that we will find the exact spare parts we are looking for in this exact village.
I should say something of the Overseer as well, she is a Franz Kafka fan, but not as extreme as anyone in the previous title, so no, unfortunately Kafka’s writing does not permeate [i]Revelations 2[/i] in the most heavy-handed of ways, and I cannot help but feel that that is unfortunate. 
Of course, there are plenty of references, and some are very explicit, but in [i]Revelations 1[/i] you always knew when they were making a reference, it was almost impossible to miss, and that is the sort of subtlety you usually see in [i]Resident Evil[/i], these references are just too well integrated, I wish there was more hamminess to it.

[h1] Presentation [/h1]
[i]Revelations 2[/i] takes place on an industrial isle but it manages to have some environmental diversity, torture prisons and torture factories blend together but that means that the foggy, green thickets and the anarchic city streets stick out more and that gives you some reason to appreciate them.
Of course, this is a [i]Resident Evil[/i] game, so there are also laboratories and some overdesigned, nouveau riche interiors. However, the best areas are only in Barry’s episodes, you can see some genuinely unsettling and disturbing visuals, even though they lack the gore of other locations they are still far more disturbing, because it is proof that you are not the only ones on the island.

As for the enemies, they are sort of a mixed bag, they are split in two varieties and you only fight one type per character, so Claire will always be fighting the Afflicted who generally look pretty generic and boring—they are your average infected with weapons—on the other hand we have the Revenants and they are far more interesting…
They are different bodies stitched together, limbs of differing sizes and shapes, multiple heads sewn as one, their flesh affixed with weapons, very visually striking, though not quite as disgusting as the bloated, insectoid Glasps.

I do not have a lot to say on the OST, it is good, and works well for the game, but on the whole, it does not stick out as especially remarkable, it blends, and heightens the atmosphere, which is good because it does not detract from the game.
[i]Theme of Barry[/i], however, is probably my favourite track in the game, it is sad, and heavy, perfectly illustrating how Barry is feeling. He regrets his actions as a father, their strained relationship, and how he has acted in the past, and now she is lost, and he does not know whether she is safe or not.

[h1] Gameplay [/h1]
If you have played a 3rd person [i]Resident Evil[/i] game you know what to expect, you fight enemies, conserve ammunition and explore a little bit.
I found that this entry could have done with a few more puzzles as most of what we get boils down to finding the key item or moving a box to the proper location. [i]Revelations 1[/i] was quite light on them as well but not to this extent, and it also had a bigger focus on exploration.

Having the missions be so linear is a bit of a letdown as well however, if you are going to do levels in an episodic format this is probably a good way to do it.
An episode takes place on the same selection of maps but Claire and Barry venture through them in different ways, sometimes the opposite direction which means it does not feel repetitive.
A couple others things makes it better than it otherwise might have been, there are unique areas for each character, and sometimes (once or twice) they are quite expansive and even the majority of the entire episode but there is also the fact that sometimes your choices affect the other character.
Claire can do things that makes Barry's episode easier or harder, and it usually comes with some sort of payoff.

However, they also brought wholesale improvements, the partner system is an actual system now with each character having different playstyles to complement their friends. Moira does not shoot but she has a flashlight to stun enemies, Natalia can throw bricks and see through walls and skin. That seems pretty useful!
This all means you will switch between characters to make the best use of their differing abilities as you go, though you will be primarily playing as Claire or Barry during shootouts. Or during the stealth sections, as they are the only ones who can preform takedowns, however, have no fear! There is no mandatory stealth, it is only used to conserve your ammunition… unless you play the Extra Episode [i]Little Miss[/i].

A system like this really lends itself to co-op, but unfortunately they did not think too far ahead, this was released at the death of local co-op games so they will allow that but not the more readily usable system of online play.
It is quite unfortunate because desperately trying to point out the literally invisible Glasps or the weak spots of Revenants would make for some very hectic and memorable moments, it is a real missed opportunity that three is no online co-op for [i]Revelations 2[/i]...

[h2]RAID MODE[/h2]
Raid mode! It has coop!
They even let you play levels from [i]Resident Evil 6[/i] which adds some much-needed level variety, unfortunately I do feel that this is a bit of a downgrade from the previous instalment. 
The fact is that the enemy variety is not necessarily there, they feel varied because they require a multitude of strategies but neither bosses nor mobs are as engaging and memorable to [i]fight[/i] as the sort of encounters from the previous games. If you like them you get a lot of content, if you do not, then you do not.

Game: Resident Evil Revelations 2

Review:

"It’s a co-op survival horror game where one player shoots zombies, and the other shines a flashlight like they’re auditioning for Ghostbusters. 10/10, would blind enemies with my best friend again."

Key Features:

Gameplay: A mix of shooting, stealth, and puzzling, with just enough jump scares to keep you on edge.

Story: A soap opera of betrayal, viruses, and questionable parenting decisions.

Co-op: One person gets all the guns, the other gets a flashlight or a brick. Truly balanced teamwork.


Personal Experience:
I played as Natalia, the brick-wielding child, while my friend screamed at me to “point at the zombie!” I pointed. They missed. Teamwork at its finest.

Relatable Humor:

Me: “Let’s be stealthy!” Partner: shoots the first enemy in the face.

The moment you realize the flashlight is surprisingly more useful than the person with the gun.


Pro-Con List:
Pros:

Fun co-op mechanics that will test your patience and friendship.

A story so dramatic it makes soap operas look tame.

Zombies, mutants, and a creepy island—what more could you want?


Cons:

Playing solo is fine, but co-op chaos is where the fun really shines.

Some puzzles are less “brain-teasing” and more “head-scratching.”

The brick may be mighty, but you’ll wish for more ammo instead.


Verdict:
Resident Evil Revelations 2 is a perfect mix of horror, action, and hilarious co-op shenanigans. Whether you’re shining flashlights, throwing bricks, or yelling at your partner for wasting ammo, this game keeps you entertained. Highly recommend—especially if you want to test your friendships under zombie-filled pressure!

Resident Evil: Revelations 2 is like being trapped in a horror movie where the scriptwriters couldn't decide if they were writing a serious thriller or a snarky B-movie. 

The game kicks off with Claire Redfield (veteran zombie dodger) being kidnapped and waking up in a prison that makes Alcatraz look like a summer camp. As you play through the game, you’ll find yourself alternating between Claire/Moira and Barry/Natalia, trying to figure out why everyone on this island is either trying to eat you or drive you insane.

Revelations 2 brings back the tight, claustrophobic environments and resource management that fans love, while also introducing a few new mechanics. The tag-team system lets you switch between characters on the fly, each with their own unique abilities. Claire’s the battle-hardened pro, and Moira is... well, she’s got a flashlight and some serious attitude. Barry Burton, Moira's dad, offers more firepower, paired with Natalia, who has the ability to see enemies through walls like a psychic surveillance camera, a kid so creepy she could have been cast in The Shining.

The game’s environments are appropriately grim and foreboding, full of dark corridors, creepy forests, and abandoned facilities. The island is full of grotesque creatures that range from standard zombies to things that look like they crawled out of someone’s worst nightmare. The soundtrack and sound effects do a great job of keeping you on edge. The story is a rollercoaster of B-movie horror clichés mixed with genuine moments of tension. Whether you’re uncovering the mystery of a villain who loves Shakespearean monologues through bracelets or trying to make sense of why anyone thought splitting up was a good idea.

Resident Evil: Revelations 2 successfully combines elements of classic survival horror with new gameplay mechanics and a compelling story. It’s a game that respects the series’ roots while also experimenting with new ideas.

Resident Evil Revelations 2 is another side story of the Resident Evil mainline series (though strangely NOT a direct sequel to Revelations 1), this time following fan-favorite character Claire Redfield as well as Moira Burton, daughter of other fan-favorite character Barry Burton who you'll also play as occasionally alongside new character Natalia. Claire and Moira have been abducted by an unknown terrorist group and taken all the way to a remote island in the Baltic Sea, where they soon uncover a new deadly variant of the T-Virus that has been unleashed on the local population. You'll make your way through dangerous environments to try to not only find a way to get off this island, but also figure out how to stop this new virus from becoming an even larger threat.

Similar to my thoughts on Revelations 1, Revelations 2 is just a bit strange at times. It's not inherently *bad* I suppose, but it's very weird. When playing through Revelations 2, I was often reminded of Evil Within in various aspects. The two games share similar stylistic depictions of gore and violence that doesn't quite fit the established norm for Resident Evil. They both share a pretty extensive skill tree system that helps boost things like damage and survivability and how well your co-op partner performs. There's a limited inventory and ammo capacity, but it's similar to Evil Within where it's limited enough to make you scared of running out of things but not so much so that you can't gun down every single enemy. Again, none of this is inherently bad, but it does feel like a game that got lost in the wrong franchise sometimes. In terms of definite positives I want to highlight that of Resident Evil 0, 5, and Revelations 2 (I haven't played 6 yet), Revelations 2 has in my opinion the best implementation of the partner system, where both characters felt useful in their own regard and fun to play as. I also think the episodic nature was handled better in Revelations 2 compared to Revelations 1, the story breaks felt more consistent going from Claire to Barry and back again with a regular, consistent rhythm. Revelations 1 felt random with its breaks and difference in gameplay styles between segments, but Revelations 2 had a very stead-fast layout that balanced combat and stealth very well. I still think the telanovella-style writing is a bit silly at times and the story isn't 100% a banger, but it has its redeeming points.

Revelations 1 and 2 sit at an odd point in the series. Neither of them are bad games necessarily, and their positives definitely outweigh their negatives. I think it's just a case of their positives not being that stellar in the first place. It's the equivalent of getting a frozen pizza as opposed to a big delivery chain or a local hand-made pizza place, it tastes just fine but it's not gonna hit the same. I wouldn't go out of my way to recommend either Revelations 1 or 2 to a newer Resident Evil fan, but for people who've played a lot of games in the series I'd say they're worth a shot, just to try something a little different compared to the rest of the mainline games.

Surprisingly good! Everything from the mood/atmosphere, level design, enemies, combat, puzzles, story, and characters is great. 

Mood/atmosphere - Trapped on an island, Claire Redfield wakes up in a prison with deranged prisoners. The prison is filled with torture devices like a outlast game and/or saw movie.

Level design - The levels within the game provide a variety of experiences in terms of movement, combat, and puzzles. Levels are revisited throughout the story and still enjoyable.

Enemies - The common deranged enemies are easily likeable and resemble classic RE zombies, other enemy types keep the game interesting and fresh in terms of design and gameplay interaction.

Combat - Similar to combat in RE 5 with sneak attacks, melee, guns, sub weapons. Dashes are included and are a separate action button in this game. Unique to this game is comboing enemies with coop partner (AI, switched to yourself, or another human) and it's reasonable and satisfying to pull off in single player. The AI partner is surprising smart and will help with execution combos, blinding, and other. 

Other gameplay - side kick characters offer unique abilities like spotting hidden items, blinding enemies and other. This game includes new injuries such as bleeding and vomit (both will blind your screen) which can be remedied by tourniquet and disinfectant. The AI will heal your ailments if they have the item. As well the AI will follow without too much issues and will not get hit by traps surprisingly; as well the player can tell the ai to stand still as needed for puzzles and stealth.  All to say is that the AI is actually good in this game. Also unique to the RE series is a skill tree players can purchase with the points earned in the game. Similar to RE:revelations, guns can also be upgraded with parts found in the levels.

Story is good. Fits in the timeline between RE 5  and RE 6. 

Overall really good horror action resident evil game with awesome setting, antagonist, and unique gameplay that is seriously fun. Revelations was good, but this game was a step up and one of the best RE games.

Resident Evil Revelations 2, developed by Capcom, takes players back to the heart-pounding survival horror roots of the iconic Resident Evil series. Set between the events of Resident Evil 5 and 6, this installment introduces new characters and unfolds a gripping narrative that delves deep into the sinister workings of the Umbrella Corporation.

[h2] Graphics and Visuals [/h2]

[✔️] 🌄 Atmospheric Environments: Revelations 2 excels in creating a haunting atmosphere with its diverse environments. [❌] ⏳ Pacing Challenges: The game's episodic structure occasionally results in uneven pacing, especially noticeable in transitions between Claire and Moira's segments and later with Barry Burton's storyline. While each episode contributes to the overarching narrative, some sections may feel slower or less engaging compared to others.

[h2] Story and Narrative [/h2]

[✔️] 📜 Gripping Narrative: Revelations 2 weaves a tale of survival and conspiracy that keeps players on edge throughout. The plot unfolds through alternating perspectives, revealing layers of intrigue and danger lurking beneath the surface. As characters confront their fears and uncover the truth behind their captivity, alliances are tested and revelations unfold that reshape their understanding of the Umbrella Corporation's legacy.

[❌] ⚙️ Predictable Moments: While the narrative is engaging, certain plot twists and character motivations may feel predictable to longtime fans of the series. The mode encourages replayability and cooperative play, providing a satisfying challenge for those seeking to test their survival skills.

[✔️] 🎮 Cooperative Play: The game's cooperative mode enhances the experience, allowing two players to collaborate in tackling challenges and solving puzzles together. I don't like it as much as Revelations 1, atleast in regards to the campaign, but it is still a fun game and well worth a playthrough. It seems like the Revelations spinoffs are a way of meshing old resident evil designs with new ones. For Revelations 1 it took inspiration from old RE map layouts and combined it with the action combat seen in 5. Revelations 2 takes inspiration from the A & B scenarios of RE2 where your direct actions in Claire's campaign affects Barry's campaign. This is the highlight of the game for me and it gives the game some replay value after a first playthrough.

My biggest issues with the campaign are that it is very short and doesn't feel as rewarding as Revelations 1. There aren't as many gun parts to collect, and I never felt excited to test out my weapon build like in the previous title. This game tries to make up for that with an upgrade tree which you can spend BP from gameplay to get certain buffs and abilities. I don't find any of these upgrades and perks to be very interesting even though they are useful. I also tend not to like BP since you will often find it in small quantities from exploring the map. Ammo isn't scarce, but I will say that I was annoyed to find BP instead of bullets every time I broke a barrel or box.

The story is okay, and again I think it is too short. It feels close to those Resident Evil CGI movies, where it is a generic villain of the week given 2 character traits to try to make them seem deeper than they are. Most of the lore I found in game wasn't very interesting either. The bright side is that our main characters are pretty good. I like being able to play as Claire again, its nice that Barry gets a return with a story that revolves around him and his family, and Moira has a nice little arc that I think is really enjoyable. Basically, everything outside of the main antagonist and this weird death game is really good.

I'm a little taken aback by how positively this game has been received. Resident Evil Revelations 2 is a co-op game that seems to actively dislike co-op. Controlling both characters at once feels very clunky, particularly with the way you are meant to highlight items with the character who can't deal damage. So the natural assumption would be that the game is intended for co-op.

Despite this, the game seems to do everything it can to make co-op an unpleasant experience. It doesn't have online support, it closes player 2's inventory when player 1 opens their inventory, player 2 cannot aim when player 1 opens their inventory, it doesn't allow two players to be in separate areas and, worst of all, the game gives you a bad ending if player 1 is too good at a QTE. If player 1 mashes a QTE in Episode 3 too fast, then you get the bad ending in Episode 4. The decisions made in the creation of this game are simply bewildering.

Even something as simple as the invisible enemies which can only be seen by player 2 are ruined by the decision to not have online play. The idea that player 2 would have to point in the direction of the enemy so that player 1 can kill it is a clever one, but it is completely ruined by the forced split-screen that comes with no online, allowing player 1 to just look at player 2's screen and see the enemy.

The story, what little of it there is, is also just thoroughly uninteresting. There's a fair bit of set-up in the first episode that just goes nowhere, and Episodes 2 and onward just feel meandering and uninteresting. Every note you find in this game feels exactly the same: "I am poor and this Wesker lady is very evil". This wouldn't be so bad if we got anything else but honestly there's just so little there.

Yes, the gunplay feels good and Episode 1 was fairly well paced, but that really feels like all the positives I can find for this game. Maybe if I had played it during that awful Capcom drought in the early to mid 2010's I'd be more inclined to be nice to it, but nowadays this game just feels like it's only a couple of steps above Resident Evil 6.

I enjoyed it however I think there are some downsides. It is clear that they were experimenting with a few things with this title, which in some ways I think paid off yet in other ways, not so much. For instance, the way the secondary character is utilized ( not being able to pick up certain things to have your partner "find" it instead ) just feels a little bit cheap and slows momentum a lot. You either have to switch to the character that has the finding ability and pick up the item then switch it to the fighting character's inventory then switch to the fighting character to use it or you have to find it as the finding character then switch to the fighting character to pick it up. A small gripe, but it goes towards a lot. Since this game has split-screen capability, it seems that a lot of how those mechanics work just in single-player turn out to be very clunky in practice. The AI a lot of times is very delayed, which for a game of its time maybe it is to be expected. Overall, I really liked it as I already enjoy Resident Evil titles and just got around to playing it so I'm familiar with the characters and setting and I knew I would probably like it. BUT on the other hand, if you don't already like Resident Evil and are just looking to pick this up with no prior knowledge of the franchise and no bias swaying you to like it, do I think I would recommend it to you... No, probably not. That isn't to say it's bad, because it isn't. But I don't think I'd really recommend it to anyone who doesn't already like Resident Evil.

[h3]THE SUMMARY:[/h3]

As a major fan of the Resident Evil franchise, personally this one is a bit of an underrated one in my opinion. While it does have its fair share of issues, bugs, and confusing access to different parts of the game (where you have to buy each episode story individually), it still offers a fun an unique Resident Evil experience that sets itself a part from the other games in a different, but fun way.

[h3]CO-OP AND MULTIPLAYER:[/h3]

One of the main points of this game for me was its allowance of local co-op multiplayer or split-screen where a friend and I could either play through episodes via remote play or locally. This was a lot of fun, and for me it offered a different experience when it comes to Resident Evil games I had not quite experienced in this way before. We had a good time playing through the story as well as going through DLC episodes this way and it was nice to play RE a bit differently with friends involved.

[h3]FINAL THOUGHTS:[/h3]

This a good Resident Evil game to give a go if enjoyed the first Revelations game, and especially if you want to try RE with local or remote play multiplayer which is something that if I am not mistaken, only this title seems to offer that I know of or have played recently. The story is a bit short, and the whole game won't be as long as compared to other RE games, but offers some replayability in the form of earning upgrades and keeping them as you progress through the game, even after beating it for the first time. All in all, I'd give it a go on sale if any of these things interest you or if you're just a die-hard RE fan like me.

Not to mention Revive Crystals, that allow you to (duh) revive on the spot after getting killed with all your ammo and heals replenished. As a die-hard fan of the Resident Evil franchise, I can confidently say that Resident Evil Revelations 2 is one of the best titles in the series. From its engaging story to its intense gameplay, all aspects of this game combine to create an unforgettable experience for players.

One of the standout features of Resident Evil Revelations 2 is its captivating storyline. The game takes place between the events of Resident Evil 5 and Resident Evil 6, and follows the story of Claire Redfield and Moira Burton as they navigate their way through a remote island filled with terrifying creatures - Featuring Barry Burton and newcomer Natalia. The plot twists and turns, keeping players on the edge of their seats as they uncover the mysteries of the island and the sinister Umbrella Corporation behind it all.

But what truly elevates Resident Evil Revelations 2 is its Raid mode. This mode allows players to team up with a friend or go solo to take on various challenges and missions. The variety and intensity of these missions make for an exhilarating experience, and the option to play with a friend adds an extra layer of fun and excitement. Moreover, the rewards earned in Raid mode can be used in the main game, giving players the opportunity to unlock new weapons and upgrades.

The gameplay in Resident Evil Revelations 2 is also top-notch. The third-person perspective and controls are smooth and intuitive, making it easy to navigate through the game. The combat mechanics are also well-executed, with a good mix of action and survival elements. The game also introduces some new elements, such as the ability to switch between characters during gameplay, adding a unique twist to the classic Resident Evil formula.

In terms of graphics and sound, Resident Evil Revelations 2 sets the bar high. The detailed environments, realistic character models, and eerie atmosphere all contribute to the overall experience. The sound effects and soundtrack are also spot on, adding to the tension and suspense of the game.

Overall, Resident Evil Revelations 2 is a must-play for any fan of the Resident Evil series. From its gripping story to its addictive gameplay, it offers everything that makes a great horror game. And with the addition of the Raid mode, it is a game that will keep players engaged long after the main story is completed. I highly recommend giving it a try, you won't be disappointed.

I am 32 years old.

My ex-wife and I have a daughter together, and we adopted our son together. Both are now 4 years old.

When we were going through our separation, I felt lost and unhappy. I was self-destructive. One day, I was so angry with everything spiraling out of control that I punched a concrete wall in a moment of overwhelming emotion. This resulted in breaking my fifth metacarpal in my right hand—the hand I worked with, played games with, and used to carry my children to bed—the hand I desperately needed to ensure I could continue providing.

Upon learning the severity of the self-inflicted damage, I became almost suicidal. Keep in mind that just a few months before this, I was the happiest man, with no history of depression or anxiety. I had never experienced anger outbursts, nor was I the type to break down and cry, but I was in a tough situation that truly prevented me from seeing the light on the other side.

With nothing better to do, I looked for a game I could play WITH ONE HAND while recovering. Somehow, I stumbled upon this game and read some of the comments. I decided it was worth a try... I must admit I didn't beat the game, nor did I play as much as some of you. In fact, I may have played this game for only a day or two. That being said, after doing so, I had a new joy and hope for life. I managed to leave behind the pain and suffering that had been thrust upon me. I could experience the joy and happiness of other people. I relaxed for 5 ♥♥♥♥ minutes listening to this music, long enough to realize that I would be okay.

After realizing this, I turned off the game and went back to work. My hand hurt a lot, but I was motivated. I stopped feeling so sorry for myself and became the father I needed to be at that moment, not the weak boy I was behaving like.

Today, I am close friends with the mother of my children. We don't fight, argue, or say hurtful things to each other. We are parents and friends.

Now I have 3 children. My third child is, wait, ALSO 4 YEARS OLD. The woman I am with was going through a very similar situation at the time of my separation, and we just unexpectedly stumbled into each other's lives. We have been dating for a year and are very happy together.

Moral of the story: you never know what life has in store for you, and if I had given up when all odds were against me, I wouldn't be where I am today. This silly little game helped me realize that.
