[i]Resident Evil Revelations 2 is by far the closest to the original horror games than any of the others in the franchise before the gameplay reboot with RE 7. It's slow, it's atmospheric and it's (mostly) well-written. [/i]

[h1]Flows[/h1][list]
[*]Absolutely great atmosphere. You are in a remote Russian island in the middle of nowhere, and there are no world-ending threats. The stakes are low and much more personal.
[*]While not open-world, many areas have a lot of room for exploration, especially in the early game.
[*]The game has an escort system that works. Basically you have two character pairs. Each has the fighter character, who carries guns and kicks @ss, and a character who finds stuff and sneaks around. Not only are your partners NOT a burden, you actually care for both of them, lorewise and gameplay wise.
[*]Said partners are a little girl and a hot barely-legal teenager in shorts with tights. Look, I'm just saying...
[*]Classic RE combat. Nothing that will blow your mind, but it works and it's mildly satisfying.
[*]Two pretty good twists, with the first being really early on and the second being the end-credits scene.[/list]

[h1]Flaws[/h1][list]
[*]The campaign is NOT co-op, the tag is completely misleading. You can only play co-op in survival missions and the like.
[*][spoiler]The villain is Wesker's long-lost sister. Whoopty ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ Do...[/spoiler]
[*]I played the game with Japanese voice-acting and English subtitles, and I have seen enough anime to know that those subtitles had f@ckall to do with what was actually being said. I'm not talking about simple paraphrasing. Character-building lines and genuine emotional moments are replaced with smartass quips about wasting zombies, completely tone-deaf. It honestly read more like a 4Kids dub than an actual translation.
[*]The second pair of playable characters has a little, somewhat-creepy girl in a white dress, as the escort/scout character. I obviously did the natural thing and after fighting a really persistent camera, I finally managed to get an upskirt shot. Turns out under the dress she's wearing... Biker shorts. At the sight, all I could say out loud was "[i]You f@cking ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥...[/i]". I'm not just disappointed Capcom, I feel betrayed.
[*]The stage mode requires you to first go to an in-game room to choose your character and gear. That's tedious. There had to be a better way to do this, through menus.[/list]

[b]RE Revelations 2 is a slower experience than the typical RE title, and that is absolutely to its benefit. It is tight, atmospheric and genuinely fun to play. Thumbs up for purchase.[/b]

[h1] Resident Evil Revelations 2: Return To Raid Mode! [/h1]

So, here we are with Resident Evil Revelations 2, and what a ride it's been. This isn't your typical spin-off; it's a compelling game that manages to please the series' die-hard fans while introducing something fresh.

First Of All... Raid mode back! Raid Mode is a fantastic concept and it's executed with flair. It combines online co-op with a leveling and loot system. After each run, you get graded and rewarded with loot and in-game currency. The gear you earn can be used instantly, and you can spend the cash in the shop for even more items. There are loads of locked characters and gear to unlock, making it highly replayable.

Kill Zombos with a buddy!

Anyway.... we should get on to the REAL review.

In Revelations 2, we've got four main episodes and a couple of bonus missions, and I'm thrilled to say it's a package that doesn't disappoint. You know, in the first episode, I pondered the essence of a spin-off and delved into its core mechanics. And through the last three episodes, the game pretty much keeps its mechanical course, albeit with a few new toys to play with. But the real show-stealer in this chunk of Revelations 2 is the boost in flair and intensity.

The initial episodes did well, don't get me wrong, but they didn't quite hit that 'wow' button. It's the second episode where things kick into high gear. Dangerous situations? Check. Intriguing new environments? Check. More formidable enemies? Absolutely.

Revelations 2 is like a blend of classic Resident Evil with a modern twist, striking a balance that fans will appreciate. It's not just formulaic; it's a slick, current experience that has tossed the old tank controls and sluggish zombies out the window.

The enemies in Revelations 2, while true to the Resident Evil spirit, offer a notable twist – speed. You spot one in the distance, just like the old days, and line up that perfect headshot. But now, they come charging at you with purpose. They leap up if you've got a height advantage, and if you miss one shot, these foes are on you in an instant, swinging multiple times in a single brutal attack. This game claimed more of my lives than any recent Resident Evil, which is a pleasant surprise. You don't just go into Rambo mode; you strategize. It's great to come across a group of enemies and contemplate your approach. This fear of the unknown, that sense of vulnerability, it's back, and it feels good.

I must give a nod to the game's environments. Darkness prevails, illuminated only by your flashlight and Capcom's stunning lighting effects. It's both a blessing and a curse, restricting your vision while offering countless shadowy corners for enemies to hide. Combine this with winding, narrow corridors, and the requirement to occasionally split up your characters (with only one having a light source), and you've got a recipe for jump scares. It's well-executed, often by resisting the obvious and lulling you into complacency.

When you finally escape these dark places into the light, it's like hearing the safe room music in the original Resident Evil. Revelations 2 makes normal light feel like a safe haven, a refreshing take on horror game darkness. It’s a subtle nod to the horror genre's tendency for dimly lit environments, and it works because it doesn’t overdo it.

As you might expect, the game involves backtracking. That's Resident Evil's signature move, revisiting the same locations multiple times. But in Revelations 2, these revisits feel more linear because Barry and Natalia's story takes place six months after Claire and Moira's adventure. There's consistency in the changes, and each segment feels different. However, this linearity is a departure from classic Resident Evil, where you knew every nook and cranny of a place after the first couple of visits. It's a small shift, but it’s noticeable.

Yet, amidst these minor issues, the game maintains its overall excellence. It's not these hiccups but the majority of the game that leaves a remarkable impact. In a Resident Evil game, it's not just the spectacular moments but also the standard enemy encounters that define the experience. Improving these confrontations automatically elevates the entire game.

Revelations 2 isn't without faults. Those invisible enemies, especially in tight quarters, are frustrating. They could’ve been more than a simple one-hit kill gimmick. However, one negative doesn't ruin what Revelations 2 gets right.

I’ve thoroughly enjoyed my time with this game. It offers an innovative spin on a classic formula while delivering intense, atmospheric gameplay. The enemies are formidable, and the environments add an extra layer of dread. Yes, there are a few hiccups along the way, but the overall experience overshadows them.

What Revelations 2 achieves that's truly impressive is establishing its distinct identity within the Resident Evil universe. It's not just another Resi game; it's Revelations 2, and it feels like a breath of fresh air.

[h1]TLDR: Revelations 2 is a bit of a weird entry in the RE series, being both the end of an era and the beginning of another. It’s a spin-off through and through but it also brings back classic characters and leans towards old-school survival-horror way more than any of the main entries. It’s a worthy sequel to Revelations, a worthy entry in the series and a very good game in general. Great campaigns with an addictive Raid Mode. Highly recommended – also, highly underrated. [/h1]

Revelations 2 is not a direct narrative sequel to Revelations, although there are nods and references to it. It’s sort of a middle-ground between classic Survival Horror with tough enemies (including zombies!) and ammo management, while also keeping RE4/5’s general gameplay feel. It doesn’t feature any of the gameplay changes that RE6 brought and focuses on a self-contained story, its characters and a solid gameplay loop.

It’s worth mentioning that when it came out, the RE series was basically all about action [i]except[/i] for the Revelations spin-offs – those were meant to be a survival horror-ish fix for fans of old. I loved the first entry, and this sequel didn’t disappoint. It’s an evolution of the RE4 formula but in a "what if" sense: what if instead of going for insane, boulder-punching action and world-ending events, the series went towards a more focused, more self-contained and horror-centric experience? 

That is Revelations 2 in a nutshell. It’s a very-well polished game that has a lot to offer. Its story is delivered in episodes and it’s a fun ride overall. These days, you can get the whole package for pretty cheap. And what a package it is: a pretty long and highly repayable campaign featuring Barry and Claire, two story DLCs and a Raid Mode that is so fleshed out that it would need its own review. Seriously, Raid Mode is very, very, VERY addictive. 

It’s nowhere near perfect though: the pacing is sometimes wonky, the story is cheesy – though that is to be expected from a RE game – and it feels like it ends on what was supposed to be the beginning of (yet) another over-arching story arc. Some characters aren’t as developed as they should be too. The gameplay is really solid and features many improvements compared to its predecessor, such as dodging and a stealth system but it also feels derivative, The Last of Us being a clear inspiration. Also, enemy variety is lacking outside of Raid Mode.

Don’t skip this one – it’s good and has little to do with the main entries, it’s a more Survival Horror-focused experience, it brings back some beloved characters and has content for days. Revelations 1&2 have more in common with RE7 really, which isn’t surprising considering that Rev’s director went on to make RE7. That’s right, this is the second game from the team that brought us RE7, RE2R and RE8. 

Here’s hoping they make a Revelations 3 one of these days. Not that a sub-series focused on horror is needed anymore since the series went back to its root with RE7, but this story arc is worthy of getting a conclusion or being merged with the main series somehow. This game is too underrated and I can only recommend it if you’re into RE at all, and/or looking for a horror game.

Perfect Game #50, Resident Evil Revelations 2.  I was very torn on whether to give this game a negative review or not, but I decided on a cautious yes.  I really want to like this game, the original Revelations is my favorite Resident Evil game, but there's just something about this sequel that is pushing me towards a no.  Let's start with what I like about the game.  

Raid Mode; my absolute favorite gamemode from the original game is back, and it's better in pretty much every way.  From character variety to more unique levels, there's not much I don't like.  I'm also a fan of the returning episodic formula, it allows for you to play a chapter and come back without missing out on the key information.  Having control of two characters can be pretty fun, but it is annoying as well sometimes.  Sadly that's about where my likes end.  

I wish there was more variety in the levels.  Playing through the same areas as both Claire/Moira and Barry/Natalia is so boring.  There is no atmosphere here; I can't remember a single time where I was tense while walking through an area or fighting a mutated monster.  I can barely think of any memorable moments at all.  I can recall at least like 5 from Rev 1, but not a single one here, it's disappointing.  The genre is survival horror but it only feels like survival, I'm missing the horror element.  Does the game need to be constantly scary? No, but I would at least hope that the sequel would improve or further excel at what the first game accomplished.

That's where this game fails me I feel.  I wanted more of the atmosphere that the Queen Zenobia gave.  I want those memorable moments of the captain yelling mayday and banging on the door or of a mutated Rachel crawling through the vents just to pop out in front of you.  I feel like this game falls so much shorter where the original game overwhelmingly exceeded.  Is the game bad? no, the gameplay is still largely solid and the exploration can be fun for at least the first time through.  This is why I'm cautiously rating it positive; it still delivers mostly on the gameplay and resource management front, I just wish it had more to offer in terms of horror or atmosphere or any memorable moments.

Revelations 2 is a great time all around.

In terms of gameplay, the mechanics are very similar to the first game but with more polished animations and a smoother camera. There are still limitations put on your character such as the camera being locked to your back during combat and only being able to run forwards (which gives you less control when you do) and these restrictions put on the player make the game challenging as the enemies are designed around these restrictions to take advantage of your weaknesses. It's not like RE6 where the controls are so smooth and you have almost zero limitations, so you can bail out of any situation meaning they have to make hordes of zombies leap at you across the map for the game to be challenging. It's more in line with the enemy design of RE4 & RE5 where the enemies are slow but can corner you if you're careless. Especially the bigger dudes.

Dodging has been reworked as a dedicated button that you can dash in any direction but the trade off is that there's no longer any I-Frames during the dodge. Most of the time, dodging backwards is reliable, but dodging to sides of an attack when applicable can put you in a better position to deal damage. So there is some skill to using it.

Melee works similarly to the first game, but this time you stun enemies by shooting them in the head instead of the arms and you can perform a follow up ground attack to deal extra damage or finish off an enemy.

The level design is a step down from the first game however. Instead of an interconnected map with a variety of shortcuts and backtracking, it's instead more in line with the linear design of RE4, RE5 & RE6. Which considering how the Revelations titles were supposed to be a throwback to old school Resident Evil...it disappoints me. It doesn't take away any enjoyment from the game as the core gameplay is a lot of fun but I do see wasted potential with setting the game on a remote Island and not making the Island interconnected. The game gives hints of this in the first and second Episode with locations that require the player to run around the map in search of items, but it's mostly dropped by the time you get to Episode 3.

A big advantage this game has over newer games in the series is that you can co-op the campaign. Unfortunately, it's local multiplayer only but if you use remote play (which I did) then you can play with a buddy online. It won't save progress for both of you however. The second player will play as Moria during Claire's sections and Natalia during Barry's sections. Both act more as support characters for player 1 instead of RE5/RE6 where the second player utilizes the same mechanics. Moria doesn't use guns, she only has a crowbar which is more powerful than Claire's knife and can be used to stun enemies if you hit them from behind. She also has a flashlight which can be used to stun enemies and leave them open for attacks (kind of like Alan Wake). Natalia doesn't have much offensive capability, the best she can do is hit zombies with bricks. But she can see enemies through walls and see invisible enemies that Barry can't. This made our co-op session very tense as we would both have to communicate positioning and aiming to take down enemies. Having player 2 be a support character makes the co-op more unique than RE5/RE6's campaigns and most co-op campaigns in general. It is also drop in/drop out co-op so that's nice. Moria/Natalia can also find items that Claire/Barry can't find such as ammo or health. In single player you can switch between the characters on the fly.

Raid Mode is back and is an improvement. First featuring a real time lobby that allows you to mess around with your friend, second it features a boat load of characters from the other games such as Jill, Leon & Chris. The raid mode mainly reuses stages from some parts of the campaign as well as Rev1 & RE6 which some may say is lazy but it does mean that the level design doesn't get repetitive when going between campaign and raid mode like it did in Rev1. Plus the stages play well and the nice part is that you don't have to play the campaign to unlock stages. You just progress the mode. Characters now have individual level scaling instead of universal level scaling like in Rev1. I like this change as it means when you unlock a new character, your stats are back to square one and the game will become challenging again even on earlier stages you could cruise through previously. This mode can played in local multiplayer, but also online with a friend. Otherwise, Raid mode works almost the same as it did in Rev1. The way you purchase weapons & obtain new items is practically the same.

There was two pieces of story DLC released named 'The Struggle' & 'Little Miss'. Both are fairly short but I had fun playing them. Not much else to say.

Story wise I enjoyed the game overall. Claire had the personality of a cardboard box, but Barry is the main star of the show. They take a lot of his one off lines from RE1 and turn them into badass action hero lines in Rev2. I enjoyed the warm and strong fatherly attitude he has with Natalia which gives some insight into what type of Dad he is and how much he cares for his family & friends as well as how determined he is to save Moria. He expresses a variety of emotions over the course of the game and it makes his reaction to the situation feel more believable as well as fleshing him out as a character. Moria does mature over the course of the game and it was engaging to see her mend the broken relationship she had with her father but some of her dialogue is irritatingly vulgar. Natalia was good too as she helps bring out Barry's softer side during downtime which helps give the pacing breathing room when it needs to. Plus I'm a sucker for the 'Strong old man taking care of a kid' trope. Her dialogue can be pretty adorable and funny as well.

Plot wise, the game is heavily inspired the works of Franz Kafka. There's quotes everywhere from his work, a lot of story aspects and character's roles are directly inspired by his work. Almost every episode contains references to In the Penal Colony with the prison setting, Prometheus's liver puzzle, A Visit to the Mine towards the end of the game, and there's even a factory you visit named 'Kierling'. I did enjoy the game giving more subtext and a deeper meaning than other Resident Evil titles, after all  this is Dai Satō as the writer (Cowboy Bebop, Ghost In The Shell: S.A.C., Ergo Proxy). The man has a deep understanding of philosophy and symbolism. However I found the subtext very surface level compared to his other work. The similarities to Kafka's work is nice and all but the game doesn't use it as a way to convey a theme or idea other than what Kafka's work itself did. For example, Ergo Proxy used Nietzsche's idea about the 'Death of God' to convey the theme of running away from a predetermined identity, so it's using another author's ideas to expand upon and give new meaning. It's still one of the better Resident Evil stories in terms of deeper meaning, themes & ideas but I found it to be disappointing when compared to the previous work by Mr. Satō.

Overall, I had a lot of fun with Revelations 2. It's definitely a better put together game in pacing and design than RE5 & RE6. It has a lot more content and replay value compared to the first game, it has local & online multiplayer features to allow a friend to join in on the fun and it's a steal in terms of price, especially when it goes on sale often. You really get your money's worth with this game. I do wish it expanded more on the level design and its deeper themes but I still had a blast playing this game. Plus, any excuse to see more Barry is good enough for me.

Was that a bit confusing? Then that's how you'll feel about this game.

RE Revelations 2 has little to do with the 1st Revelations and acts more as a direct sequel to Resident Evil 5 and somewhat of a bridge to Resident Evil 6 with slight mentions of Resident Evil Revelations...

It follows a pattern of episodic series similar to Life is Strange, 4 in total, and brings gameplay elements from RE6 and 5 back.
In RE5 your character felt very stiff whereas 6 went for a go-all-out type of play.
Revelations 2 removes some of the freedom from 6 but adds a dodge mechanic.

The story's about Berry from RE1 who's searching for his lost daughter Moira on a death island. You'll encounter deathly traps, some horror elements here and there, invisible enemies, and normal enemies.
Sadly there's barely any variety of enemies in the game.

Now here are some of the positives.
It feels...good, the gameplay's pretty solid and the atmosphere rocks at certain parts in the game but unfortunately, it doesn't stick with you since a lot of the areas you'll proceed through are so short which makes them forgettable.

The gunplay's solid and feels somewhat more impactful. It's a fun game.

The downsides of it are the bosses and the AI CO OP.
The game lies to you: There's no CO-OP...you cannot invite someone to join and play with you via multiplayer. They'll have to join through Remote Play and they better own a proper controller or you better download some fixes because I wasn't able to play with my friend in CO-OP through Remote Play because the game wouldn't recognise the 2nd player despite the fact that it worked with any other game.

The bosses are creative, well, some, not all. 
But the main issue is - while most of the enemies are a fun challenge to deal with, sadly, the bosses are Destiny-level type where you have to waste bullets upon bullets, and the game barely gives you any during the boss fight. On normal difficulty, there's no freaking way for players not to have encountered this problem unless they stockpiled a bunch of ammo beforehand by knifing their way through the level or just plainly running away from enemies.
Out of all the Resident Evil games I've played, the bosses of this one were the most frustrating due to the lack of ammo you can get.

The other thing is AI... If you thought RE5 and 6 had bad AI...oh boy, wait until you get a load of this one. The AI will just stand there and do absolutely nothing and in a lot of cases will go in ways that will mess you up even more.

They came up with the idea to play both characters, which, makes sense and it's a justifiable method to progress this type of level design and sequels but they completely obliterated the partner AI.

You can now switch between characters in the fight, which may take a bit of getting used to.

But then, the worst part is that ONE character will use normal health herbs - a limited type of health while the other has a REGENERATIVE type of health.
This is complete bollocks but made for some hilarious moments.
So when Claire runs out of 20 shotgun shells while fighting the boss, then just switch to Moira and go smack the boss with her pipe, get hit, wait for 10 seconds to regen your health then go back to waking the 10 meters super mega boss again because...that's how it works...and pray that the AI of Claire won't jump in front of the boss' attacks.

All in all...it's just Not-Very-Good.

The story's meh...very meh... the premise is good, and the journals you'll find are pretty okay. I like the atmosphere in certain parts, you do feel trapped on an island filled with death traps and deadly enemies but the story ends up taking itself both severely serious and so awfully cheesy that you don't know how to feel by the end.
RE5 and 6 had a consistent mood for the story where as RE Revelations 2, just like its gameplay mechanic doesn't know what it wants to be...too serious or too cringy/cheesy.

The DLCs, Little Miss, and Survivor are so lackluster...one's just a walking simulator and the other is basically a Gauntlet mode that starts interesting but ends up being quite boring with some story context slammed here and there. It should've been cut in size, and been in the main game, not a thing you have to select from the menu.

The game is challenging, however, more so than 5 and 6 which is pretty good. You'll have to be more thoughtful about your approach and stealth is actually useful in a lot of cases. There's reason to switch between characters in order to find resources and ammo and the interface is pretty easy and simple to navigate in most cases.
The best part about RE Revelations 2 is Mercenary Mode.
It is, hands down the best Mercenary Mode out of all Resident Evil games.
Many challenges, a bunch of stages, mostly from previous games such as Resident Evil 6, and lots of characters that most people won't give a damn about so I have no idea why they decided to shove these characters in any way like Neil and 2 other dudes that die in the main story and who are completely irrelevant NPCs while Jill, Chris, and Wesker are hidden behind grind or DLC paid content.

If you're looking for a Mercenary Mode to play that's really good, then this is it.

So to sum it up
+ Story mode that goes around for 7-10 hours of gameplay
+ Good atmosphere
+ Solid gameplay
+ The best Mercenary Mode to play
+ / - Decent, very mediocre story that's so predictable by the end
- Horrible tanky bosses
- Bad DLC overall with nothing new in it
- Lack of enemy variety
- No Co-Op in Singleplayer as advertised and IS misleading

Not the best RE game, but Revelations 2 is a solid entry. It has a good variety of enemies, decent story, and well-paced gameplay. You get to play as Claire and Barry in two parallel narratives, each accompanied by a new character. 

Claire is accompanied by Barry's daughter, Moira, who is armed with a flashlight and crowbar. She can shine light in the enemies' eyes and hit them with her crowbar. Barry is accompanied by a young girl, Natalia, who can point at things, see enemies through walls, and throw bricks at enemies. 

Each secondary character is essentially a support character, and you can swap between your primary and secondary characters at any point during the game. When playing as the secondary character, though, the primary character is useless and barely attacks enemies (even after unlocking a talent that says they do). That was one thing I disliked about the game. 

Barry's story gives big 'The Last of Us' vibes, in that he's dressed spookily similar to Joel from TLOS, and the gameplay consists of sneaking around, crafting molotovs, throwing bricks, and protecting a girl from zombies.

Do note: this game is made up of 4 chapters, each of which you need to purchase separately. There is no way to buy the full game alone.

A captivating storyline is one of the game's highlights. The story takes place between the events of Resident Evil 5 and Resident Evil 6 and follows Claire Redfield, an iconic character from the series, who is kidnapped and wakes up on a mysterious island. Together with Moira Burton, daughter of the legendary Barry Burton, they must fight to survive and uncover the truth behind their capture. The narrative is well-crafted, full of twists and revelations, keeping players intrigued and eager to discover the next chapter of the story.

The game features classic Resident Evil gameplay, combining action and horror elements. Players alternate between Claire and Moira, each with unique abilities that influence the gameplay. Claire is skilled in combat, while Moira provides support with a flashlight, capable of finding hidden items and temporarily blinding enemies. This dynamic between the two characters adds strategic layers to the game, encouraging cooperation between players in the cooperative mode.

The game's enemies are scary and varied, including zombies, mutated creatures, and other grotesque monsters. The oppressive atmosphere and dark environments accentuate the sense of imminent danger, creating intense moments of tension. The game also presents challenging puzzles that require reasoning and careful exploration of the environment to solve. This combination of combat, exploration, and puzzles keeps players constantly engaged.

The soundtrack of Resident Evil Revelations 2 plays a crucial role in enhancing the atmosphere of suspense and terror. The sound effects are well-executed, increasing immersion and contributing to the sense of fear. The visual quality is also impressive, with crisp and detailed graphics that enhance the dark and terrifying environments.

In addition to the main campaign, the game offers a mode called Raid Mode, which provides an additional gameplay experience. In this mode, players can tackle a series of challenges, earn experience, and unlock new abilities and weapons. The Raid Mode is highly addictive and offers a good dose of replayability for enthusiasts who want to prolong the gameplay experience.

Resident Evil Revelations 2 is an excellent addition to the Resident Evil franchise, offering a blend of thrilling survival horror elements, engaging gameplay, and a compelling storyline. Whether you're a longtime fan of the series or new to the world of Resident Evil, this game is definitely worth experiencing. So grab your flashlight, brace yourself for the horrors that await, and prepare to embark on an unforgettable survival journey.

I am going to be fully honest here, I came to Resident Evil Revelations 2 with a sour taste in my mouth after REALLY disliking Resident Evil Revelations... I have to say... ReR2 is NOTHING like RER. It improves on every single aspect that I hated from ReR. It actually felt like a Resident Evil game from start to finish and the story kept me hooked the entire time. I did not take a break at all... I legit sat and played it for 15.5 hours straight. DOUBLE the time it took me to play ReR... that's saying something. 

[h1][b] Pros [/b][/h1]
⚫The main characters in this game are fantastic. Barry, the father that goes solo and armed to the teeth to find his daughter Moira who went missing 6 months prior. Talk about father of the year award right here.
⚫Playing the game solo was a blast. It felt so good. I was not bored in the slightest.
⚫The story was so interesting from start to finish. "What virus is this?" "Why does this look like the Uroboros Virus?" "How is the little girl able to see them through walls and footprints?"... everything had me hooked.
⚫It does away with the "Scanning" feature from ReR that I despised and replaces it with something that ACTUALLY makes sense. "Its to dark to make out what this object is - use the flashlight". Fantastic improvement. It kept me immersed the entire time and actually prompted me to use Moira much more to look for objects.
⚫It fixes one of the biggest issues from ReR too, the mouse sensitivity. I did not need to adjust it at all in this game. It also did not go super slow when my reticule got close to a target.
⚫The game surprised me at times here and there and it made me jump. Horror was on point.
⚫Graphics are MUCH better than ReR too. No stupidly overstretched polygons on face's/outfits.
⚫Animations were smooth and on point.
⚫Audio was done perfectly for voices and enemies. I could locate the invisible enemies easily.
⚫It has a Raid mode which adds so much more content to play.
⚫Each "Episode" has medals you can earn and collectables to collect which gives the campaign replay-ability. This is rare for most games. Fantastic!! I can go back and have some fun!
⚫Has a pretty sweet soundtrack behind it

[h1][b] Cons [/b][/h1]
⚫Raid/Multiplayer mode is dead. Makes sense though. 
⚫The game is NOT online-COOP. It is couch COOP sadly.
⚫You have to buy the game in "Episodes". If I buy a game I want all of it.
⚫It has the same "Episodic" transitions as ReR. I despise this as it goes "PREVIOUSLY ON RER2"... I am right here you know... playing it... maybe only do it if I come off the game and go back on to remind me.

[h1][b] My Verdict [/b][/h1]
Resident Evil Revelations 2 improves on almost EVERY single negative aspect of ReR drastically and for this... its 100% got my positive review. A solid survival horror experience here that sticks true to the Resident Evil franchise.

Compared to its predecessor:[list]
[*]Even more atmospheric and creepy.
[*]Better, slower gameplay, and higher enemy variety, without such dramatic shifts like in Rev1's flashbacks, so it's more consistent.
[*]Dodging that's just a button press instead of requiring vague conditions to execute. Dodge animation was reused in Resident Evil 3 Remake.
[*]Music just as good, if not better, than in its predecessor.
[*]Contrary to Revelations 1, which could be very corny at times, its sequel is one of the least goofy ones, while being simultaneously one of the bleakest in the series. The story is better written than most of the franchise. It even touches upon issues like gun ownership and presents them in both positive and negative light, sparking discussion. The relationship between Barry and Natalia (similar to The Last of Us), as well as Barry himself, are the highlights of the story.[/list]

New features:[list]
[*]Re-introduced the A/B scenarios where A can influence B. It’s more meaningful than RE2 Remake’s A/B at any point.
[*]Coop in lieu of RE0, but done in a way that doesn't make you want to shoot yourself. 
[*]Stealth kill mechanic, which seems borrowed from The Evil Within, and returned in RE4 Remake.
[*]Invisible and Countdown modes are challenge modes: they aren't much fun to be honest, but do provide a good challenge. Barry gets the short end of the stick since his episodes 3 & 4 are significantly harder than Claire's. The AI in Invisible mode can be either very helpful, or completely useless, nothing in between. It can really make your blood boil. Finished both modes, got the achievements, never gonna touch them again.
[*]Two endings, though getting the good one requires performing an action so counter-intuitive that many people, including multiple professional reviewers, assumed that the bad ending was the only one.[/list]

It's a major improvement over Rev1 in virtually all aspects. I think it's forgotten about since it's a spin off (though canonical). Well worth the purchase.

:edit:

Now that I think about it:[list] 
[*]Resident Evil 3 Remake copied the dodge mechanic and animation,
[*]Resident Evil 4 Remake copied the stealth system,
[*]Resident Evil Village copied most of Barry's story...[/list]

The resource management and limited ammunition further intensify the sense of vulnerability, keeping players on the edge of their seats.

[h2]Replayability[/h2]
Resident Evil Revelations 2 offers replayability through its varied gameplay modes and multiple difficulty levels. The game features a cooperative multiplayer mode, allowing you to team up with a friend for a thrilling and challenging co-op experience. Anyway, the game isn't awful. Some people might enjoy it to some extent. It's just a very bland and rather soulless experience that never felt like a part of RE franchise. Maybe except for that one "master of unlocking" reference... 

First, the environments. There isn't much encouragement for exploration, just a few items here and there. So you just rush forward without enjoying the sights - not like there is much to enjoy, though, since locations are incredibly generic. You've seen the same type in many, many other games, but likely done much better. They all look so... barren. Especially some outside areas where you sometimes have some huge block-y chunks of rocks, a handful of trees and a few assets scattered around. It feels low effort and so. uninspired. I suppose that level art team was as bored of these environments as I was. Incredible.
 
The enemies are also painfully uninteresting. Some over-designed psycho guys that look like they are trying too hard to be scary, but are just annoying. Some under-designed zombies that are as scary as a sleeping puppy. And then some other monsters that are at least semi-funny when glitching through solid objects and doing unintended dance moves when prompted. Combat isn't awful, though feels somewhat inconsistent (like 2-3 enemies in a row dying from a single headshot, but next enemy of the exact same type tanking 4-5 headshots without even a stagger). 
I'm also not a fan of how enemies are forced to be "scary" by just appearing all of sudden. Like the very first enemy which appears from literal nowhere. It just cheapens the experience. 

At least the music sort of tried to get somewhere, although it never reached any true heights either. I did hear strong inspiration from Silent Hill games, though - so at least ONE thing tried to get inspirations from an old classic in horror genre. Cause I sure didn't notice inspirations from other leading horror titles... Nothing like - what was the name...? "Bad House"? No, no, it went something like "Vile Village". Or wait, was it... "Not-a-good Mansion"? Hmm, no, I cannot recall. But neither can the developers, apparently.  

The story had some potential, though. I'll give it that, at least.

I've also attempted to like this game twice. First played a couple of years ago, didn't like it, really wanted to like it, so I gave it another go now. But nope, still as bland as I remember. Or to be exact, I remembered nothing. I was playing it for the second time and constantly thinking "Wait, I have never seen this before. Have I? No, no, impossible". And then realizing that yes, I did see it all, because I have the completed save files, so the heck. And mind you, I'm normally the type of person who can recall details in favourite games dozen of years after playing it. So. Yeah.

Still, for anyone who managed to enjoy this game, good on you. People should enjoy games they buy. But for me, it will likely be the first RE game that I will never finish. Not like it's much of a RE title in the first place though.

Resident Evil Revelations 2 is a very good survival/horror game, the story takes place between Resident Evil 5 and 6. The game will make you play Claire Redfield again but also Barry Burton and approaches a new story with several references to the previous games.

Like the first Revelations, this game is more focused on the story than the other opuses, with many cutscenes and a more advanced scenario. The game is again divided like a series, with episodes (chapters) and summaries at the end of each of them. The story is quite intriguing and the horrific atmosphere is very successful, reminding sometimes The Evil Within.

The new thing in that game is that you can now switch from one character to another manually, allowing you to play up to 4 characters. Each character has its own abilities and its own inventory, so you have to switch between them regularly to progress in the game. There is like in the first one, the weapon upgrade system, you can now also improve the skills of your characters and craft different items.

In conclusion I recommend the game to any fan of the license, this game brings a new style of game to the license and the gameplay and the story are very pleasant.
If you are looking for a survival horror and you are not familiar with the license, I recommend you to start with the first games before doing this one in order to have all the references and to better understand the story.

Imho, one of the best RE games for a relatively low price. With graphics that still somewhat hold up. The only RE game I've disliked so far was RE5, just too clunky and boring, despite the epic cutscenes and fights against Wesker. I'm glad though that they went with the gameplay from this and similar RE games for their remakes.

The game is split into 4 episodes with 2 "campaigns" each. One is Claire and Moira, the other is Barry and Natalia. In both campaigns the first character is the one that does all the shooting, while the 2nd one is necesary to complete puzzles, open chests or find hidden objects, but otherwise doesn't do anything, which is a bit of wasted potential.

The campaigns each take about 1 to 1.5 hours to complete with the exception of 4.1, which - for some reason - is only about 5 to 10 minutes long ... very weird decision. 4.2 is much longer then to make up for it, I guess.
Story and characters themselves are mostly okay, though Moira's swearing gets irritating soon enough. I get that she's a young rebel kind of gal, but damn, she was just about to start her job at Terra Save, but honestly she behaves like a 15 year old brat. 

Gameplay wise it's smooth. The gunplay is good, the variety is what you'd expect from an RE game, the upgrade system is the same as in Revelations 1, just a bit smoother, like everything really. You can run and gun so to speak, you can sneak, you can backstab and insta kill enemies, you can still kick them in the face. Inventory management is mostly manageable.

The only thing that really sours the whole are the 2 DLCs, which aren't worth playing (or paying for), but they're part of the package, so whatever. Moira's DLC gives you more insight into what happened between chapters 4.1 and 4.2, and is basically a wave-based scavenging mode, where you have to hunt and look for ammo, then fight off hordes of enemies. Very boring, timed missions with a potential game over that has you start from the very beginning (or you can get soft locked into an impossible situation as well). Natalia's DLC bridges the gap between chapters 4.1 and 1.2, if I remember correctly, and is one big, long, irritating, trial and error stealth mission with instant failure states, but at least with decent check points. Still. Also not worth playing, since you don't really get any interesting story out of it. 

Ultimately, as a package, it's probably the best of the old RE games that you can still play on modern hardware. Or maybe the best of both worlds: Old game with still decently modern mechanics, as opposed to the really old games and the newly made remakes or the 1st person Winters duology. Well worth playing.

Best 'modern' RE game. Keeps many horror elements in play, yet still is an action game. Movement is responsive and clean, with a great dodge mechanic. Points from completion encourage replays, as you can replay the base game with new unlocks such as longer dodge I-frame windows, or more melee speed/damage. Weapon upgrades are both limited, and exclusive based on type, so do you put in the high damage on your pistol to save the most ammo, or on the magnum to delete bosses? Scavenging for items feels in line with the game, and you can have excessive ammo if you search every corner, or just enough ammo even if you barely touch the mechanic. Feels good and rewarding without being fully required (outside of harder difficulties maybe). Invisible enemy and Countdown modes encourage further replays, as extensive knowledge of enemy placement and routing are rewarded. Raid mode is a decent enough Mercenaries equivalent, and even allows online with a friend. The loot is a bit stingy though, and the xp/gold is somewhat grindy. For an action game, this feels the most like RE. Personally I would rate the action game REs accordingly Rev2 > 4 > 5 > Remake 2 > 6 > Rev1 > All other RE engine games. I enjoy all of these as action games (other than the RE engine games), but Rev2 feels the most like a classic RE game with a fun action game polish.

Probably the most aggressively mid Resident Evil out there - literally, now that I think about it. This comes smack dab in the middle from the dark ages of the RE franchise where Capcom wasn't sure if it was a horror or action series. The story is as dumb as any of RE4, 5, and 6's, but with way less bombastic action and intuitive controls - simultaneously, the "survival" """horror""" aspect is so rudimentary that it feels route. 

One of the stranger aspects of the game is the fact that it's episodic - which, now that all the episodes are out, adds absolutely nothing to the experience. Having two sets of survivors you play as only adds a minimal amount of mechanical intrigue - you go back to places you've been before and now can open things you couldn't! And something about killing certain enemies in one campaign affecting the other, but you'll be shooting them dead regardless so it doesn't matter all that much. 

The story consists exclusively of cheap fanservice - and it's not all bad. It is a genuine delight to see Barry back in action. If you [i]really[/i] care about the plot elements of Resident Evil 5 and 6, there's plenty of references to that too - but in a day and age where those games are a bad memory, it's more grating than anything else. Don't worry, it's a spinoff, so nothing that happens in this game will ever be acknowledged by the series again!

I don't plan on playing much more of Raid mode, but it has it's fans and is probably the best reason to pick this game up. 

The PC version doesn't even have co-op (split screen or otherwise) like the consoles, so you don't even get to have the "fun with friends" experience. 

Revelations 2 ironically feels like a mutant science experiment being pushed out on an unsuspecting public. Capcom evidently wanted to see how they could push Resident Evil forward without any commitments, and it shows. Horror without horror. Story without stakes. Episodic content without --- well, episodic content never really had a good reason to exist. 

RE series completionists need only apply.

Review for: Resident Evil Revelations 2 Deluxe Edition Bundle
Played on: Casual & Normal Difficulty

Resident Evil Revelations 2 is a fantastic entry into the franchise, returning to the B-Movie story lines and schlocky dialogue that the original games are best remembered for. There's still plenty of action to be had but exploration and resource management are usually emphasised over straight combat. 

The main campaign lasts around 6-8 hours and consists of 4 episode split into two chapters each. The first chapter of each episode follows Claire and Moira with a larger focus on horror, whilst the second chapter with Barry and Natalia tends towards being more action heavy. 

While Claire and Barry act as the main 'combat character' for each of there respective chapters, with Moira and Natalia are taking up support roles. The game-play is at it's best when splitting up the characters to make use of their unique abilities. While Moira is able to blind enemies with her flash-light and open barred doors with her crowbar, Natalia can craw into small gaps in the wall and sense nearby enemies, which often comes in useful for a stealthy approach or spotting enemy weak points. Both support characters can also spot hidden objects and are needed to find collectables hidden throughout the game.

The game looks fine graphically, and there isn't much to say about the sound design. There are some performance issues at times (normally when loading into a new area), but there's a mod that can help with that and it's never so bad as to make the game unplayable. At worst it's a minor annoyance which is quickly forgotten.

Although the story-line (never a strong point with Resident Evil games) is nothing special, the locations are mostly forgettable and the enemies aren't anything amazing, it's a definite step-up from the first revelations games.

There's a lot of fun to be had here, and a good amount of replay value on offer. Actions in Claire's Campaign impact on Barry's and there are two campaign endings on offer. Each of the main campaign's episodes offer 4 difficulties, with 2 additional game modes (Countdown and Invisible Enemies), in addition to a range of challenges (Medals and Records) and collectables (Kafka Drawings, Insect Larva and Tower Emblems).

At the conclusion of each chapter the player is awarded with BP which can be used to unlock new player skills, or spent on new campaign skills, Figurines, Concept Art, Costumes, Weapons, Screen Filters and more.

Raid mode is the real highlight here though offering some serious longevity outside the main campaign. The progression feels fair, especially with the rest bonus and daily challenge mechanics. There's plenty of maps, characters, weapons, weapon parts and skills to unlock, with a much larger variety of enemies to be found than in the main campaign.

The gist: This is a good game. It's not great, but it has some really solid scares, nicely replayable, but needs to be bought all at once. The episode gimmick is just that -- a gimmick.

Gameplay:
Revelations 2 not only has cooperative capability, but it also allows you to switch between the characters if you're playing solo similarly to RE0. The good thing is that this mechanic is implemented in a fun and unique way with little to no wait between switching characters. The bad is that I can't imagine this is super fun as a co-op simply because each character has different abilities and weapons. Claire and Barry get knives and a collection of firearms (with each having different firearms) while Natalia is able to see enemies and throw bricks and Moira is armed with a crowbar and flashlight to blind enemies. Natalia's powers are much more necessary overall than Moira's flashlight, honestly. You can go the entire game without blinding anyone.
Another thing to note is that Claire's campaign is much more horror-action oriented while Barry's is centered more on stealth and puzzles. This is really cool but something to be aware of.
There's also quite a lot of potential glitches. They're mostly visual  (like an item falling and not disappearing) and won't impair gameplay, but Revelations 2 certainly doesn't have that final polish.
The Story:
The story quality is honestly a little confusing and half-baked. Claire in this is often called "mischaracterized" which I'll agree with. Moira comes off as very annoying at the beginning for her refusal to use guns in a life-threatening situation (Claire seems to know why, but the player does not find out until a few chapters in,) and honestly? She curses way too much. It gets really cheesy.
Both campaigns start out straightforward. Claire and Moira want to escape, and Barry wants to find his daughter. This gets more convoluted with the addition of the Overseer (no spoilers, but the twist isn't implemented smoothly, and it's kind of a disappointing use of the character), T-Phobos, effing Neil, and the relationship between Moira and Barry (it's tense) and Natalia and the Overseer (it's creepy).
While the game doesn't deliver the story in a clean and polished way, I do believe that the story is very fun overall with a lot of cool scares and interesting puzzles. The DLC stories are also great to fill in some of the gaps in the main campaign.
I also have to mention that this game has two endings. The choice that decides your ending though? Happens in Claire's part of the forth chapter, so if you get an ending you didn't want? You have to replay both chapters to get the other ending. It's pointlessly sneaky and not even a good "twist" though it makes sense from a character perspective.
The End?:
I really do love this game despite my issues with it and the flaws. Particularly if you can grab all the chapters and DLCs on sale, get it! It gets massively reduced, and I've had a lot of fun with it.

Highly balanced difficulty. Some challenges, you can expect to die. Capcom won't let you off easy here.
Supports multiple playstyles. You can do a no-ammo run, for example, and it's not like some endless knife dodging. Alt characters use unique weapons systems, or you can just go ahead and fire away.
Difficulty is highly tuneable. If you're scared of dying/difficult games, put it on easy or normal mode and you get unlimited ammo. If you want a Resident Evil-style challenge, select the hardest difficulty instead. The hardest difficulty is still playable and gives a respectable challenge, without being some darksoulsesque gimmick.
Diverse assortment of enemies to fight.

Cons:
Easy and normal difficulty are both unlimited ammo. You get around 40 rounds of ammo for every enemy in the game under these modes, and enemies only take something like 3 - 10 bullets to kill. Within minutes you cap out on available ammunition with full magazines. 
Hard difficulty replaces ammunition drops with perk currency to tailor the game to your preferred playstyle. It unintentionally gives you a better experience, but a lot of people pass over the hard difficulty by just being intimidated by the concept. Hard mode is the actual way this game was designed. Easy and Normal modes are bugged, and they are not the version that was initially released. They give you too much ammo, and enemies die almost instantly. It's not fun, compelling, or Resident Evil at that point. This is a con because it's not implied or intuitive, and can lead players to a poor experience under normal circumstances. If you don't select the hardest difficulty, the game is going to look and play very stupid. You can be armed with a paintbrush and one-shot bosses by just walking into them.
The graphics are inconsistent. Some parts of the game look like a 2003 flash from the past, others look like modern gaming. It's kind of weird.

[h1]A good Shooter-Survival and a good RE : Spin off[/h1]
[h1]Score : 70%[/h1]

[b]Summary [/b]

Resident Evil Revelations 2 was supposed to grant the series a big breath of fresh air while returning to the Survival Horror gender.
Well... even if we are still far away from the survival, the game is proposing very interesting concepts like the constant double character and the possibly to switch between each other’s to unlock path or gameplay options and the return of stealth.

We can finally play again with Claire Redfield which was absent from resident Evil since Code Veronica (can't wait for the remake - there's rumors it's in preparation) which sadly fall AGAIN into an island and in a prison (very unlucky girl).


[b]Gameplay[/b]

The game proposes a good level design but mainly linear as it's trying to tell us a story, which can be annoying for some players but the good news is that there's a bit of exploration and back-tracking in order to max-out your points and equipment.

The multiple options and the come-back of the gun upgrades system from the first Revelations title is a strong combination and being able to find objects using the flashlight from Moira or the superior vision from Natalia is far better than the scanner system from Revelations 1.

Shooting is classic for such TPS configuration but it's great fun and you will have to be careful on your ammunitions !
 

[b]Character design[/b]

All characters of the game received great attention on their mindset / story / dialogues, from Claire to Barry passing by Moira and finishing with Natalia.
Even the main villain: Alex [spoiler] Wesker [/spoiler] have a good treatment.

I would just pass a word on facial animations which are a under what we would expect from a 2015 game but as we are not every time looking at our partner or our own face it's really a side point.

Enemy variety is superior to Revelations 1 but still too low. We have around 4 different enemies’ types (7/8 if we count the 4 from Barry's side) with very little different model numbers.

[b]Music[/b]

Once again Capcom and Kota Suzuki offer us a great composition of excellent quality, it was expected considering the work from Kota Suzuki on resident Evil 5 and 6!


[b]Engine[/b]

Game graphics are quite good for a side resident evil entry and the game is well optimized.

Hair work is absolutely fantastic in my opinion (especially on Claire).
Animations are great, moving with our character is feeling good, not clunky and there's even a bit of " gun security awareness " while selecting your pistol.

Nevertheless, some textures seem to have received less effort from the designers or have been re-used from the console versions as their definition is far inferior from others.
There's also some texture pop-in from background and light problems on some box objects appearing.
Effects are below 2015 standards.

And i which we had more options in the graphics menu as the game is having a big problem with " film grain " making some moments looking like an ant colony on your screen more than a pitch-black room.


[b]Conclusion[/b]

Resident Evil: Revelations 2 is a good game with a good life-span playing only the 4 episodes (even more if you play in commando mode, raid mode, extra episodes and new game+) and is worth for the experience he is delivering as well for being able to see Claire and [spoiler]Chad[/spoiler] Barry again in a Resident Evil game. Not necessary for " main games " plot but really cool for RE storyline fans!

RESIDENT EVIL REVELATIONS 2 is an awesome game, and it really feels like a direct follow-up to not only Revelations 1, but also Resident Evil 5.

Revelations 2 officially returns RE2 star Claire Redfield, also introducing her new partner-in-horror, Moira Burton, daughter of Barry Burton. Barry & Moira's relationship is... definitely far from even the slightest of good, but there's a big reason why and I won't be spoiling it for you. 

When I said Claire & Moira are "partners in horror", I don't mean in an agency like the BSAA or anything, I mean they get wrapped up in a messy nightmare, and they are placed together.

Revelations 2 carries over the episodic gameplay of Revelations 1, but also introduces a double-campaign per episode. There is the Claire & Moira campaign, and then the Barry & [mystery character I won't spoil] campaign. These campaigns take place in the same areas, on the same island (that's not a spoiler is it?), but at two different times. Even though these campaign's play during two different time frames, each one reveals info about the other, which I think is an awesome way to reveal lore and Revelations 2 does it extremely well.

Revelations 2 mechanically plays basically the same as Revelations 1, which feels really nice and plays well. Although, Revelations 2's sprint button is odd to me, and I had to end up swapping the sprint & sub-weapon buttons. Of course this comes down to personal preference, though.

Revelations 2 feels like a direct sequel to Revelations 1, which is great, but Capcom also made a main plot-point be a follow-up to Resident Evil 5, and they do it very well. There are many mentions to the events of the first Revelations, and the main villain of this game heavily follows after Resident Evil 5. Of course, this means the player would have to play both Revelations & RE5, but they are both great games in my opinion, so I recommend doing it before you hop into Revelations 2.

Compared to the first Revelations' 12 episodes & numerous sub-chapters, Revelations 2 plays through 4 episodes with 2 sub-chapters each. Revelations 2's episodes all run longer than Revelations 1! The game comes out about the same length as the first overall, at least for me, but it feels more streamlined as there aren't so many episodic endings & beginnings like Revelations 1 had.

Overall, Revelations 2 was awesome & it feels like a direct follow-up to both Revelations 1 AND Resident Evil 5.

I'm honestly not sure if I prefer Revelations 1 or Revelations 2, but I won't ponder on that thought for too long. All that matters to me is that I enjoyed them both a lot, and Resident Evil Revelations is an awesome RE Side-Series. (Revelations 3 when, Capcom?)

Revelations 2 is a very polarising experience, and I sympathize with fans of the series in February of 2015 who had the pleasure of waiting for this mediocre story to drag on for four weeks with its episodic format which was a prevalent trend within gaming at the time. The game follows a split narrative between two pairs of characters: Claire Redfield with Moira Burton and Moira's father series veteran Barry Burton with a young girl Natalia six months after the events of Claire and Moira's segments.

Revelations 2 is so frustrating because in concept it does sound intriguing, sure we have seen Claire Redfield trapped on an island with bio-organic weapons before in Code Veronica, but in this case, the inclusion of a new young and vulnerable side protagonist in Moira Burton should add a new layer of tension, also upon the opening segments the story seems to be neglecting the series bloated and often abhorrent lore in favor of a more self-contained narrative, however upon the games third chapter it, unfortunately, falls back into familiar territory with a cringe-worthy reveal that the games "overseer" character is the sister of series main antagonist Albert Wesker, because of course she is why wouldn't she be? this series has showcased an innate insecurity to deviate from the original umbrella corporation trilogy even as far back as Resident Evil 4 with its bonus separate ways segment featuring Ada Wong and Albert Wesker respectively. Even the likes of the soft reboot that was Resident Evil 7 Biohazard and Its sequel Resident Evil 8 Village have struggled to neglect the series' absurd narrative with the forced inclusion of Chris Redfield in Biohazard's conclusion, then transitioning into main character territory with Village. honestly, I just must ask how old are these guys? The outbreak at Racoon City was in 1998, yes? For how much longer must Capcom drag out these legacy characters that might I add weren't particularly interesting in the first place, for little more than cheap fan service?

Rant aside, the gameplay here seems to be a lot more interesting than its predecessor with its split between two player characters however, I must state that playing this game exclusively as player 2 must be no fun at all with no offensive attack options aside from an iron bar for Moira and laughably a brick for Natalia. Of the two campaigns I would have to say Barry's segments are the more fun to play with some interesting level design involving the two characters cooperating through environmental challenges as well as some stealth segments in which Natalia can spot enemies for Barry, some of these incorporate invisible flying enemies that distort the player's vision, I have to say that these were awesome! And I would love an enemy like this returning in the series' future but with more speed and aggressiveness. 

The game's worst aspect is undoubtedly some of its horrible dialogue, I am not being dramatic when I say that some of the lines in this game are the worst, I have ever heard particularly from Moira who while likable in some cases resorts to using the most awkward combination of swear words imaginable, especially after a particular boss fight, just in general the frequency of swear words used feels so strange and out of place. 

The game features two endings, which one you receive is entirely based upon one choice at the end of a boss fight, the "good" choice ties into Moira's tragic backstory and trauma tying into the themes of the game which leads me to ask why this is a choice? and not simply a mandatory cutscene/quick-time event, especially considering how underwhelming the "bad" ending is. the game has two dlc one featuring Moira and a new character that feels like a fun action gauntlet that also expands upon the story with Moira filling in some noticeable gaps in the main plot, the next dlc featuring Natalia while interesting in premise with Alex Wesker manifesting herself as a dark version of Natalia feels awful to play as it is stealth-based…. for a game that is not built for stealth. Finally, the raid mode here has a substantial amount of content and from the little, I have played I can confidently state that it is a vast improvement from the original and is great fun in short bursts.

In conclusion, while a strange game in both premise and execution, I would recommend Revelations 2 to any fan of the franchise as it ultimately isn't a half-bad action horror game.

Resident Evil Revelations 2 is a really enjoyable experience that delivers a strong story, solid gameplay, and great atmosphere, even if it doesn’t fully surpass the first game.

The biggest highlight here is the story. It’s more engaging, emotional, and mysterious compared to the first Revelations, with better characters and a much more interesting villain like Alex Wesker. Playing as Claire Redfield again was great, and the dynamic between her and Moira, along with Barry and Natalia’s side of the story, kept things interesting throughout.

Gameplay is good, but it has its problems. The addition of stealth, a skill tree, and more puzzles is a nice improvement, and I enjoyed how each character has a unique role. However, combat feels less satisfying than the first game, and enemies aren’t as engaging or threatening. The map system is also pretty confusing, which made exploration frustrating at times.

Visually, the game looks great for its time, and the environments and character models still hold up well. The sound design is also strong, with great voice acting and music that enhances both the emotional and intense moments.

Replayability is decent, with Raid Mode, extra content, and DLC episodes like “The Struggle” and “Little Miss.” That said, I personally didn’t feel a strong reason to replay the game after finishing it once.

Overall, Resident Evil Revelations 2 is a solid Resident Evil title. It may not be as fun gameplay-wise as the first game, but its strong story and characters make it worth playing.

When I found out that RE had once again theirs games in sale, I just couldn't REsist. I am a big RE fan, so I was incredibly hyped. I bought the game and started playing. I set my hopes high, due to Resident Evil Revelations being my personal favourite Resident Evil game. The beginning of the game felt like a huge disappointment. Claire was there, which was cool, but Moira...well, let's say that I firstly was truly annoyed whenever she would open her mouth. She felt like a stereotypical teenager (even though she isn't, since she's working for the company where Claire also works). By time I got used to her and at the end, I even was liking her. Just a little bit xd. The premise of the story didn't amaze me, an average okay rating would be fitting, but I definitely liked the gameplay. After playing RE6, this actually made me feel, like I was playing Resident Evil once again. Though I did have thoughts of bringing back that slide mechanic when running and pressing the right mouse button xd. It wasn't scary, but it gave off some of those creepy vibes. That marionette type of enemy (if you played the game, you know what I am talking about) would give me the heebie jeebies every time they'd show up. Those two story lines at first didn't make sense to me (The Claire story line and the Barry story line), but after what came during the final 20 minutes, it all clicked perfectly. I must say, that even if I like Claire, as much as I do, Barry's story line was more fun, scary and overall much more Resident Evil-ly. I especially liked Natalia's ability to sense monsters. This turned out to be usefull and it made an unique gameplay. Claire story line has also some great moments. Alex Wesker was a greatly designed antigonist that could be coming back soon. I loved the references to Kafka's The Metamorphosis. I don't know why, but Revelations has these book related references. The first game uses Dante Alighieri's The Divine Comedy, and the second one uses Franz Kafka's The Metamorphosis. As a Czech, this brings a smile to my face. The end was outstanding, I haven't enjoyed a finale like that for a really long period of time. The defeat of Alex, the daughter of Albert Wesker (Albert - one of the best villains in gaming history), was ended in a classic RE fashion with a rocket launcher. It felt amazing. 
To summarize it all, the game started with various emtions of love and hate, halved emotions to be specific, but ended with joy and happiness, peace and tranquility. Even if the game started nightmarish, I fully enjoyed the scary middle and the dope ending with the grotesque metamorphosis. 
A Kafkaesque experience. 7.75/10

Resident Evil Revelations 2 is the first truly fantastic Resident Evil game to come out since Resident Evil 4, however despite three other games coming out since the release and many improvements being made since then, Revelations 2 is still not without some major glaring problems.

(First of all, and I need to get this out of the way, please stop putting "Previously On..." cut-scenes in video games. They supplement absolutely nothing and are annoying to have come up any time I boot a level.)

Annoyances aside, onto the Campaign mode; starring Claire Redfield and Moira Burton for one half of the game and Barry Burton and Natalia for the other half, the Campaign mode is structured in the same manner as Revelations 1 where the missions frequently make jumps in the timeline between the past and present events. I feel that they did a better job with this in the sequel because in Revelations 1, I found that some of the flashbacks where a bit confusing at first and hard to follow, but in Revelations 2, they decided to simplify it to just a six month jump back and forth each mission. I find this to be a major improvement gameplay-wise as well because in the previous game when playing as any character other than Jill Valentine, the game gives you preset weapons and ammo which makes the game a bit of a chore to play through on new game+ since Jill is the only character that can use the overpowered post-game weapons. This was fixed in the sequel since the story focuses on two characters who use guns whom of which share weapon unlocks.

Speaking of characters, some of the new ones introduced I have a few problems with. Moira for example I think they tried way too hard to write like a Borderlands character, swearing every other sentence that utters from her mouth, and her chemistry with Claire is about as interesting as dog water. In the story they also introduce three other supporting characters, named Pedro, Gabe, and Neil, three members of a non-governmental human rights agency named TerraSave, who have very little personality between the three of them and you may quickly forget about unless you've beaten the game seven different times to unlock everything like I have. One of the trio they even try to imply some kind of romantic interest between him and Claire, which I didn't think made any sense. We all know the only man to continue the Redfield bloodline is Leon. On the brighter side however, the chemistry Barry and Natalia share as a sort of father/daughter relationship was really sweet, and seeing the two of them interact with each other was probably a highlight of the game for me.

To speak more specifically on the gameplay, it's a major improvement on the past three games. Where Revelations 1 takes many steps in the right direction for the series, Revelations 2 takes it a step even further. Instead of having a scanner to tediously scan every corner of the room for pickups, they've streamlined the process by having the partner character see sparkles on their screen and be able to point at it to be able to be picked up. And speaking of the partner mechanics? Revelations 2 puts much more emphasis on "cooperation" which I would argue on one side makes the game less fun as a co-op game since only one character can shoot guns, (but then again you could just play raid mode) but on the other I would say the gameplay and puzzle mechanics are much more tightly designed than Resident Evil 5 and Resident Evil 6, especially considering the fact that you can switch between characters on the fly instead of having them awkwardly follow you around and make you question why they're even there during gameplay. However this brings me to one of the first major problems I have with this game, which is the lack of any online co-op for the main campaign. Why Capcom decided to go down this route is beyond me since this would be an extremely fun co-op game. There's couch co-op for console and lan for computer, but the neglect of an online co-op option is just baffling...

Another problem I have with this game is Capcom's manipulative advertising practices for this game. A lot of people who have bought this game bought it without knowing they were only buying episode one and the rest of the episodes were in the DLC section for the store page. This was especially telling since the first episode was always the episode to get the biggest discounts. I think Capcom has since realized this and made sure the episodes are all discounted evenly, but to this day, they still have yet to replace the episode one purchase link on the literal top of the purchase section with the full game bundle. Early-Mid 2010s Capcom was quite quirky like that.

As for Raid Mode, I thought it was a little disappointing. It's basically the same mode as it ever was in Revelations 1 with a bit more depth, and more characters. In this mode you'll be fighting either enemies from Revelations 2, RE6, or an Executioner Majini from RE5 in locations based on Revelations 2 and RE6. That's it. Personally I think they could have added so much more to this mode, such as El Pueblo from RE4, the Town Assembly from RE5 or more variety in enemies would have been nice as well, like the Chainsaw Majini, El Gigante, Regenerator, etc.

To close, Resident Evil Revelations 2 is a great game. Flawed, but the least flawed in regards to the previous titles post-Resident Evil 4. Don't go into this expecting a fun co-op game with a friend though, unless you want to play Raid Mode, in which case you're good. Definitely worth playing.

Yes, it was claustrophobic at times, but it still didn't feel like that much of a horror survival game.

With RER2, the story is intriguing and has me guessing. I'm only into episode 3 (of 4), but so far, the game play has been excellent, the tension high, and the I'm getting completely immersed into the story. Also, this game definitely rewards on stealth in various areas. Also, exploring the areas definitely rewards you in more items you can use on your adventure. And it is creepy. Not necessarily scary like say RE1 or RE2, but the creep factor is high in this one. RER1 the monsters were not scary, and just didn't really intrigue me at all. Here, there are are a more variety of enemies in this game IMHO than in RER1 and they are definitely disturbing at times.

Yes it has a tag along player, but the AI does seem better than in RE5 and 6. Also, you can easily switch between the two, and unlike RE 0, the inventory management is much better, and there are strengths and weaknesses in using both. In fact, for me, a lot of the fun in the game was discovering when to use each characters.

You play as Claire Redfield and as Moria, Barry Burton's daughter. When you get through their story, you switch over to Barry Burton and he teams up with a little girl, Natalia. Again, between the two, there are strengths and weaknesses and certain areas you learn when to use one or the other, and then switching is pretty easy as well. It didn't take me long to figure out when to use one character over another and I enjoy the dynamics it provides to the game play. For example, with Natalia, she has the ability to sense enemies that are not seen but close by. I can then switch to Barry once I know where they are and sneak around to see where they are. If I can sneak up behind them, it's an easy stealth kill. With Moria, if you can get Claire to knock the enemy down to the grown, Moria with her crow bar can do a killing blow. It's this dynamic and ability to switch between characters and utilize their strengths that makes the game play and battling the enemies enjoyable.

The graphics are definitely an upgrade from the first Revelations game. Of course, from RE 7, RE 2 and 3 Remakes, and RE Village, there is no comparison. This would be a major downgrade, but they are still pretty impressive and the sets are definitely creepy, as is the music.

The controls are pretty responsive for me and I haven't really ran into any glaring glitches. There are some boss fights that are tough, but learning the weaknesses helps. I definitely feel the controls in this game are much better and feel more responsive than in the first Revelations game.

As you collect items and do certain actions, you can earn BP that can then be spent to increase various skills across the 4 characters you can control. You can upgrade after you finish one story in an episode, or after exiting the game and before loading up where you left off.

Yes, it had some twists in the story, but it never really had me guessing too much. RER2 still has me guessing into episode 3, and there have already been some surprises that shocked me and delighted me. I won't spoil it for those that haven't played yet, but I am so eager to find out how this ends.

I keep returning to this game specifically for Raid mode. The gameplay loop is really fun and addictive, and the monster variety is wide and clever enough to force occasional changes in strategy.
For those looking for a more story-focused experience, the campaign is definitely more of a mixed bag. The setting is interesting, and the parallels the game draws with Kafka's work is compelling at times. However, the attempts to innovate the co-op gameplay fall a bit flat, with companions being endowed with comparatively dull abilities and roles in combat. The core gameplay for the main characters is fundamentally solid, but the constant shift between different characters and backtracking of levels breaks up the pacing and much of the tension. Character dialogue varies significantly in quality. Some characters are quite likeable, believable and seem to show the RE writing style has matured. But then you encounter some characters that are about the same as or worse than previous titles in terms of cheesiness and lack of nuance.
For those in it for a horror experience, while some moments and enemies are visceral, the game isn't especially scary, and it's even less so in co-op. 
Overall, I'd specifically recommend this for fans of RE4/5/et al.-era combat who are looking to scratch that esoteric itch.
