I'm generally not too easy to scare but I did find myself getting caught off guard or a bit apprehensive to enter the next room a few times. I've been playing on the normal difficulty and it feels somewhat forgiving, enemies go down quickly once you learn how to handle them, and I often find myself with more ammo & health than I can carry, though I have the feeling that's going to change as the game progresses and difficulty ramps up. It's not completely linear, there is some backtracking, but definitely not nearing the levels of the Spencer Mansion or RPD where I feel like I could find my way through it blind. It does feel sort of cheesy sometimes, especially when the decor feels like it's just there to be creepy or gross instead of serving any real purpose, but I respect what they're trying to accomplish. I had some issues with slowdown and frame drops, even when I turned down my graphics settings, but that was mostly during transitions and not unbearable. I don't care for the episodic format, it feels out of place to have "Previously on Resident Evil" and "Next time on Resident Evil" like I'm watching a TV drama or anime rather than playing a video game, but all in all, I really do enjoy this and can confidently recommend this to anyone looking for a good late-night, lights down, headphones on kind of game. [h1][i]"God... You owe me a pair of underpants"[/i][/h1]
[i]Resident Evil Revelations 2[/i] is an episodic survival horror and a two-player split screen co-op game. You can play four different characters; Barry, Claire, Moira and Natalie. I have to mention that I didn’t like the first game; it was bland, the writing was bad and the enemies were generic, so I stopped playing it halfway through. Because of that, my expectations were low for the sequel. Just finished it and it is far better than its predecessor.

[h3]Pros:[/h3]
✔️ [b][u]Creative co-op:[/u][/b] Player 1 uses weapons to blast zombies and monsters, while Player 2 doesn't use any, but has special abilities which helps Player 1 solve puzzles and defeat monsters. Too bad it’s just local, not online, so it’s splitscreen. 
✔️ [b][u]Fun gameplay:[/u][/b] Like any [i]Resident Evil[/i] game, the gunplay is solid,melee combat is fun, and it is satisfying to headshot zombies. 
✔️ [b][u]Good replay value:[/u][/b] you can collect guns from the campaign, find and shoot plates to get more guns, three different difficulty levels that you can get an S-rank on. There is also the excellent Raid mode, a run-and-gun where you can play and upgrade different characters with their own special abilities and weapons.
✔️ [b][u]Graphics aged well:[/u][/b] It’s a 2014 game, certainly not the most beautiful game, but it still looks good.
✔️ [b][u]Excellent soundtrack:[/u][/b] The songs are pretty good, especially in the raids, they are an adrenaline rush.

[h3]Cons:[/h3]
❌ [b][u]Average storyline and bland writing:[/u][/b] According to the other steam reviews, the story is “one the best” and “ amazing”. Not sure what they were smoking when they wrote that, but the story is okay at best, and the writing is cringe. If you are aiming to buy the game only because of the story then you’ll be disappointed. 
❌ [b][u]Not scary:[/u][/b] let’s be frank, the new [i]Resident Evil[/i] games aren’t scary to begin with, that is until they released [i]Resident Evil 7[/i]. To be fair, it made me jump once (it was quiet and an enemy came out of nowhere).

***First, I would like to thank my dear friend, Bachito, for gifting me the game.***

Game Mechanics & Ideas:
I really enjoyed the game. If I would to rate it out of 10, I will give it a 10 simply because the flow of the game was very smooth & not super complicated to follow. The storyline was also very nice & unique. The characters of the game have also contributed in making each of them have his/her own style & benefits to their partners. Furthermore, the Weapons' mechanics, sound, & power are all very balanced. In addition to that, the weapons that were given to each of the characters fit perfectly to their style & specialization. The inventory was unique & very easy to manage. I liked mixing the items to get a final product & the idea of Sub-Weapons was also very creative. Now for the controls of this game, I can't say anything other than it was AWESOME! Why? Because you can move & shoot, dodge, crouch, switch weapons really fast, & the upgrades allows you to enhance your weapons & there are also skills that you can buy to enhance your characters' ability to accomplish things at a better rate/speed.

Graphics: 
The graphics are very nice & detailed. They did NOT put a filter that removes away the true colours which is a good idea. The visuals & mapping design is very creative & not super complex. For me, I really liked it as it seemed to have the same style of "Resident Evil 4". The glow, colour saturation, details, shadows, lighting, environments (Ground/Tunnels/Inside/outside/Houses/Sewage), are all PERFECTLY well made!

CONS:
- Bosses are very fast for their magnificent size. 
- They can instant kill you right away. It's a little bit confusing. 
- Understanding current game "Objectives" can be confusing. 
- A lot of unnecessary partner switching to accomplish simple tasks. 
- It doesn't have a Mercenaries mode or supports Online Duo. 
- It primarily features "Remote Play" which isn't nice due to LAG.

Overall, the game was really nice! I definitely look forward to playing this game with my siblings on Christmas. (:

The Claire scenario was actually decently scary, ♥♥♥♥ these jumpscares lmao. While Barry's scenario didn't have any jumpscares, a certain type of enemy is just awfully creepy to look at. The setting gives off the same vibe as the first Resident Evil Revelations, though in that game you're stuck on an abandoned cruise ship in the middle of the ocean, in this game you're stuck on a remote prison island in the middle of the ocean. Still a place I wouldn't want to be at ever.

I'm at a 50/50 with the partner characters each person has though. As soon as the Life Is Strange guest character Moira picks up the Crowbar, I pretty much swapped to her and had Claire follow. Moira can just stun the enemies with her flashlight, then bash the ♥♥♥♥ out of the monsters with the crowbar, knocking them down, then Claire, Moira, or both together do a finisher combo. Pretty neat if you're like me and try to reserve as much of Claire's ammo as you can.

Barry's character, Natalia, though? Pretty boring. I like their dialogue together but that's the only thing Natalia has going. She can point at the enemy or throw bricks. She can also sense enemies that are out of Barry's vision. But let's be honest, this is a Resident Evil game, there's always gonna be an enemy or two around the corner DUH.  Point at the enemies' weaknesses that only she can sense, which lets Barry reserve ammo something I realized during the last ten minutes of the episode oops. But honestly during the boss fight no one would consider switching to Natalia when Barry is the only one doing the damage. She can throw bricks to cause the weakest enemies to trip or stun them, then you can swap to Barry and do a followup attack. I feel like this character should've even need to be swapped to, like an AI can easily have her do these things.

I give it a 6/7, definitely gonna check out the next episode.

It's a mixed bag, to be honest. I wish I could give it something in between positive and negative. Note that I am giving this review based on the actual game; not online/raid or whatever the multiplayer is about. I'm not interested in that portion of the game at all.

Things I like about this game:

-Good horror atmosphere
-Pretty nice graphics for its time
-Amazing sound design. Probably the best gun sounds I've heard in this kind of game.
-Good gunplay.
-Barry and Claire

Things I don't like:

-Uninspired game design
-Uninspired story
-Bad mouse implementation. Acceleration is always on like in RE5. Not sure why as Revelations 1 did not have this problem.
-Controls can be clunky sometimes. Weird button combinations/functions.

I love the RE franchise. Been playing since RE2 in N64. I don't have a preference for the classic or the new and I find enjoyment in both. I didn't really expect much from the Revelation series, but since the first one exceed my expectations, I imagined this game would be as good. Unfortunately I find this game to be somewhat tedious, often boring and bland. The sense of wonder of what might come next is pretty much nonexistent once the game reveals you're in an island. Everything around you looks pretty much the same and having to replay the same areas with the second character doesn't help at all.

I get what they were trying to do with the enemies, but unfortunately, they are just a mess in design. There are only like 3 or 4 different enemies, they all look as if the designers were forced to make them look creepy, but they didn't feel neither original or memorable. RE5 did their own excellent twist on "Ganado-Type" enemies with the Majini, RE6 took it a level further with the J'avos. But these "afflicted" don't really add much. Bosses are interesting enough though.

During my playthrough of RE games next year (which I do every year for fun), I think I will be skipping this game unfortunately. At the moment, I just want this game to be over. Hopefully it will get more interesting in the last two chapters.

So far, I have to say that I am very happy with how the game is created. You relive the horror you had as a child the first time you played, which I personally got in Resident Evil 3: Nemesis.

Really have nothing to complain about when you can both enjoy the game yourself or with a friend.

The only thing that many more than I can think is completely to hell, is that you have to buy different episodes to be able to take you further in the game. Apart from that, definitely a worthwhile purchase in my opinion.

I seldom play horror games and when I do play I usually do not last long. The big exception to this rule Resident Evil: Revelations 2. It is a horror game, but not in the normal alone-in-the-dark kind of way. The game has you guide two couples through the story. Which is a bit less scary. This could disappoint horror fans, as isolation is a cornerstone in any horror story, but it allows squeamish people like me to play it. Perhaps one can say that it isn't a real horror game?

Revelations 2 strongest part is probably the team system. It should allow the team members to be played by different players in a sequel, but in this one one is controlled by the player and the other by the computer. You can switch between the two at will and you have to, as it will help overcome obstacles. You can also give the other member commands. Each member has certain strengths that you can use to the teams advantage.

The first couple is Claire and Moira. Claire is the older of the two and the fighter. She gets to handle the weapons, such as the pistol and shotgun. Moira is a teen and has some special abilities. She can blind adversaries with her torchlight and has a crowbar that she can use for bashing attacks and followup attacks.

The other couple consists of Barry and Natalia. Barry takes the role Claire has and is the fighter. Natalia, a child of around twelve has special abilities in that she can sense danger, spot treasure and see invisible enemies. She can't fight so Barry has to do all the fighting, but she can tell him where to shoot.

The trick is to have the members of a couple work together. Especially Natalia's ability to see invisible enemies will be important.

Each couple finds itself on the same forlorn island that used to be operated by the Soviets until it was abandoned to the local populace. After a while a group of people representing a company showed up to ostensibly operate the mine. But the inhabitants started to get suspicious when people started to disappear or change. The island itself eventually became dangerous as evil creatures start to roam around.

Claire and Moira are the first on the island because they are kidnapped and locked up in a prison. They manage to escape and try to flee the island but find that the only way to get away is to find the one who is in charge. The path to freedom leads through the heart of danger.

Barry arrives six months later to find Moira, his daughter after she has send out an emergency broadcast. When he sets foot on the island he encounters Natalia. Not knowing what to do with her, he takes her along, and he soon finds out that she can help him with her special abilities.

The nice part in the game is the interaction between the two members of a couple. Especially that between Barry, as a replacement father, and Natalia. Claire and Moira act more like friends. Time is spend on making this connection believable. Another is the one that links Barry with Moira.

The progress over the island is less impressive. There are various dangers, felt more keenly because of the lack of ammunition, especially by the first couple. There some traps, puzzles and boss encounters, nothing really surprising when you think of it, but coupled with the team system it works nicely. The narration isn't top notch for a book or a movie, but for a game it is good.. An additional factor that makes this installment better is that the movie has a different atmosphere as it's direct predecessors. It more resembles the earlier creepy resident evil installments than the action oriented later ones.

The lowdown: Resident Evil Revelations 2 isn't a very remarkable game, but with it's team work mechanism, creepy mood and more story based angle allows for a much needed revitalization of the Resident Evil series. It shows a possible way to go, but it depends Capcom to take that route. Will it improve on this or will it take another road entirely? It remains to be seen.

TL:DR : RER 2 is way better than the first one, but still has a lot of flaws. I'd say it's as good as RE0, better than 5 and 6, but not as good as RE2 or Remake. Still totally worth it if you like RE games.

The good :

- a better duo system than RER 1 and RE0, and it can be played in co-op like RE6. I like the characters, playing as Barry and Natalia, despite being totally copied from The Last of Us, feels new.
- better controls, they actually added a key for dodging, and we can run too ( yay )
- probably the RE game with the most moves/options. You can dodge, dash, crouch, stealth kill, quick melee with a knife, throw sub-weapons like molotovs, smoke genades, decoys, bricks, blind enemies with a flashlight, and there is even a skill tree to unlock more moves, like using a knife while running or making a follow-up attack with your partner.
- speaking of skill tree, I think this is the only RE with one. Not really sure it's a good thing though, seems a bit useless at first.
- stupid sexy costumes
- good balance between action and more stressful moments, the pacing is good but suffers near the end.
- good atmosphere, at least on your first run when you don't already know the game
- some good ideas for enemies, like the invisible ones that only Natalia can see and you have to follow her guidance to shoot them.

The bad :

- the difficulty seems a bit all over the place. On easy it's waaaay too easy, especially compared to RER 1, there is so much ammo and enemies die so quickly that I had to throw ammo away to make room for other items. And with the skills upgrades it becomes even easier. But then on normal mode, even with fully upgraded weapons and all my stuff from the first run the game was quite hard. A single hit almost kills you and often makes you bleed and you have to use a special item ( tourniquet ) to staunch it, but I didn't find any shortcut for it so you have to open the inventory ( doesn't pause the game ) to use it in the middle of a fight. Some enemies are also bullt sponges, like the big guys with an axe, taking one grenade/molotov plus 4 shotgun or magnum shots ( fully upgraded with the best mods I had ) to die.

- somehow they ♥♥♥♥♥♥ up the aiming with the mouse. It was perfect in RER1, which was a DS port, but here even if you turn the acceleration off it's still there and the mouse speed can change when you aim and make you miss. Playing with a gamepad isn't ideal to aim either. It wouldn't be too much of a problem if enemies didn't move so weirdly, and they are often fast, running sideways before jumping at you or swinging their weapons in every direction, or you have to shoot weak spots moving all over the place due to their animations.

- the AI is abolutely worthless in combat, often staying close to the enemy instead of running away, they act like there is no danger at all. The problem is that in every duo only one character can use guns ( Claire and Barry ) while the other has more of an utility role ( holding the torchlight, opening passages, finding hidden objects, lockpicking, etc ). It's not much of a problem on easy, but on normal enemies do a lot more damages and we die faster. It's probably better in co-op.

- lots of red herrings and a few plot holes, which I won't spoil. The story is OK and split in two, in each chapter you first play as Claire and Moira ( Barry's daughter ), stranded on a Russian island which looks more like a gulag and trying to escape. Then you play as Barry and Natalia ( a weird little girl who survived here we don't know how, she probably eats bricks or something ), trying to find Moira who disappeared  6 months ago. It makes you go through many of the same places, and even if it's nice to see the changes ( the enemies you killed as Claire and Moira have mutated into new monsters ) it feels a bit cheap. Fortunately there are also new places, especially later on.

The ugly :

- Claire's face. What did they do to you girl ?

Side note on the extra content :

On top of the usual Raid mode, the game has two "side stories" to fill the gaps about Moira and Natalia. Unfortunately this is like the Survivor stories from RE2 Remake : there is barely any story in it, and it's more like a mini game with different rules from the main game.

With Moira you have to kill animals to get food, which is used to retry a failed mission. If you run out of food you'll have to start over, your save is deleted. And these short missions kinda suck, theyre are often timed, and it's just horde mode and ♥♥♥♥♥♥ stealth with insta-fail if you get spotted.

Natalia's DLC is even worse, it's all about stealth, it's slow, boring, and you die if you get spotted too.

It's such a waste imo, Capcom should focus on adding more story with their DLCs instead of these ♥♥♥♥♥♥ mini games.

I enjoyed Revelations 2 as a unique novelty experience, but I don't think I'd want more of it.  The setup is cool.  In the first half of each episode you play the climatic events as they're unfolding, while in the second half you follow up the events six months later, retracing what happened.  It's intriguing.  In each section you play as two characters with complementary roles.  You can command your partner to follow or stay and you can easily switch between them.  The AI is very inconsistent with shooting enemies though.  I imagine this would've been better as coop rather than singleplayer, but as a solo experience it functioned okay.  The story wasn't anything mindblowing, but it accomplished what it set out to do.  The true ending is locked behind a single choice that you make during a QTE, which I think is pretty dumb, especially since the non-canon ending feels more like a Game Over than a resolution to the story, except this "Game Over" requires you to redo multiple hours worth.  The game does rank you independently for different difficulties and lets you replay any half from each of the 4 episodes from the title screen.  That I liked.

However, one thing that almost stopped me from hitting the Recommended button is the game's performance.  It's buggy and it stutters forever.  The game stutters and stutters and stutters.  It does this constantly throughout the entire game.  You either get used to it or give up, because no configuration of graphics settings will fix it.  I tried.  The stutters are micro, lasting mere milliseconds, so I was able to put up with it.  There's still no excuse though.  On top of that, the game has a couple of massive bugs in the final chapter that straight up lock you into a cutscene and prevent you from playing.  After researching, I found that you can fix these instances by capping the game to 30fps and then restarting from the last checkpoint.  This bug is all over the Steam forums and it's ridiculous that it hasn't ever been patched.  

Overall, I recommend Revelations 2 for the interesting approach it took with it's setup and tag-team characters and a story that was just interesting enough to keep me invested.  Nothing else about the game is worthwhile.

I've been playing the entire franchise in chronological order, and this is the first entry that felt like a chore to get through. Looking back on it, the story is actually pretty good, but I feel like I would've enjoyed it more were it not for the distraction of the AI breaking all the time.

Friends and foes alike frequently glitched out, running in place or getting stuck. I'd hate to give spoilers in a review, but I need to bring up specific examples:

At the end of the prison section during the Clair half of episode 1 you try to hold out while Moira gets the door open. I retried this section a few times, it was hard and I was playing on survival, until all the enemies just walked past me and into a blade trap in single file for reasons unknown. I have to admit however it was funny to watch.

In the Clair half of episode 2, Neil kicks down a ladder and you need to get both your characters to join him on the roof. As Clair I climbed up immediately, but Moira would never even try to approach the ladder, so I switched to her to make her do so manually, but then Clair jumped off the roof to join her and got herself killed. I retried this part about a dozen times and it was a never ending cycle of making one character climb up, the AI controlled one jumps down, I switch, make them climb up, while the other one I just moved up the ladder jumps back down. Wait and Follow commands didn't help much. By the time I finally got both characters onto the roof, Neil's AI got stuck and would never unlock the gate no matter what, forcing me to restart the episode from the beginning.

There were plenty of other smaller occasions where an encounter would be harder or easier than it was supposed to be because an AI clearly wasn't behaving as intended. I much prefer Resident Evil 0's much simpler AI companion that was less proactive and thus never got in the way.

By the time I got to the final act I just didn't care about the story and characters anymore and wanted to get it over with. I don't doubt that others will and have enjoyed this game more than I did, but I can only speak for my own experience and the utter disappointment I felt. I tried youtubing other people's playthroughs and the AI didn't seem to have the same errors mine were displaying, so I guess I'm just unlucky.

I have over 1400 games in my Steam account, and the vast majority of them are still unplayed. So I'm dedicating an hour to each of these games and writing a series of One Hour Reviews. An hour isn't very long to judge a game on, so think of this as more of a first impression, and take this review in the spirit in which it's given. Be sure to read other reviews from players who have spent more time in the game.

One Hour Reviews #72 - Resident Evil Revelations 2

So I freely admit I'm going to have a pretty outsider perspective with this review because until now I've never played a Resident Evil game.  So this is a very weird one to start with.  But that said, I didn't really feel like I was missing out on that much as I played, other than I felt like I was supposed to already be familiar with the characters.

The game starts out with a bit of exploration, as I find myself basically trying to break out of a facility that I've been been imprisoned in.   It definitely tries to be atmospheric, like to the point that it almost felt formulaic in the way that everything has this grungy, under-lit look to it, and the almost ridiculous amount of random blood splatter everywhere.  

I'm playing as Claire but I have also been kidnapped along with Moira, who I quickly break out of her own cell.  It's not long before I realize the facility I'm locked in is host to a number of messed up experiments going on, and lots of gory remains.  I get a jump scare with what I assume is one of the failed experiments, but otherwise the game keeps it to a slow burn as I continue to explore.

I'm kind of joking to myself at this point about what it must have been like to actually work in this facility.  Like okay, maybe the ridiculous amount of blood splatter came after they lost control of the experiments or something.  But it's like nobody ever cleaned a single thing here ever.

Eventually I do start running into some of these failed experiments as the game finally introduces me to some combat, and a chance to use the gun and ammo I had picked up before.

So about halfway through my playthrough, I start getting smack-talked to by a mysterious voice, and soon I realize I'm not going to be able to escape until I can re-activate the power in order to be able to open a door that leads to the exit.  So now I'm working to find the power generator. 

And again, I find myself laughing as I pass this contraption which is basically a bunch of buzzsaws mounted to a wheel on a rail.  Like, gee, I wonder if I'll be dealing with this thing when the power is back on.  I guess this is supposed to be for defense in case the experiments get out?   I feel like you just kind of have to suspend your disbelief here and the designers are just putting things in because they look cool, or because you're expected to have them in a Resident Evil game.

At this point, the combat is definitely ramping up, and I'm getting introduced to other weapons like the shotgun and the molotov cocktail.  There's also some puzzle elements that come up which involve switching perspectives to play as Moira to get to areas that Claire can't.

I did eventually get the power restored, and it led to kind of a final sequence where a bunch of the failed experiments got out and I had to basically fight my way out, but in the end I did make it outside of the facility, where again I get smack-talked to by the same mysterious voice.  And that's where I ended up stopping, technically a little over the 1 hour mark, but I really wanted to make it outside before I stopped.

Overall I had fun, even with some of the unintended humor and suspension of disbelief.    I can't really relate this to the other Resident Evil games, but to me it came across as a pretty typical horror game, so I think if you are a fan of that genre, you'll feel right at home with this.

The game is pretty fun but the fact that they offer to sell it for one episode at a time when the entire game is now available for purchase is a bit strange. People are likely to see the very low pricetag and assume that they'll be buying the full package for only a dollar.

Luckily I didn't make this mistake, I purchased the whole lot in one bundle for £12 which isn't so bad, especially for all the content that there is in this title.

The singleplayer story mode which I played the most is enjoyable and well-made, there are collectibles, challenges, and special modes such as invisible enemy mode for each chapter, which makes them very replayable.
After a lot of grind I did manage to get all of the achievements in this game, but I must say that it really did become somewhat difficult to do after a while, this is mostly because there are a fair number of sequences in each chapter which force your character to move at a walking pace while some dialogue happens in the background, these [b]cutscenes are unskippable and must be done each time you play the chapter.[/b] If the option to skip all of this were present I would probably enjoy replaying this as much as I do other entries in the series like RE4 and RE5, but unfortunately that's not the case.

I played this game with a PS4 controller so I can't comment on how well done the controls are for keyboard and mouse, but the controller support is exactly what it needs to be, no issues there. Visuals are great, Capcom have this grainy sort of texture compression that has applied to their RE games since the remake of RE1 and the original RE4 which I think brings a charm to the graphical style and allows it to age surprisingly well.

Disappointingly, despite the game's story swapping you between two pairs of characters alternating with each level, [b]it is not possible to play co-operatively over the internet in this game[/b], it is only possible to do this locally or by using Steam's "Remote Play Together" feature which I have never tried as it requires quite a strong internet connection to minimize input lag.
I did not play much of this game's Raid mode, which is a side mode that is the definition of grind.
You play as one of a number of characters with their own experience level and collect levelled guns and levelled abilities which you can use to to replay the same chopped up sections of the singleplayer story filled with enemies with inflated HP based on their level which are placed in different configurations, the general goal is to kill them all and reach the end of the level.
Perhaps if I owned this game for a mobile console this mode would have more appeal, perhaps if I knew someone who owned the same game on their portable console we could regularly co-op some raids and enjoy the grind.
Raid mode is a chore playing solo. This is coming from someone who maxed out the singleplayer campaign's content completely, achieving the max rank for every level on every difficulty.
Despite its flaws, there is an online multiplayer function to Raid mode, which makes the fact that this function is missing from the story mode even more of a kick in the teeth.

Overall I would say that this is worth playing, storywise it's alright, gameplay wise it's alright, atmosphere and replayability-wise it is stellar, with only the few unskippable semi-cutscenes in each chapter cutting into the game's replayability.
If you buy this on sale you will definitely get your money's worth through the singleplayer content alone, even if you only play it once.

There's a solid game in there, but the release is quite a mess and should be approached with a lot of caution.

The gameplay itself is quite fun and it feels like a very modern game. Tight, responsive controls, comfortable shooting and camera. The partner mechanics overall are working out pretty well, though at some points they feel kinda forced. Looks like the entire game was designed around being able to play in co-op, and it feels that the plot could have benefited from more times where the player is acting alone. Inventory management system is pretty generous, but that just raises more questions about why the slot system is even needed any more.

So about those negatives then. First of all, the game is released as bunch of separate DLCs and episodes. I think I may have purchased it directly from my wishlist page and didn't realise I'm not even getting the full main story, which is broken down into 4 episodes. Buyer beware, I suppose, but it still could've been package more clearly. Then the gameplay in each episode is kinda broken down into 50/50 chunks of one team, then the other team, breaking immersion a bit and sacrificing plot development opportunities.

The game really loves throwing previews and recaps at you at whenever it has a chance, probably with the assumption that the episodes will be coming months apart... And thanks, but I don't want the next two hours of gameplay spoiled right before proceeding. I also haven't forgotten what I did two minutes ago either. Feel free to re-package the trailers in a Extra section, but if you can see I have the entire thing purchased please don't do that.

Internet connectivity all the time is assumed, and I'm guessing that adds up to a lot of loading times, as the game tries to sync with the servers. It'll work in offline mode, I assume. You'll miss out on the leaderboards or something. There's a very real and frustrating way this affect actual gameplay though. Imagine you approach a door towards what you can tell must be the big boss. You approach some object of interest and the game cuts away to a 15 second black loading screen to launch a pre-rendered cutscene. The cutscene ends with you in imminent danger, trying to fight back the big bad thing. Loading screen. 10 seconds, 15 seconds, 20 seconds. I refused to believe that has anything to do with having to load anything from the SSD and seriously suspect some sort of network shenanigans. Otherwise, a seriously horrible decission/oversight.

And then there's the big Raid Mode where you partner up with random people to fight meanies or something. Lots of leveling up and unlocking and acheivements... Yeah, you guessed it, it's dead at this point. If it was ever alive. No option to play with a bot. No indication of what the odds of a person actually joining are. You just run around a tiny little room and hope that a miracle would happen.

So overall, it could really be salvaged if the developer chose to re-package it into a standalone game, but right now there's a few too many things that feel broken or even scummy in terms of not being clear what you need to purchase.

RE: Revelations 2 is Capcom's foray into episodic gaming during a period where other episodic titles like Telltale's The Walking Dead were very popular (NOTE: Be sure to get the Deluxe Edition which contains all campaign episodes plus the bonus episodes. I suggest waiting for a Steam sale). It's a refreshing change of pace from the action-packed set pieces of RE5 and RE6, as Revelations 2 is more focused on exploring, backtracking, stealth, and simple puzzle-solving. Co-op companions return but the co-op elements this time are far more intuitive and integrated directly into the gameplay — your partner is no longer just there as a meatshield or inventory mule.

There are four episodes in total, and each episode has to be played twice: First as Claire Redfield, and subsequently as Barry Burton. The story takes place between RE5 and RE6, and gives some much needed character development for both Claire and Barry (more than a decade of in-game time has passed since we last saw them in their respective RE games). An interesting new villain is introduced, which fits in nicely with the RE lore.

Your actions as Claire will effect what Barry encounters later. For example, if you make the effort to defeat a certain enemy as Claire, Barry's portion will be slightly easier. If you activate a certain switch or contraption, that contraption will still be in play for Barry. Similar to Resident Evil 2 (1998), you can also choose not to pick up certain items as Claire, leaving them for Barry later.

Both Claire and Barry have partners accompanying them throughout the story, and it is this co-op mechanic which makes Rev2 shine. You can swap back and forth to take control of your partner, similar to Resident Evil 0, which is necessary to solve certain puzzles or to access some hidden areas. While your partners cannot use firearms, they can still help out in combat by using throwing weapons such as firebombs or smoke grenades. Moira in particular, can stun enemies by shining her flashlight on zombies, allowing Claire to follow-up with a knockdown attack. One annoying new enemy (which I won't spoil too much), requires teamwork from both characters to defeat.

Once you've completed the main story (it should take you around 18-20 hours), if you don't mind replaying the game again there's an insane amount of unlockables and many alternate game modes for you to try. There's also a semi-competitive online mode called Raid Mode, which can be played solo or co-op. Your objective is to race against time to obtain a high score for... you guessed it, more unlockables.

Revelations 2 is by far, the most replayable Resident Evil game to date, jam-packed with unlockables and oodles of game modes to appeal to both the solo casual and hardcore online player. Highly recommended for any RE fan.

Capcom sells you a game it knows you will not be able to finish under certain circumstances. Let me explain, if you have the unfortunate luck to die during the last boss battle, everytime after that when you restart the battle, you will not be able to move anymore. The game goes on as expected eg: the boss comes out and lashes out at you, but you can't move or do anything for that matter. So in essence you have to reload your save everytime you die. This is unacceptable as not everyone is tech savvy and can look on the internet to fix your broken game. A game when sold should be fit for purpose, the purpose of a game is to be finished, if it can't be in normal playing conditions, it is not fit for purpose and should be fixed. So I tried resident Evil 6 because lately it received some kind of a resurgence of positive reviews. These new ways of looking at Resi 6  all claim the same thing, Resi 6 is an underappreciated action game that is in fact very good. Well let me put this to rest, no it is not , it is not very good, it's a poorly tuned action game, there are thousands of better games out there at doing the action thing. There are some good bits in Resi 6 but as a whole it is not a very good game. Now fast forward to Resident Evil Revelations 2, it has never been very well received either, but has not enjoyed a revival such as Resi 6 did, so I didn't look at it at first. After my Resi 6 disappointment, I decided to give it a go and let me tell you it was worth it. Let me start with the bad things first, it is episodic, and for a game from 2015 if you want all episodes it will cost you way too much. Better wait for a sale, and still the price will be much higher than resi 6. But besides that, Rev 2 is a true survival horror game with some action sequences. The coop play is interesting due to the different skill set of the 4 protagonists. Disclaimer here, I only played local coop, with split screen. The game advertises online coop but I didn't want to pay twice for the game and still, I read quite consistently that online coop doesn't work on PC so, now you're warned, you'll probably have to play in a tiny corner of your screen if you want coop but it's workable. I also realised that playing on the same screen with someone makes it special as you share you're partner's emotions much more than with online coop. Other good point, the atmosphere is enjoyable (even if not very scary) and the graphics are fine. All in all it is a good coop game, in my view much better than resi 6. Let me give you a few examples of things that Rev 2 does better than Resi 6: 1) the Camera is at a decent distance from your character and FOV is wide enough 2) No quick time overload 3) You can actually see whats going on (most of the time) 4)  There's a story, it kind of makes sense (as much as it can given Resident Evil Lore) and was written by someone who actually gave a ♥♥♥♥ 5) The characters actually sound and seem human, as opposed to the one dimensional comic book archetypes of Resi 6 6) there is pacing, as opposed to the constant 1.000.000 volt 9 billion megaton atomic explosion that Resi 6 tries to pull off (spoiler: it doesn't) 7) The inventory is useable and consistent between characters, none of the one line inventory ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ with a different skin for each characters in Resi 6 8) after a couple of hours I actually enjoyed myself VS I wish I could get my 20+ hours back from Resi 6...

The campaign in this game isn't particularly the greatest. There's barely any exploration, unlike the first Revelations game, and in general feels more like the more action oriented Resident Evil games than the classic ones (although it's certainly not as action based as say, Resident Evil 5).

It also technically has multiplayer, but imho it's not very good. You basically play as one main character that does all the fun stuff, and a supporting character than can find items and help a tiny bit with enemies.
While this does sometimes lead to cool scenarios, it's basically like handling the broken controller that you don't want to use to your partner. Plus, it has no proper online multiplayer, so you're stuck with either local play or remote play together, with a weird split screen mode that wastes a lot of screen space.

Not only that, but the campaign is quite short. Each episode has 2 scenarios, one with Claire and Moira, and one with Barry and Natalia, and each scenario lasts about an hour and a half for each episode. That is, except for the last episode, where Claire's scenario lasts about 15 minutes, and Barry's lasts about 2 hours. If you're only going to play the campaign, it may not be worth the price.

However, the game includes an expanded version of the Raid Mode from the first Revelations game. Now, this one isn't without its fair share of problems either, like the fact that most maps are from Resident Evil 6, which gets repetitive, but it's a lot of fun to play, specially with friends. You have multiple characters to unlock, many different weapons, different upgrades for each weapon, a lot of levels and multiple difficulty settings. It's a serious time killer. Most of my playtime is from Raid Mode.

Basically, get the game if you have a friend who also has it and wants to play Raid Mode with you, you'll get your bucks worth. If you're only going to play the campaign, then try getting it at a discounted price.

Resident Evil Revelations 2 seems like the natural evolution of Resident Evil 4 with similar level design and some of it's own unique and creative ideas which makes this game stands out as a more toned down and a serious tone. The main mechanic is the partner system where you have one underpowered partner that helps you with their abilities and certain areas the main characters can't get to. This system is great in my opinion and handles the partner system even better than Resident Evil 5 did which is fairly impressive. However, while I recommend not playing this in cooperative play, there is local splitscreen but not online which is just dumb and jarring especially since Resident Evils 5 and 6 had online. The story is also great which contextualizes you go back through older areas in an interesting way and it never feels stale due to different paths and enemies to encounter in each story which is split between Claire Redfield and Moira Burton and Barry Burton and Natalia Korda. The second story takes place six months after the first and the areas feel old and festering as it should. With great atmosphere and a really heartfelt story, Resident Evil Revelations 2 is certainly worth picking up and it essentially a more modern Resident Evil 4 with it's own handful of unique mechanics and designs.

TL;DR - An absolute love letter to longtime Resident Evil fans, that's paired with an asinine pricing model.

At Length: This game is actually excellent as a follow up to Revelations 1, and improves on that game in nearly every way. The controls feel tighter and pretty much everything in terms of gameplay feels better designed, and the graphics are definitely better since I think this is running on the RE6 engine. The enemy and level design is also quite good for an RE game made during the "Action" RE era - not much in the way of puzzles unfortunately (there's only one that requires any thought at all and it's completely optional), but the enemies are well designed to have appropriate variety and the levels are well designed to work with them. And you don't really get too much ammo, so there's still enough of a survival horror experience here to matter. 

In a many ways, this game is a synthesis of almost every RE game that preceded it: the story is a fairly engaging tale centered around a situation reminiscent of Code Veronica - Claire Redfield ends up on a prison island where a madwoman lies in wait soon to be followed by an older male protective figure, but it's Barry Burton this time rather than her brother. The story also has some elements from RE2 (original) as at least a few things you do in Claire's game affect Barry's game. RE3 dodging is back like in Rev1, but it's improved by being given its own button (finally). There's character swapping as in RE: Zero, since both Claire and Barry are working with a partner character, Moira and Natalia respectively, and it's sort of like RE4 in that their partners are notably a bit less capable than they are in combat, kind of turning the game into a semi escort mission, except the partners can also initiate combo attacks like in RE5 and Terra Save was only ever in one of the CGI movies before making that canon and . . . 

. . . well you can see what I mean when I say this is an obvious recommend for fans. If you've played a lot of the prior titles, you can recognize the influences and references here clear as day. If you're not, just know that you're getting a game experience here that coming from 20 years of iteration, so it's pretty well honed.

One thing that surprised me after finishing everything is that this game really is Barry's story. It features Claire, sure, but really the core emotive impact here centers around Barry's relationship with his daughter Moira, and the little girl he discovers and protects like a daughter, Natalia. This is the "Dad Game" entry in the RE series I suppose. It also does a bit more than normal to actually highlight the characters in a good way - Claire, Barry and Moira all feel a lot more human and down to earth than some of the other RE protagonists who are cool-as-ice supercops and secret agents. So, while the story of this game is smaller than found in Rev1, which tried to emulate a spy thriller, I do think it's more impactful.

Plus a note must be made on Raid Mode: it's a LOT better here than in Rev1. I actually found the overall design of the secondary game much more compelling here. The weapons and levels are distributed more evenly, you carry progression on individual characters rather than using them as simple skins. The levels are better designed to work with Raid mode in particular and are mostly pulled from RE6, so there's not as much repetition from the main game. And the larger enemy variety and the larger number of enemy variant options make it much more engaging. I've actually spent more time playing Raid mode in this game than I have the main game and found myself really enjoying it, even in solo play..

In fact - over a month later, I'm still playing it! Raid mode is extremely compelling.

Which leads to the big obvious downside to this game: the way CAPCOM is selling it as an episodic package.

I'm sure when this game launched the idea of an episodic RE game was en vogue and seemed really cool to players. But ultimately it just inflates the price and there's no suspense about what comes next all these years later, so the novelty of the model is gone. 

The total cost of all the episodes and bonus episodes is about $32 but if you add on all the other Raid mode fluff and bonus costumes it gets up to $70ish. This makes the $30 price tag of the deluxe edition a good value if you like Raid Mode, but bad if you don't. However, you probably won't know if you like it until you play it, which means buying at least the 1st episode on its own, as a pseudo demo. But if you do that and do like it enough to get the deluxe edition, they don't deduct that prior purchase from the total and all of this just feels like a frustrating entry in nickel & diming a customer to death rather than just settling on one flat price and providing a free demo like a normal game.

In the end, I'd still recommend the game for those looking for another fix of Resident Evil, especially if they liked REmake 2 and want to see where Claire ended up, or anyone curious about what an alternate take with RE6's engine could have looked like. In fact I'd argue that this is definitely a better game than RE6, and should probably be considered to be on par with RE5 in terms of overall quality, meaning this is a series side game that's better than some of the main games in the series.

I didn't expect much from this going in, as Revelations 1 was so so (and only Resi 4 has been good for yonks now), but it was pleasantly surprising. Coming over like a mega-mix of the best bits of previous games, and with a few neat touches of it's own. It's an action game first and foremost, but there are still some moments and gameplay mechanics where it pushes forward from the template set in Resi 4.

However: If you're expecting survival horror then don't bother with this. Whilst it's actually much more successful at being tense in some sections than any of the other games it's also fairly generous with the ammo, so the survival aspect isn't really there. 

I'd also have to add that this being a positive review doesn't make it a great game, and that it's only a good Resident Evil...which still means it's a bit crap, and far from troubling the likes of Dead Space or The Evil Within. I enjoyed it, but as a series RE should have died off years ago before they released about thirty billion different games with awful narratives trying to suggest there's some overarching story worth keeping churning them out for. 

Like all the other games the plot is a load of old steaming sloppy bum outpourings, though this title at least knows that it's terrible and is written with what is clearly a deliberately cheesy tone. The sole reason I give this a positive review is purely for the gameplay mechanics which are, as I said before, somewhat of a pick and mix from the best bits of previous games. As an action game the controls are up to the task, and you can at least dodge attacks which makes it feel like more of a modern title than Resi 2 Remake where the feature was absent.

Play is split between pairings of different characters and each has their own emphasis. Claire Redfield and Barry Burton are the experts with weapons, another has a flashlight that can blind enemies and temporarily stun them, and then there is one who can sense enemies through walls and spot their weak points. It's always the case that the two characters with lesser combat skills, but another useful ability / tool, will be in tow with an armed character. They can be computer controlled or switched between at will, and the game makes some interesting uses of these dynamics.

They're not groundbreaking but there is the sense of them trying to do a bit more than just regurgitate past glories by aping Resi 4 (though it does do that too) or the tired, clunky old skool design of Resi 2 Remake. Given that I can no longer stomach the latter I enjoyed this more as a "wham bam thank you mam" title, than if it was "here's a gun, but oh! you can't shoot it for most of the damn game and BTW - you're utterly useless at defending yourself in any other way" type thang. 

In other aspects it's okay. The graphics are reasonable, as is the voice acting. Though the cutscenes have a horrible look to how they're presented. The enemies don't look as stupid as they do in the other games, although they still have the tendency to think monsters sprouting eyeballs all over the place doesn't look utterly rubbish, or that it isn't by now somewhat overdone in the twenty plus years since Resi 1!! Why not do something unique and have them sprout, ooooh! I dunno....noses on their elbows, or ears on their kneecaps...

Well...it's Resi so that's kind of accepted as their thing by now, and it's still not as crap as the designs in Resi 6 so that's at least something. Overall this is trying to do something new with a generally tired formula, and whilst I wouldn't rave over the end result I can't deny I did enjoy the 18 or so hours it took to complete. As a single player campaign, and for the cost, I have no complaints - so a recommended it is. 

But this teases a sequel and I really, really, really! hope they put this crap to bed as far as the story goes, because there just isn't one worth bothering with. The gameplay just about makes up for it here, but that's like 12 games or more built around any old guff they can cobble together and the justification for the narrative is getting paper thin.

[h1]A great game offering many different forms of gameplay [/h1]

[b]Single-Player[/b]

Single Player campaign is a good horror/zombie-shooter game similar to the original RE Revelations but this time with more emphasis on the survival horror aspect with more puzzles, more running and less shooting.

If it's shooting you want though, try raid mode which I spent literally hundreds of hours playing. It's basically a smaller version of Left 4 Dead. 

The "Little Miss" DLC for this one of my all-time favorite TRUE survival horror games being literally a game about being an unarmed little girl with paranormal powers which you have to use to get past lots of dangerous enemies whom you can't fight.

[b]Coop[/b]

Raid mode is a great coop zombie shooter (it's basically a smaller Left 4 Dead) and with couch coop and Remote Play Together, it's a great story coop game as well. 

If Remote Play Together does NOT work at first, try plugging two controllers into the host's computer. If you do that, you will be able to enjoy a decent story coop experience together provided that the person you invite has a working controller plugged into his or her computer as well. 

[h1]Drawbacks[/h1]

The gameplay is very good as are the weapons though the fact that there are differently-leveled versions of the same weapon is an unnecessary complication I could have done without. 

I hate this system in Borderlands and I hate it here. Either just have one type of each weapon or let us level up the weapons rather than having to constantly sell old ones to make way for higher-leveled versions of the same thing. 

[h1]Final thoughts[/h1]

8/10

This is a good Resident Evil game. It came out in a time when Resident Evil was the least Resident Evil-y it's ever been! This felt like a breath of fresh air. Mostly, anyway.

Claire is back along with Barry, along with Barry's daughter, Moira, and a mysterious little girl, Natasha. Claire and Moira gets kidnapped and thrown on an island full of monsters and they need to find a way out. The way the story unfolds is kinda interesting. You play as Claire and Moira in the past, trying to survive on the island, and Barry and Natasha in the present trying to find them. There's also a secret lab involved with evil experiments and stuff. It's a Resident Evil story. There's a rocket launcher scene at the end!

The gameplay is like Resident Evil game with a little of the Last of Us attached. You can crouch now, which is new, along with an instant kill stealth attack. The game encourages you to play with a little stealth, which is nice and all, but it's not the most polished stealth system out there. I always end up getting caught and use my guns anyway. Aside from the stealth, the game plays like a more movement-free version of RE5 and RE6. You can move while you shoot, and you don't feel as stiff as you do in 5 or 6. It feels good in my opinion.

There's a lot of replay value here. You get a rank for each episode you complete, a decently sized skill tree to unlock, a bunch of unlockables to get, and raid mode is ADDICTING AS TITS! There's a lot to like here. Even though it's not as scary as RE1 or RE2, it is scarier than 5 and 6, so that's a plus!

There are some issues like crappy mouse controls, minor performance issues, and the difficulty gets unbearable above normal though. It's overall a solid game. Give it a shot!

In some ways it's a return to form for the Resident Evil franchise while in others it still has a semi action oriented feel to it. The story is best described as tale of two stories. On one hand you have Clair and Moria who have been captured and are trying to find a way back home. While on the other hand you have Barry and the little miss trying to rescue them. The episodic structure is certainly different and maybe a turn off to some while others may view this as a different approach and an interesting idea. The upside to this is that if it turns out you don't like it then the price of admission is low especially when it is on sale. The downside is that if you like it then you either have to buy remaining episodes separately or purchase the deluxe edition with all the DLC. So certainly a mixed bag across the board. 

Gameplay wise it's best described as an ideal game for co-op as one character can fight foes while the other acts as a supporting character by calling out foes or helping to locate items and such. What's even more interesting is that the progress you make like item management will carry through to each episode and considering that ammo and items can be hard to come by at times it makes item management key.

In closing if you want to try this new format for yourself or are just curious then either try the demo or buy the first episode on sale and see what you think. On sale you can get it for under $1 so no real heavy risk involved if you decide to go that route.

I can't tell you how many times I have gone to pick up an item and hit the wrong button. The addition of a running feature is good, but considering how cramped the maps are, this addition is moot. Would have been better in the previous title.
Claire's campaign is undermined by the addition of having to essentially escort Moira, who is playable to a minimal degree. Her required tasks feel shoehorned into the gameplay as a means to justify her inclusion. The overall feel of their campaign is less like an RE title and more like horror titles like Outlast. The confusing motivations and blatant lack of logical direction going on is more annoying and tedious than engaging.
Barry's campaign with Natalia is far more interesting by the inclusion of her sensing and eagle eye attributes. While also technically an escort scenario, her abilities and total lack of an ability to do more than stun enemies is justified by her being only 10 years old. Moira is an adult and should be able to fight like one. Barry's gameplay somehow is smoother in transitions from one stage to the next and feels more like a traditional RE game.
The overall gameplay and setting are nothing new to this series. The setting hearkens to Code Veronica, but the engagements of enemies is more like RE 4. The lack of fresh things or lovingly nostalgic creativity inherent in the first Revelations title make Revelations 2 a disappointing turn. The episodic format also holds the game back as it makes you wonder if finishing the game is worth buying the next part. It also had me wondering when this would all be over so I could say I tried while also not allowing this to be a waste of money.

The game itself tries to get back to its roots when it comes to the horror survival aspect, especially on harder difficulties. I believe I did it on the regular difficulty and had small ammo and health problems, compared to say RE6. The plot itself is pretty interesting, in that you play two different campaigns at one time. It's almost similar to RE2, but rather than different scenarios, the two sided campaign go hand in hand for the story. The story DLC that you can get fill in a few tiny plot holes in certain character's locations, and add to the game. The game itself feels a lot more like Evil Within, where stealth is an important aspect and ammo reserves can be rough at higher difficulties. It gets further away from RE6, which is back to back action compared to horror survival. The game itself is heavily influenced by CoOp, you have a partner at all times, and you either control both or one with a friend. The only issue I had with it was that your partner has specific skills and abilities that aren't shared with the main characters. Due to how the characters are not the same, it's something to consider with a co op buddy. My only real gripe with the character swapping was that the secondary characters can spot extra ammo and items (you have to aim at the shinnies) and you will not see it if you're the main character. I found myself swapping quite a bit. It runs very smoothly, and fps runs like butter (some stutter coming from a loading screen, goes away and stays away immediately). I had two critical bugs, and the discussions helped me resolve them. Some people, like myself, couldn't start the game and the screen would stay black. I was unable to do anything, almost like a freeze, and was forced to restart. This was fixed by putting your game in compatibility mode for Win 8 or 7, and running as administrator. The second critical error is a game glitch, in which your character was stuck during the final boss fight. I fixed this by putting my fps cap at the lowest possible (24 I think), restarting the checkpoint, going through the cut scene (in which you should be able to move again), and then swap your fps back to it's default. Since they were easy fixes, it did not cause any issue for my gameplay, and I can highly recommend this to anyone who enjoys RE or Evil Within.

One of the most ambitious RE titles, Revelations 2 is plagued by many issues, but it still manages to stand out with its complex structure.

This is also one of the most purely survival-horror-oriented titles in the franchise, as ammo tends to be extremely scarce, and there are many sequences in which you need to use stealth and combine abilities efficiently to progress. Each of the characters also plays completely differently, which offers many opportunities and keeps things spicy.

Plot-wise, this game features one of the most interesting villains in the franchise and also one of the more serious stories, with a bit of philosophical undertones (but nothing too deep, ofc). It still retains some of the typical RE silliness (such as via costumes and the sort), but far less so than other games in the series.

Its episodic structure can be both interesting and annoying, however, as you will often have to play through the exact same sequences with different characters, except doing different puzzles and utilizing different abilities and gameplay elements.

Overall though, this is definitely worth trying if you're a fan of the RE formula. However, it might not be the best starting point if you're new to the franchise.

For a Resident Evil game, the story is pretty good. Each episode is rather focused so meandering is kept to a minimum as you progress along. Unlike the first Revelations, you aren't bogged down with characters and b-plots that you don't care about *cough* Jackass and Grinder *cough*

The atmosphere is really good. The bloody prison you start in should give you an idea of how the rest of the game is gonna feel. The monster design is top notch and either really disgusting or outright horrifying.

I played the game solo and, despite your partner not having a gun, keeping them alive isn't hard and they aren't useless. Firstly, they can't really die so you can use them to tank hits or draw aggro away from you. Second, they have utility. Moira can stun enemies leading to a combo that saves ammo. Switching to Natalia lets you see enemy weak points to make taking them down easier.

In terms of gameplay, I found ammo conservation and inventory management really important. Finding a lot of ammo meant something was going to happen soon. It was sometimes beneficial to avoid fighting and just GTFO. Claire's scenario plays a bit like RE4 and 5 I would say, while Barry's puts more emphasis on performing stealth take downs (Natalia makes life easier).

Combat isn't particularly difficult so long as your aim is true and you have a handle on positioning. You will occasionally run into enemies that will blind you with either goop or your own blood and that sucks. My advice is to not get hit in the first place. Unlike Revelations 1, you can dodge at any time so you should take full advantage of it.

The puzzles aren't obnoxiously easy nor are they nonsensically difficult. Some of them need you to switch between characters to solve. The only one I really had a problem with was in the spike room.

All in all, I wouldn't put this on my top games of all time, but I really enjoyed my time playing it. It was fun, challenging but not too difficult, the story wasn't boring, the atmosphere was good, I didn't have to babysit AI, the monsters were pretty scary, but nothing really phenomenal.

Final rating: Good, but wait for a sale.

An improvement over the first Revelations game. A great game, but with a few issues that hinder the game from being even better.

Revelations 2 maintains the same gameplay as the first game, with a few tweaks. Guns can still be upgraded using custom parts found on the way, though this time characters can also be upgraded by spending BP to learn passive skills, which is a good improvement, but the skills also feel a bit weird and too situational for the most part, like damage bonuses that only apply when crouching or for a few seconds after switching between characters.

Story-wise, it was great to see the return of Claire and Barry as the main characters. The story is also pretty good, even if not perfect, telling two stories that are connected but not parallel.

For the most part, the game is great - gunplay is good, there is a decent ammount of challenge without feeling too frustrating and the enemy design is interesting.

There are, however, two main issues with the game that hinder its potential. The first is how both scenarios have two characters to be played, each character having a specific functions - Claire and Barry are the ones using guns, while Moira and Natalia can find items that Claire and Barry can't, plus Moira also has a flashlight (so Claire depends on her when in the dark) and Natalia can sense nearby enemies, including invisible ones.

The problem with this is that the player has to spend most of the game playing as Moira and Natalia instead of Claire and Barry in order to be able to find the hidden items, which often provide extra BP to be spent on skills later on, which is something that I didn't specially enjoy.

The second issue is the lockpicking mechanic. It's needlessly complicated, to the point I had to look for a Youtube tutorial on how to lockpick, and definitely not needed since all it does for most of the game is test your patience.

Crafting in this game is also something that could have been removed entirely. You find items that you can then use to craft different types of explosive bottles or healing items, but for the most part, what they do is clutter the inventory (which is also not great - I much preferred the inventory in the first Revelations).

The two extra chapters are not spectacular, but they're good in the sense that they add more to the story of the game. It is worth noting, however, that the second extra chapter ("Little Miss") is entirely a stealth mission that auto-fails if you get caught, something that I find to be absolutely no fun at all.

The Experience:
This one was a lot better than the revelations predecessor, it is unfortunate that they have to reference the lame backstory for it. The whole Terra Save and Terragregia really just give the game a cheap feeling when the rest of it is actually very well done. While the antagonist comes across as annoying and corny, the interactions between our protagonists grounds the experience pretty well. Moira is a bit of a potty mouth and some may not like that, but the story is still driven well. The game does actually become a good bit scary, and your partner isn't useless even though they cannot use guns. The game actually plays a nice balance in giving the secondary characters worth in their powerlessness comparatively speaking. This strikes a nice balance to keep the game feeling like an action game à la RE5 and RE6... if only you could play it online. The collectibles, enhanced raid mode and dlc additions are a neat inclusion.

Like Resident Evil 0, in Resident Evil Revelations 2 you control two characters at the same time, but unlike only two characters in Resident Evil 0, there are four characters, consisting of two pairs, and each pair is formed by one main character and one side character. Only the main characters are able to shoot, while the side characters possess assistive abilities that fit their characters, which can help you go through the game more smoothly. Switching characters now feels natural and convenient, but this design is not integrated into gameplay as much as Resident Evil 0 – you don’t need to decide which character is better for the situation, nor you have to use one specific character for some reasons. You only have to switch characters for a few puzzles, but those are brief. For the rest of the game, you can just keep using the main characters if you don’t care about hidden items. The only complaint I have regarding dual characters is that the game does not support  online coop, although it allows local coop.

Revelations 2 story is okay, well-structured and decently long (12 hours or so), unlike Revelations 1 being a bit short (about 8 hours). The whole story gives me some The Evil Within vibe, talking about horror and human mind stuff, though they all connected to bioterror at the end.  Still, I think it is a bit too supernatural for Resident Evil, but that is just my nitpicking. 

Other than the main incident, the story focuses on the relationship between Moira and Barry, which is not normal for Resident Evil to put effort into emotional side of things. This father-daughter relationship thing is cliché but turns out okay. Moira is the most accomplished character of the bunch, showing the audience both her tough and fragile sides with her loads of bad languages and her genuine personality, though there is some mild inconsistency in characteristics. Barry, on the other hand, is kind of stereotypical being a clumsy father who has a tense relationship with his daughter. I guess he is more of a fan service because he is beloved and we know how much a family man he is in Resident Evil 1 (and here we are finally meet his family). As for the other two, Claire, an important character in the series, seems to be completely forgotten by the scriptwriters. She has the least story to tell. While Natalia is an adorable and lovable character who probably the most helpful kiddo you could have in a video game. The game did not fully explain the mystery around her and leaves players a cliffhanger. I wonder if the future Resident Evil will do anything to this character.

This game is a standard third-person shooter, but it adds back the inventory management which is a little problematic because of excessive types throwable and healing items that you hardly use (but carry all the way and take up inventory space). Map design varies from different sessions and many require some backtracking like old Resident Evil. The shooting is solid, however, even the minimum sensitivity is still too high, you have to readjust mouse DPI to 300 or 400 in order to aim comfortably. The raid mode is a surprisingly fun add-on and I spent lots of time on it. All in all, I am glad to see the game went back to be a horror game with good atmosphere, although I would call it unsettling other than truly scary. I also really enjoy the chitchats while walking, as it makes the characters feel real. Still, there are three flaws I want to point out: during autosave the game would freeze or the frame rate would drop; the vision is too blurred to see anything clearly when bleed or injured; the good or bad ending depends on a quick event in Episode 3, which is not a good design since a lot of people might be unaware  like I did for my first playthrough. 

Now that Resident Evil turns first-person and features the new character Ethan Winters, I would very much love to see the old characters make a return in future Revelations series.

In Resident Evil Revelations 2, you (and ideally another player) initially play as either Claire Redfield, Chris Redfield's sister, or Moira Burton, Barry Burton's daughter, who have been kidnapped at a TerraSave gathering (because "Terr" doesn't have to end with "ist") and find themselves in a mysterious abandoned facility filled with monsters. Barry Burton, accompanied by a mysterious young girl named Natallia, follow in their tracks hoping to find out what happened to Claire and Moira.

Resident Evil Revelations 2 is a cooperative survival horror game which is a good mix of the old school and modern designs of the Resident Evil franchise..

Pros
- Good mix of modern, actiony behind the shoulder, and old school, survival / puzzle solving / methodical, Resident Evil gameplay that should appeal to a wide-range of players.
- Great asymmetric coop core gameplay with four different characters to play as, each of which plays quite differently from one another.

Cons
- Story is a little too "out there"; one could probably qualify it as being just plain bad.
- You get a good or a bad ending based on a excruciatingly small choice in one of the episodes, the bad ending is extremely anti-climatic compared to the good ending and having these two endings doesn't add anything to the game.
- Gameplay gets a tad repetitive towards the end of the fourth (and last real) episode due to the lack of enemy variety and new gameplay elements.

If you're a fan of the Resident Evil series or if you're looking for a fun horror coop game to play with a friend then you can't go wrong with Resident Evil Revelations 2.

- The story is better off in this one as it isn't just the classic routine of someone betrays someone else to gain power. Revelations 2 gives a lot more cryptic moments and twists to keep it interesting throughout the episodes.
- Claire and Barry are already great characters but the partners work wel ltoo even if at times they can be a little odd to listen to, especially Moira who has the biggest potty mouth out of anyone.
- Claire's chapters focus more on combat and Barry on puzzles and logic which separates them in more than jsut the story, it's something to look forward to when switching.
- Each episode takes around 2- 4 to complete, if you're taking your time, making the game last about 11 hours which is decent for a survival horror.
- When doing certain actions you gain XP which you can spend on skills and abilities which really help you survive.
- There's a decent variety of enemies which are remiscent of ones from 3 - 6. Classic zombie type enemies, some ganado type and other boss types that have a big glowing orange blob that screams "shoot here!".
- The online co-op mode is really fun if you can find a friend to tackle it with, lots of replayability and unlockables.
- Same goes for achievements and single player unlockables, plenty to go for.
- The graphics are pretty nice from both gameplay and cutscenes.

NEUTRAL
- You can choose which weapons your AI characters use but sometimes they will swap to the knife randomly which gets annoying when you need them to cover you.
- The final bosses are usually somewhat tricky in each game (minus one or two tricks) but in this one it's pretty easy.
- There are two endings that is defined by one choice made in one episode. I usually wouldn't mind but it cuts a chunk of the end of the game if you chose the wrong one. It's not even a good/bad choice either so it's hard to tell.

CON
- Partner characters can be a little annoying when they get killed because they won't run away from the enemies and instead try to take them on with a knife.
- I get that they want to make the AI more useful so they need to give them their own thing. Natalia can spot enemies and Moira can blind/stun them. But why are they the only ones who can find items?

Revelations 2 is a really fun game and a must have for any fan of Resident Evil. You'll find a lot more here than you did in 5 and 6 as well as some great additions.

[b]Resident Evil Revelations 2[/b] is a third person shooter game set in Resident Evil universe. It's not a direct sequel to any of the previous games, even though it has a number in the name. The story focuses on characters, who already appeared in the series, but it also introduces some of the new ones as well. Game is divided into 4 episodes like a TV show. Each episode is divided into two parts, in the first part you play as Claire Redfield and Moira Burton, who were kidnapped by terrorists and placed on some god-forsaken island full of monsters. In the second part you play as Barry Burton, Moira's father, who's trying to find his daughter. He also has a partner, a little girl named Natalia, who just happened to survive on an island full of monsters. 

The gameplay is almost identical for both character duos, Claire and Barry have guns and Moira and Natalia can find hidden items and unlock special crates. You can switch between characters at any moment or play local coop with your friend. You go through mostly linear stages shooting everyone in sight. When playing as Barry you can also make stealth kills, but you probably don't need to waste your time, because you always have a lot of ammo. Sometimes you come across a simple puzzles or on open-ended level, where you have to go through one path, then go back and open the other.  It feels like any other third-person shooter. There aren't many enemy types and there are no unique weapons, so it gets boring pretty fast.

The graphics feel cheap, textures resolution is noticeably low and lighting is somewhat strange. Animations are ok though. Moving on to the sound, voice acting is great in this game and dialogue feels more natural than in the Resident evil 1 and 0. Soundtrack is almost unnoticable, so it's ok.

Now onto the goodies. 

Setting:
I like the setting of this game. Setting in between RE 5 and RE 6. Uroboros virus is now in the hands of a new antagonist in an island. There is a lot of F***ed up s*** going on in the lore of the place that it is creepy. I wouldn't say that it is scary, but creepy. You're in an island and on this island, people are infected and experimented on through physical torture to trigger the virus. You get to see and read about people who were tortured. Also they show you what happens 6 months after you arrive in the island through Barry's story which I thought was cool. This is definitely the creepier one among the third person Resident Evils.

I like that in some instance, what you do in Claire's story affects Barry's, like if you kill the boss 6 months before, you won't have to kill this boss 6 months into the story. 

I thought the good ending of this game was really good. It sets up so many possibilities for future Resident Evil titles using a well known antagonist in the game.

Raid:

This is a really good Resident Evil game that suffers from a consumer-unfriendly business model, and lack of information as to what you are getting/supposed to get.

Instead of buying the Deluxe Edition, just buy the main game and the RER2 Episodes Two, Three, and Four. That's already the complete story.
