One good thing about the game that isn't pointed out much is that it has the most replayability out of all the Resident Evil games that preceded it. Its Raid Mode is not just you replaying missions - each mission is instanced and different from the main campaign, with character progression that unlocks costumes, upgrades weapons and skills. Once you're done with the main campaign, you can spend the rest of your playtime doing the Raid Mode in short bursts. Since the zombies here are classic slow RE zombies (as opposed to the fast ones in RE5 and 6), it's a more accessible mode even to casuals.

Don't know what everyone is on about this one. Clearly says "Episode 1" if you purchase the first "game". Reading, people, is a handy skill. 
 
That being said, the deluxe edition is very often reduced by 66-75%, and even at 50% (every episode/dlc is in that one) this game is a steal if you dwell in nostalgic memories of actual survival (horror), like RE 1/2/3/4, where the first playthrough really feels unique and charming. Just shooting won't get you anywhere here, except on casual difficulty. More or less likeable characters/quotes, but the world and the gameplay feels great, especially the first time you start each episode up. None really dissapointed, except maybe the 4th part with Claire which seems like a budget cut (because it's really short). Enemies and (mini)-bosses feel mostly fair to be fought against - the more you fight them, the easier you will get rid of them. So everyone can git gud with a bit of dedication. 

Raid mode is pretty decent given it's an addition with quite a good amount of missions, that can be done on various difficulties, cramping up the challenge quite a bit. Resident Evil: Revelations 1 and its raid mode is way harder and requires a lot of grind/help from others, because the difficulty is so damn out of hands starting around the middle of the mode itself. 
Revelations 2 takes a step back there, adds the ability to use skills with every character (and negating the annoying set-character-trait from its predecessor) and, in general, brings a good, arcade-style-vibe in it. Not necessarily something for everyone, at least not getting the most overpowered items and upgrading them to oblivion, but nonetheless fun for a while. I enjoyed playing it on my own with a bunch of characters (only 1 is level 100 though), co-op is definetely an option, but not necessary to perform well. Enemies come in different variants, with multiple, possible traits, from both revelations 1 and 2, so that's also a cool thing (you get for free).

If Capcom would have given the Revelations-Series a bigger budget and more experienced developers, this game could have been a lot bigger. Kinda feels like some aspiring developers got a bit of money from mother Capcom and made Revelations 1 and afterwards the 2nd part, which is a lot better in almost every regard. Seems like based on the progress made here, they decided to re-work Resident Evil 2 in this kind of way. Gonna be fun, at the very least, I can imagine - Probably overpriced, but looks fun.

So, to summarize, buy the deluxe package on a good sale. The campaign is fun (co-op is local only though), has a bunch of different modes for a bit of replay-value, and there's also the arcade-style-shooter (with lvling up) called raid-mode, playing solo or co-op (online, this time, is a thing). Overall, a good recommendation for 10-15 bucks. Easily one of the best of the modern Resident Evil series, just fell short on budget sadly as it seems. Big hopes for a possible Revelations 3 and a bigger development team behind it.

Quick Summary: Resident Evil Revelations 2 is a Third Person Shooter with light puzzle solving mechanics, and is more action packed than Revelations 1, but less spooky. If you liked the first Revelations game, you should enjoy this one too. Raid Mode, which was the best part of the first game has been expanded this time around and is easier for the most part. Unfortunately, there aren’t many people playing online anymore, so if you want to play Raid Mode cooperatively, you’ll need to bring your own friend. There is no online campaign co-op (I believe split screen is available). 

The game’s story takes place some time between Resident Evil 5 and 6, with some quick mention of the events in Resident Evil Revelations 1. You do not need to have played the first Revelations to understand what’s going on here, but it certainly helps. None of the characters from Revelations 1 return in this game though (except as playable characters in Raid Mode). This game follows 2 “teams” of people that you may recognize if you’ve played the earlier RE games, Barry Burton and Claire Redfield. Your overall goal is to escape a mysterious island infested with various people/monsters who are infected by something similar to the Ouroboros virus from RE5, including a few bosses. The game’s main villain has weird-ass motivations, but who cares since you’re mostly just trying to stay alive.

If you’ve played Revelations 1, the gameplay will be extremely familiar. The camera follows your character from about 6 feet behind so Claire/Barry takes up about 25% of the screen. Most of the enemies in the game are fairly slow once they get close to you, so you should have no difficulty blasting them with your guns. Melee combat is generally a bad idea unless the enemy has been stunned with a headshot, then you can run up and use a powerful punch/kick, just like RE 5/6/Revelations 1. Ammunition is only semi-common so using the contextual melee attack is a good way to avoid wasting it. Note that enemies do not drop ammo when they die, and you don’t get experience/money for killing them during the campaign. This means it’s often a good idea to just run past enemies whenever possible, especially on hard mode. They won’t follow you through doors, but a few of them are fast enough to catch you, so keep an eye out. 

The game’s campaign is broken up into 4 episodes (about an hour and a half each if you like to explore), and each of these episodes has 2 sections: One as Claire and her companion, the other as Barry and his companion. Revelations 1 also gave you a partner through most of the game, but this time around you can switch between characters at almost any time with the push of a button. For example, Claire’s companion Moira has a crowbar and a flashlight, allowing her to open doors and boxes that Claire can’t open, and Moira can use her flashlight to blind certain enemies (a little like Alan Wake) or reveal hidden items (like the scanner in Revelations 1). Claire is the one with the guns though, so most of the time you’ll probably be controlling her in combat. Inventory management is a challenge, just like previous Resident Evil games, so if you like to collect everything you find you’ll end up throwing a lot away throughout the game to make room (like the various bandages). Fortunately, all your characters have separate inventories. So, if Claire’s full of ammo and healing herbs, move extra items to Moira’s inventory.

There are also a couple of difficult “challenge” modes that you can unlock for the single player campaign: Countdown mode and Invisible mode. In Countdown, there is a clock that starts around 3 minutes, and constantly runs down toward zero, and you need to play through the single player campaign as fast as possible before your time runs out. Killing enemies adds a few seconds to the clock, depending on the strength of the enemy. The game difficulty for Countdown is locked on “normal” and you can’t bring your inventory from previous playthroughs (in regular campaign mode, you can replay episodes with your current inventory, like a New Game+). I barely beat the first episode on Countdown mode and didn’t even try the others, too stressful. In Invisible mode, the enemies cannot be seen unless you use your companion’s detection ability to make them show up briefly (for example you need to switch to Moira and use her flashlight to see the enemies, then quickly switch back to Claire and blast them before they move too far). Invisible mode is locked on “survival” mode, the hard mode difficulty, and making enemies invisible certainly doesn’t help. I only got half way through the first episode before I gave up. Just like Countdown mode, you start from scratch with no gear, so there’s no “cheating.”

Just like the first Revelations, there’s a chance that you’re only playing the game for Raid mode, which is where most multiplayer comes into play. In Raid mode, you choose one of about a dozen different Resident Evil characters (some characters are DLC), each with different “skills,” to take on short missions in familiar environments. The levels are from previous Resident Evil games and you’ll probably recognize a few of them, including the enemies that show up there (a lot of them don’t show up in this game’s campaign, only Raid mode). Every character levels up independently by completing missions, but you share money / weapons / upgrades among all your characters. I mentioned earlier that Raid mode in Revelations 2 is easier than in the first game, and what I mean is that these Raid missions are very linear and short. There’s no “Ghost Ship” type mission that takes 30-45 minutes of exploring. Most of the time you just need to run to the end of the level, killing about 30 enemies along the way to finish (about 6 minutes per mission). There are more enemy types and more “elite” enemies, but as long as you keep upgrading your guns you shouldn’t have too much trouble until you’re in the real hardcore levels. It takes a really long time to reach level 100 though.

You should play Revelations 2 if:
+You enjoyed the first Resident Evil Revelations game, or Resident Evil 5 or 6. These are action games taking place in horror environments, not exactly survival horror. The locations are creepy and the enemies are disgusting, which is probably what you’re looking for in a Resident Evil game.
+You have a friend that you want to play co-op with in Raid mode. Don’t go in thinking you’ll find some random person to play with on the matchmaking system. There’s nobody playing anymore. 

You should Not play Revelations 2 if:
-You thought the first game sucked. It’s mostly the same type of game. You don’t need to hoard door keys in Raid mode this time around. There’s still some backtracking in the campaign because Barry goes through most of the same areas as Claire, sometimes in reverse order.

Resident Evil as a series is a little unpredictable. For every good one, there are some real stinkers. This game therefore sits in a unique position of being a good game, with it's own stinker attached. Some take issue with the split campaign, and find one better than the other. I'm of the mind on the other hand that both are good, but both have a character that sucks to use, and the shifts between the two are the main cause of contention between the player and the game. This is mostly because of the games episodic structure -a trend I'm so glad we got out of- which pumps the breaks on each character right as things get interesting.

Here's the thing though, despite those facts, I think it's a really solid entry in the series for a few reasons. For one, the gameplay when playing as the attacker of the 2 characters feels good, it's derivative of Resident Evil 4, sure, but that game felt good to control and this one feels fine by extension. More importantly though, the story in this one feels pretty good by Resi standards. Sure it's as absurd as any Resident Evil, but it's of the fun, tries to be scary but ends up a weird mixture of camp but also unsettling just like Resident Evil 4 type. If you're beginning to notice a pattern, good, you've been paying attention. What I guess I'm getting at is that this game is pretty much Resident Evil 4 diet. It's not quite as good, but it's still fun, and if you want another good Resident Evil 4 type game, this one is pretty quality.

There is one last thing I should mention though, because it is so good. The aesthetics of this game are fantastic in looks, sound and general feel. The theme of the game is Kafka, and while it's not exactly as nuanced as that would imply, this means the narrative of the game involves not belonging, fear, pain and general isolation. The monsters are tremendously messed up and the environments are horribly run down and threatening. It's the kinda thing you feel like you need to take a shower and wrap yourself in a blanket after playing because it's just so miserable. To give you an idea of how much of this game's quality comes from it's bomb-ass designs, I'm giving them their own paragraph just to gush about how good they are. They take a normal Resident Evil 4 style game with it's unique mechanic debatably causing more harm than good, and bump it up to some high tier stuff. It enriches the story, gameplay and overall experience.

Pick it up if you want something like Resident Evil 4, but that isn't Resident Evil 4.

And well, it's feels like Revelations title but also different enough. This time campaign levels are linear, you don't backtrack. Well, instead you get to play as two characters that share some locations. Some. Claire and Barry. Yes, Barry bloody Burton is back. And he is badass, a daddy and cracks few jokes and game even makes some of the original RE1 stupidness canon. Too bad he is not the Master of Memes this time around, even if he is self-aware. And he gets to do stealth killing. Claire can do it too technically, but monsters aren't positioned for that in her levels. Yea, there is a bit of stealth to spice it up. He gets more ammo for frontal attack too, for some reason.

The more unique thing is asymmetrical coop. Each one of our two main character has their own supporting character. Who usually can't do much, they mostly do stuff like pointing or throwing a brick in. There is some chance that players who play as them will end up being bored but dunno, I haven't tried. Good for non-hardcore friends. Sadly, Capcom decided that it should be for local splitscreen only, there is no online option. WHY?! Also, this option is semi-hidden in PC version too. I heard that you are required to have two controllers to get it.

Otherwise, you have to play with AI, switching between them to find hidden objects in the room, so you will mostly explore new locations as support characters. Good thing is that somehow made switching between character feel comfortably fast, somehow I wasn't annoyed at all. Quite a rare accomplishment. I also was really mad at AI partner until I learned that support characters regenerate health. And if they take heavy damage, you can recover them. So never switch to support characters during fight.

There is a good and bad ending. Which one you get depends on what you do at one point in the game. So be worried, it might end up being a tragic tale, mhm. Well, the plot is pretty fine. Not too unique. And sometimes you do get boring big sewer locations. At least this game can be proud, for it was able to give few actually creepy moments where I felt uncomfortable about going forward. Quite an accomplishment for Resident Evil series, before RE7. Especially the forest.
Actually, it managed to scare me too. But it had to do with me sprinting like an idiot at some point than a proper jumpscare.

But dunno, this game doesn't feel like a complete positive experience for some reason. Can't tell why. Just feels like devs didn't get to do it fully. It probably has to do with one of the mechanics of Revelations 1: putting weapon parts that increase stats into weapons. I guess that there was not enough of them or it didn't play big enough part of it. Or maybe the game was not inspired enough at times. Yea, that too. While other parts are great. And it does feel somewhat more Resident Evil calm, there is not a single turret section, for example.

Still, if you have two controllers (or just console versions) and got a friend for local coop, it's worth a try, I am super sure. But I feel that Revelations 1 was more complete, proper experience. Felt better. This one is nice too. Loved atmosphere.

Oh, there is Raid mode too. It feels like a proper mode now, compared to Revelations, having unique arena levels from RE6 where enemies spawn in when needed. And more of interesting leveling, I guess. Not sure, it feels like a complete experience. Too bad that people say that it's too easy in this game, unlike Rev1. Oh, and I should mention that the combat in this game, like in Rev1, is simplified compared to main games. Even tho this time you got a proper dodge button unlike who-knows-how-to-do-it in Rev1. So it's not as good as Mercenaries modes in main games, instead doing Raid things that is leveling up and other RPG stuff of grinding and special properties on both weapons and enemies.

Resident evil revelations 2 has been a fun package so far and I'm still playing to do finish up achievements and I've barely touched raid mode although I have played a bit.
The entire main game is split between 2 parts of a story, one where you play as Claire and Moira trying find out why they are on the island, how to get off and how to stop what's going on whilst the other half you play as Barry and Natalia wanting to save moira and finding out about an enemy fimiliar to Barry with each episode having a bit of both, first Claire and Moira, then Barry and Natalia. 

I quite like the gameplay, it's not super complex but it doesn't need to be. Most of the combat consist of shooting at enemies and dodging with some differences in what you encounter during Claire and Moira's part and Barry and Natalia's part.
As Claire and Moira ammo is often a bit tight but you'll only have to fight off against simple enemies for the most part. The lack of frequent ammo finds makes it important to preserve ammo for when you do have to face off against a more difficult enemy so for that you have moira's flashlight, as Moira can't use guns she uses her somehow mega bright item detecting flashlight to stun enemies by shining in their face giving Claire the opertunity to knock them down where Moira can then perform an excecution, her flashlight can also be used to find slightly less obvious items to stock up and a hidden collectable called Kafka Drawings.

When playing as Barry and Natalia you come better equiped and you find more ammo to face the enemies on the island and so you face a wider aray of enemies that require you to get to their weakspot and pump that full of lead. This time Barry has the guns AND flashlight, however for some reason it's not bright enough or something to reveal hidden images, items or stun monsters. But for not having that you have a small girl with you called Natalia that can use her short length to crawl trough small spaces that Barry can't get through. Natalia also has a special power where she can detect monsters through walls and see where their weakspot is located, she can also use her magic finger to point out where items are that you previously had to use Moira's flashlight for. When playing as Barry and Natalia you also sometimes encounter parts where you are able to stealth past enemies, sneaking up behind them and finishing them off with one quick execution.
For those who think of stealth sections in disgust, you have to note that stealthing is very much optional and there is no real penalty for just shooting them or even just running away besides from saving some health and ammo, and even then, I still recomend trying it as it's really not bad and I quite enjoyed sneaking around.

As for the story, it's a neat experience to experience with some questions arising early on with more along the way and a couple of twists as you alternate between the Claire and Moira story and the Barry and Natalia story that weave together eventually leading to a fun conclussion. And as someone who has never played any other resident evil games I can say that I was easily able to understand the story minus some parts like reoccuring names and stuff although you don't NEED to know those, it mostly makes it more interesting for people who have played the other games.

For the raid mode, the little I have played of it I played with a friend and we were having a blast the whole way through, it's a way more arcade-y shooter where you clear out the enemies but that's just the fun distraction some people need, it opens up more as you progress through the game and even has some things not present in the main game for added enjoyment.

Now there are of course some gripes I have with the game and I'd like to adress them here.
In the way of unlocking extras the game feels a bit unsatisfying to me as when you unlock something you don't actually get it, instead you get the ability to buy it with ingame points that you also use to upgrade your character which to me at least kindof undermines your acomplishments. Some enemies also felt WAY too tanky to me whilst being able to utterly obliterate you in 2 attacks like the Dhurlga you encounter at multiple points during Barry's parts and [spoiler] Mutant Pedro having way too hard to hit weakspots sometimes whilst having an instantkill attack where he rushes at you with his drill, it was way too easy too fall off the crane in barry's episode 4 [/spoiler] and some parts send you back a bit too far when you died in my opinion. I also find it weird that there is online multiplayer in raid mode but the main story is local only.

Now to adress some problems I frequently see people talk about.
Yes, the game is episodic but when you buy the game with the 3 other episodes or get the deluxe edition it's still around the same price or even cheaper than some of the other games in the series. And to those who were angry about not buying a full game, they make it quite clear that this is just the first episode, both in the name, the about section and the DLC list.
You must also know that this isn't a full on horror game, besides from a couple of quick spooks for the unaware and some enemy designs I guess it really isn't so if pure horror is what you're looking for you might not like this. However, as an action game it's a fun experience with a slight amount of ammo management.

Concerning the price, If you're only planning to play through the story made and not touch it again I might suggest waiting until a sale to get it but if you take your time to try and go for the achievements and/or you sink some time in the arcade style fun that is raid mode with a friend you might be able to consider getting it even at full price.

All in all, I think this game is great fun and definitely worth picking up at least some time.

In RE:R2, the Complete Edition, the game is splitted into 4 Chapters (+2 Bonus Chapters) and the Raid Mode.
The 4 Main Champers are also divided into 2 seperate Campaigns. 
One, where you play as Claire Redfield & Moira Burton.
One, where you play as Barry Burton and Natalia. (6 Months after the Events of Claire's Campaign)
You will visit some of the same locations twice, but with different enemies or twists.
Claire and Barry are your Weapon Users, while Moira uses a Flashlight to stun enemies for a strong Combo Attack and Natalia can use Wallhack Abilities, I mean, "sense" Enemies through Walls. 
This Abiliy is mostly used to see Weakspots of Enemies or for one Special Enemy Type, which can't be seen by the bare eye. I loved this Enemy in Barrys Campaign and how Natalia's AI worked in those Situations.
Total Playtime for the Campaign ca. 10 Hours.

"The Struggle" is a Bonus Campaign, where you play as Moira. It's really short and you have to do different tasks here, like go hunting animals, reach the goal before time runs out, or defent yourself agains a set amount of enemies. It's also Story related.
"Little Miss" is the second Bonus Campaign. It's kind of like a stealth-puzzle task you have to do. You play as Natalia and you have to avoid all enemies with Stealth and reach the end. You can't fight, if you're getting spotted, you're dead.

Positives:
+ Barrys Campaign (Loved it! Cool Enemies & Locations, Partner AI worked really well here, Stealth Possibilities)
+ Raid Mode is awesome as ever (diablo-esque gameplay, gather loot, level you character, etc.)
+ It feels like action survival horror (low on ammo, items, enemies are a threat)
+ Good and Clever Puzzles
+ Story is fine for a Resident Evil Game
+ Character Models look detailed

Neutral:
- Playing as 2 Characters (Awesome in Barrys Campaign, Disaster in Claire's Campaign)
- Graphics overall are really poor or even ugly, but the lightning effects and dark areas makes it look fine in some areas.
- Soundtrack was nothing special. I really loved the Music in Revelations 1, that's why I was hoping for some cool tracks here, but didn't get it.
- not as creepy in atmosphere as the first Revelations, but it has it's moments. Most of the time, it's just flesh and gore.
- Claire's Campaign: It had some cool ideas and moments but (See Bad)

Bad:
- The Partner-AI in Claire's Campaign (Oh my god, it was TERRIBLE! They get hit all the time, huge Green Herb Waste! Melee options are really efficient for saving ammo, but AI won't leave the melee area after performing a combo attack and can't dodge attacks, so you either waste Herbs for AI or your precious Bullets)
- Difficulty in Claire's Campaign can feel cheap or even unfair (too many enemies, fast and bulletsponges, areas are often times too small when you're fighting enemies, Rare Stealth Possibilities)

I recommend this game. It isn't as good as the first Revelations Game in my personal opinion, because this game just has too much flaws in Claire's Campaign which frustrated me, but if you can deal with some unfair situations, you will enjoy this game.

Resident Evil Revelations 2 is a very underrated RE game with a brilliant atmosphere and control scheme dynamic that allows you to switch between two different characters. Throughout the campaign, you will play as different pairs of characters--one pair as Claire and Moira and the other pair as Barry and Natalia. Their stories intertwine by crossing the same setting and areas, but displayed from a different angle and story.

The characters are likeable, but the character development never fleshes out into anything meaningful. Just when you get to a point in the game where the characters could develop an emotional connection, Capcom loses sight of that and throws you back into the old Resident Evil trope. This isn't necessarily a bad thing if you have played Resident Evil games before. It is kinda what you would expect with this franchise.

"Resident Evil Revelations 2" is an emo 3rd person, over-the-shoulder shooter with a disappointily sleepy pace.

The movement system is absolutely as good as it gets in Resident Evil. It allows us to dodge and weave while aiming or shooting and gives us a wide view of ourselves in the world. We can crouch, sneak-takedown, and change characters to interact with the environment in new ways. Mobility was a crucial piece that's been sorely lacking in every Resident Evil game. Here, it has arrived.

But more than that, the mood here is chilling and the zombies take exactly the right number of shots to drop so they genuinely feel like zombies. There are multiple characters we can swap between in-game, and the way one set of characters manipulates the environment before the second set arrives, is both stirring and rewardingly new (for the mere 2 chapters that it is allowed to happen). Add to that first rate graphics and "Resident Evil Revelations 2" feels like the adventure this overrated series has been striving towards since Day 1, pretty much. The first Chapter feels like the best RE game you could imagine!

Except that actually, it's all just a little boring.

As well-designed as "Revelations 2" is, the game beyond Chapter 1 is also incredibly low energy, some might say, sleepy. This feeling is made worse by the fact that the world lends itself to wandering, the puzzles are highly tedius, and overlooking the path to the next stage of the game is far too easy. A lot of time is wasted in this game running about trying to sort out 'what next?' We often forget about having Fun. Fights are hectic but brief. There is very little gaming momentum here at all. 

So what's the state of a series when simply having a functional clean interface is enough for the highest score of the series? No. That's the bare minimum. We deserve more from the actual gameplay!

"Resident Evil Revelations 2" is a well-designed game which drags its weary self across a lifeless finish line.

Even though Resident Evil: Revelations 2 is a spin off, this could have been one of the best Resident Evil games. It had the potential. But many flawed design decisions make it only a good Resident Evil game. I recommend this, but not for full price. You're better off with Resident Evil 7.

Here's why, in case you want to know:
Resident Evil: Revelations 2 have a bit of horror, few resources and less super human characters(as Revelations 1 also did). The gameplay is good and responsive (besides being a little strange when using mouse. Mouse aiming doesn't seem to be well implemented in this game). You are in control of two Characters at the same time. It's similar to Resident Evil 0, except you can play almost the whole game without changing characters if you want. Some people do not like this two characters feature but, in this case, I don't think it's a real issue since, as I said, it's not mandatory to change characters, except for a few times in the game. And you have two campaigns: Claire/Moire and Barry/Natalia. But you can not choose between the two, they play one in between the other and you do not have the option to not play Claire/Moire or Barry/Natalia campaign for instance. The story is also kind of interesting, specially Barry's segment and the ending moments of the game, presenting a potential new big villain for the series.

The problem is: It's only interesting during Barry's campaign. Claire's campaign is a bit more action based. But it's not really fun, honestly. Claire never was a great character, in my opinion, and in this game is even worse. She seems to be there just for fan service. Moira, which is Barry's daughter and a boring character, in my opinion, even manages to be more interesting than Claire. Their story segment is also not really interesting, being mostly about Moira's bad relationship with Barry (She uses Claire to vent most of the time and that's almost everything about their campaign). 

On the other hand, Barry is a more well developed character in this game. Revelations 2 managed to turn Barry from only a "Jill Sandwitch" and "Master of Unlocking" reference, to one of the best RE characters for me. His Campaign is about protecting a little girl(Natalia, the other character you control) compensating for his failures with his daughter. Also, he's trying to find his daughter. But, because he is trying to find her, in his campaign, you'll play once again in the same areas that you've been in Claire/Moira campaign, and this turns very repetitive in about 30% of the game, which is one of it's biggest flaws for me(If only we could not play Claire's campaign...) 

Also, the setting of the game is not really attractive for these initial 30% of the game, which makes everything more of a struggle to complete. You're mostly in some generic Russian Island setting, with generic old villages and generic abbandoned places. The setting becomes great, though, when you make it to the factory, which is amazing. From this part on is where you begin to really play Revelations 2 on it's best. You'll be on this factory, sewers, mines, labs and even, once again, in a Mansion. But, not everything is sunshine and rainbows for this game's design. As I said, there's many flaws during the levels. Specially with the invisible enemies that can kill you with one single hit.

These enemies turn the 60% of the game into a very frustrating experience some times. Natalia is supposed to see these invisible enemies and point them for you to shoot. But the AI is not very well made for this... She tells you where to shoot, you shoot, and the monster is not there. Not to mention the frequent times when she doesn't tell you a thing at all and you have to guess all by yourself or change characters and try to find the monster, then change back again to Barry and, even doing this, you may still miss the monster. All of this results in an absurd waste of bullets. And I didn't even mentioned yet that most of the time these monsters appear in the game, they're accompanied by many other enemies and you have to manage all the situation without touching the invisible ones, otherwise, you'll face his touch of death. There is times where these monsters appears in those classic RE countdown sequences, where you have to run your way to escape collapsing places and BAM, there's an invisible touch of death monster ridiculously placed in a tiny corridor and you're dead. Very anti-climatic.
To end this huge review, I would like to mention that boss battles are not very funny, also. They're mostly bullet sponges and all you have to do is run far away from them, shoot, shoot, and shoot, repeat. There's some more challenging sequences with normal enemies and sub bosses during the game, actually.

If it were not for these tiny and easy to solve, but very annoying flaws, this game could have been amazing. Unfortunately, its not. But it's a good game if you can buy it for a cheap price and it's a decent RE game to pass you time if you do not have anything great to play(like Resident Evil 7).

Long time till I didn't feel so satisfied while playing a Resident Evil game. This is what I will truly call a "return to the origin" for the series. What I truly don't understand is why this game is so underrated and watched with skepticism, while RE 7 is considered like the messiah of the survival horror genre. For sure nobody like games divided in episodes, so probably this choice is what affected much the credibility of Revelations 2. I will like, to my opinion, to compare a bit the two games.

Revelations 2 has an interesting gameplay, rooted in the best way to what modern RE games has to offer, but without forgetting the survival nature of the game. The ammunitions are few, and the physical attacks are useless with the 90% of the enemies. I never felt bothered by the forced coop, and always find alternative tactics like using Moira to blind the enemies or killing them with a stealth attack very satisfying. Some cheap solution like the almost immortality of Moira and some abilities that can be acquired can damage a bit the gameplay, but without any dramatic changes. 

Regarding RE7, the game is a sort of FPS without any true root with RE. The game is more like Outlast with a combat system, a very simplified and boring combat system, as well as the general gameplay. True, the exploration is great with puzzles to solve and a truly scary environment, but this is valid only for the first half of the game. Then RE7 even lost these positive points.

In Revelations 2 some chapters are better than others, especially chapter 3, while some moments can be a bit annoying. The enemy design is very original and interesting, with creatures that looks like to be inspired by Hellraiser, tormented and twisted in body and soul. There are many enemies and few bosses, each of them required a specific tactic to be defeated. A sort of invisible insect can be identified only using Natalia, and can kill you with one touch when too close, while other abominations can be killed only identifying their weak points hidden under the skin, also using Natalia. One of the strongest point in every Resident Evil game was the enemy design, and Revelations 2 truly do a brilliant work to provide new and terrifying foes. Also there are no "common faces", every enemy is new so forget about seeing the usual Hunters or Lickers. Also the abominations are more believable, so there are no giant monsters obscuring the sun or people with Dragonball-style superpowers.

RE7 offers very few standard enemies (like 4 i think), without any difference in the strategy to kill them. There are few uninspired bosses, and some immortal stalkers during the main game. So "the best RE in decades" also lost one of the best fature since RE1: a variegate and creepy enemy design. 

Some of the main characters, like Barry and Natalia, are very interesting, well developed and the player will have a natural bond with them. The island is an interesting and scary environment, with a constant sense of dread. The history is nothing special, with few plot holes, but it is enough interesting to keep you playing, especially for a very well defined and creepy main antagonist. The final boss is scary, twisted and a very deep and interesting fight, one of the best in the saga. Also the history is well rooted in the saga, with connections and references with other games. Finally the game offers a very mature plot, without cheesy, over the top or forced comedy moments... well maybe a couple of things, but the overall experience is mature and tense.

RE7 has very flat characters with a very anonymous protagonist. Some members of the family are a bit interesting, but they also look sometime too much an excessive caricature, more than a truly scary enemy. They are also there "just to be there", without any truly purpose or main goal. The plot is also totally forced to fit inside Resident Evil, with viruses and experiments that looks totally out of the atmosphere. 

Revelations 2 is also full of secrets, with several modes like Invisible enemies, time attack and the usual Mercenary style. There are also many hidden weapons to obtain, from giant power drills to the usual infinite rocket launcher, this will keep you busy for many hours. Also, only to finish the main campaign at normal difficulty will be necessary around 13 hours.

RE7 has very few replayability and a couple of secret things. The main campaign can be finished in like 8 hours.

So why RE7 is considered the best game in the saga in decades, and Revelations 2 is so underrated? Do we really just want a scary FPS from this saga in the future?

This is just my quick opinion and a comparison of the last two Resident Evil games in the saga. Both are interesting games, but I think the way Revelations 2 was developed is the future of the saga (except dividing it in episodes), not RE7.

I grew up with the RE series, and if I'm honest, I really disliked RE6, I thought this would be more of that, and I wasn't entirely wrong.

I'll leave a [b]TL;DR[/b] at the very end if you don't want to read a novel from some nerd on the internet.

[h1]Overview[/h1]

RER2 is an episodic resident evil game that focuses on short two part campaigns, which themselves focus on individual pairs of characters (Claire Redfield and Moira Burton, Barry Burton and Natalia Kord, etc.)

Each episode is fairly short, about a 30 minutes each part, so 1 hour total. there are 4 episodes (6 if you include the extra episodes), though, and each has additional modes liked Timed, where you have a certain amount of time to finish the part, and invisible enemies, which you can guess what that does.

Each episode is about 6 USD, which intotal will cost you about 30USD total to get all the episodes, or the full game if you will.

Accompanying Story Mode is Raid Mode, which is where the majority of this review will be focused (since I mostly play that.)

[h1]Gameplay[/h1]

[b]Story Mode[/b] is fairly tough, you get just enough ammunition and healing items to get through, you need to really be careful with how you spend your resources, which I very much like. Unlike RE6, you don't just go into a room with an assault rifle and hold the trigger down until either your rifle melts into a puddle of molten polymer, or everything in that room is dead 4 times before it hit the ground.

Healing items are fairly easy to get a hold of, which can make it fairly mistake friendly, though, the enemies will mostly 2 - 3 shot you even in the medium difficulty, so again, you really need to watch yourself.

Ammunition is hard to get a hold of and enemies can take a lot of shots for the most part. You can stun them and kick them in the face to kill them easier, usually.

Each character has their own [i]'thing'[/i], Claire has a lot of guns, Moira has a flashlight that stuns enemies and locates items. Barry/Natalia's part is pretty much the same, but with the exception that Natalia can't stun enemies, but see them through walls, like a Combat Arms player.

[b]Raid Mode[/b] is where I found a lot of the fun, it's basically an RPG mode. You pick a character, level them, their skills, and get loot (parts and guns), the more you play and higher level you are, the better the guns you can find/buy. Think Borderlands, but [i]without[/i] Mr. Torgue.

This mode is repetitive, but there are a HUGE amount of stages/enemies, many times spawning with unique traits such as a frontal shield, being covered in ice, stuff like that. Almost all the stages from RE6 return here, as well as stages from RER2. It's all just enough to keep it from getting stale.

Raid Mode is very grindy, I have 25+ hours in it alone and my highest character is level 71, max level being 100. If you need a good time killer, Raid mode is a good choice, and you get a decent amount of it's content with just Episode One (base game).

My biggest issue with this mode is that leveling will be very inconsistent without multiple episodes. I've been getting by with episode one and two, and at level 58 I needed to grind to 62 to take on the next level of content (66+).

There is a LOT of DLC you kind of need such as storage space since you'll be getting tons of parts later game, you start with 75 slots, which isn't much, and can buy up-to 300 slots! You can of course combine 2 parts to a higher level one at the Toolbox, but...

... The tool box requires episodes to upgrade. If you don't have episode two, you'll be full of level 4 parts that you can do nothing with, if you don't have episode three, you'll be full of level 6 parts, and these things go up to level 13!

In the end, I love raid mode, it's fun to progress, and you can play co-op in it! (Not in the story mode, though, just a heads up.) You can even play as HUNK!

[h1]Visuals[/h1]

Graphically, it looks alright. It's a 2015 game so don't expect next gen graphics. It's comparable to RE6 in terms of looks.

The story mode set pieces are very pleasing visually. They're just dark enough to merit a flashlight, but you can still see well enough without one if you so choose. (oir if Moira decided she didn't feel like holding it right now...)

Characters look great, there's some good details in the story mode such as seeing your weapons on your back/hip and the character interacting with them. Enemies look great as well, they're all quite gross/intimidating.

One thing I need to note is in Raid mode, Gestures are very stiff and awkward, I swear they had two different interns make these in their spare time.

[h1]Sound[/h1]

Sound is overall very high quality as expected, lip syncing for the characters can be a bit questionable, but the voice actors all sound excellent and the characters voices fit great, enemies sound great with the exception of the Hunter, they don't sound as scary as they have in the past, they mostly just click at you.

Guns sound alright, they're a bit weak sounding but otherwise fine, they're distinctive enough to tell the difference between them. In Raid mode, the mosin nagant with a charge shot is amazing sounding, and probably the best sounding weapon in the game!

However, in Raid mode, some characters have some off putting lines. HUNK for example, his Sorry! line is very clearly [i]not[/i] the same voice actor who dubbed the rest of his lines.

[b]TL;DR[/b]

[h1]Good[/h1]
+Story Mode is slow and difficult as it should be
+Raid Mode is fast and fun as it should be
+Game looks good
+Sound overall is very good
+Base game is only 6 USD
+HUNK is playable!
+Wesker is playable
+Co-op in Raid Mode

[h1]Bad[/h1]
-There is a LOT of DLC that can be needed to progress in Raid mode
-Raid mode gets extremely grindy
-Some animations are very questionable in quality
-Episodes are way too short
-No co-op in Story Mode
-Bonus Story Mode difficulties are fairly dull (Timed, Invisible Enemies.)

Ending Note: If you can get the complete edition, a few of my complaints are null, raid mode is a lot easier with all the storage upgrades and gauntlets. Also, HUNK is in this game!

I didn't know what to expect from either RE: Revelations game going in, but I think Revelations 2 might be one of my favorite titles in the series as a whole. Like the first, it brings back a sense of tension and unease that is sorely lacking from, say, Resident Evil 6, and in particular improves upon the controls and general mechanics of the first.

Taking place between RE 5 and 6, This installment sees series regular Claire Redfield, promoted-from-background-character Moira Burton, fan favorite and professional papa bear Barry Burton (complete with modified revolver) and a strange little girl named Natalia pitted against the mutated horrors of a strange russian mining town on a lonely island in the middle of nowhere. It's split into just six episodes, four main and two bonus episodes, compared to the 12 of the first game, but altogether several hours longer, so don't be fooled.

This is probably Capcom's most competently executed PC port, which admittedly isn't saying much. Regardless, it runs well, looks nice, and has speedy load times. It also controls quite well. I wound up with a surplus of ammo in most levels thanks to precision aiming. You can use the assault rifles essentially as large pistols here. I can't help but wonder if the other Resident Evil PC ports handle this well. I haven't tried 4 as of this writing as I'd already played it twice, on Gamecube and PS2.

There is a bigger emphasis on conservation of resources in this title compared to Revelations 1, but its still not as punishing as Resident Evil 4 in this regard. One thing In particular I really liked was the addition of a manual dodge mechanic instead of the half-assed timed input of the first revelations, which pretty much worked whenever the hell it wants to. Combined with the new skill tree, you can upgrade this dodge for increased distance and safe frames, and even use it to cancel out of other actions, though the latter is prohibitively expensive.

Collecting and upgrading weapons remains the same as the first game, but there are far fewer guns and upgrades overall and furthermore, certain actions in Claire and Moira's levels can either cause you to find or prevent you from finding some items in Barry and Natalia's levels. I was locked out of picking up an AK for Barry, so be warned.

Overall Revelations 2 is a surprisingly decent game. I didn't expect it to be bad, but I did expect it to be cheesy- and it most definately was not. I could do without the hampering additional mechanics of the bonus episodes, but I can't deny that the fights of "The Struggle" episode were suitably nerve-wracking. Series veterans and story shooter fans should pick this one up. I'm looking forward to trying Raid mode if I can find someone to play it with.

The Revelations sub-series follow an old school style, closer to the first chapters of the original Resident Evil.
I absolutely love it: dark scenes, low ammo, high tension.

It's Resident Evil: The Last of Us.  That's what you wanted, right?

Gameplay is now built around single-player co-op using two characters.  Essentially, you have an assist partner that finds items/enemies and use your main character to fight.  The AI is absolutely terrible but the partner regenerates health and gets downed instead of dying.  Inventories are huge so you can carry basically everything, and there's a crafting system but it's only used for a few items.  Workbenches for gun part upgrades return as well, and there's a skill system now to buy character upgrades.

The problem is that the game is walking down hallways again, even worse than RE6 since it doesn't even have the interesting set pieces.  Your objective at any given time is almost always to keep moving forward until you get a cutscene, then repeat.  It's at best going through the motions of survival horror, and it's hard to care when it barely feels like the game does.  As a parting insult, the final area of the game is a mansion, but the path through it is still completely linear.  

None of it adds up to anything interesting either.  The dialogue has been updated to be a bit more interesting and personal, but the plot goes absolutely nowhere, instead having the majority of time spent just moving from area to area.  It kind of makes the whole game feel like filler.  The extra episodes try to fill in some plot details, but are very short for the price and have absolutely atrocious gameplay, so you may as well just look them up on youtube.

On that note, just youtube the whole game, there's very little here worth your time.  Play the first Revelations instead.

Resident Evil: Revelations 2 is the most fun I've had playing a game in the series since the fourth one. It has an interesting premise with precise controls fitted for mouse and keyboard with competent level design and good pacing. Frankly the differences were jarring coming right off of Resident Evil 6.

Any fan of the series will have a blast with this game. There are several humorous callbacks to the early installments involving sandwiches, masters of unlocking and Samurai Edges. The monster designs are very creative in the sense that different types of enemies force you to consider different types of strategies. Just shooting at anything that moves isn't as effective. I especially liked one particular type of monster where you have to use one character to spot it and then switch back to the other one to shoot it. This may sound overly complicated but it's actually quite fun to do, even in single player.

Unlike Revelations 1 this game actually had a revelation about something in one of the main character's past. Though it's not lore-shattering the game at least tries to live up to its own title this time. That always bothered me while playing the first one. Barry and his daughter Moira's story is engaging and heartfelt and leagues beyond any narrative plot in the first game. I thoroughly enjoyed their arcs from start to finish. I also found it humorous that in Barry's story he becomes a surrogate father to Natalia in the same vein of Resident Evil Gaiden. And even though Gaiden isn't canon it's still interesting to see how many similarities its plot and ending shares with Barry and Natalie's story in this game.

The game is goofy but grounded in reality in the same way that Resident Evil 1 was. Especially towards the end when the plots starts getting cartoonishly campy with you having to infiltrate the most evil-looking tower ever. It all screams classic Resident Evil and it plays like it knows all the ridiculous things in the previous games really happened and then running with it.

Resident Evil Revelations 2 BH is honestly a fun game. It includes the original features of a horror/scary theme. The game doesn't really follow much of the original RE games, but does feature a character that was spoken/mentioned in previous games. (Clare Redfield). Also following a sequel of Resident Evil Revelations.

It has it's pro's and cons, so why don't I list them out;

Pro's:

-Dark themes
-Voice acting is done well
-Menu is clean and sharp
-Raid mode is fun
-A lot of secrets to find
-Ability to play as both parties in each chapter, either as Claire or Moira / Barry and Natalia
-Each character has different/unique abilities
-Storyline is presented clear and understanding
-Some jumpscares literally made me jump out of my seat because I didn't expect them to come out from that location

Con's:

-In the story itself, not so many variety of enemies, a bit of a repeat of some of the undead
-Raid mode leveling up can be oddly questionable (Not a con for everyone)
-One thing I'd like to point out that I very dislike, is how they broke up the episodes and you gotta buy them oddly seperate (example, I bought episode one for about 50 cents on sale, and later I picked up the whole game as a bundle, but I've heard people having to buy each episode independent (don't know if that's true tho)).

Additional features of the game; 

Invisible mode; it's self explained. The enemies are all invisible during this gamemode, you play through all chapters as normal but with a challenge. In order to reveal the enemies, you have to switch to Moira to get her flashlight and reveal the enemy, or switch to Natalia and point them out.

Countdown mode; A mode where you race agaisnt time, I haven't tried it but I'm sure I'll like a challenge on highest difficulty and racing through the horror.


Additional thoughts/details; I read a lot of reviews before buying this game, I saw people mentioning that they get a lot of fps drops and the way camera movement was awful for them, I didn't run into any of these problems, maybe because I skyrocket on a i7-6600k with 16 gigs of DDR4 with a GTX 960, I ran on max settings at 120 fps cap. Now, towards the screen situation, I found it flawless, it was smooth and enjoyable.

Would I recommend this game? Absolutely, you don't need to play the previous games in order to understand what is going on here.

Thank you for reading. I hope it helped to those who are debating to buy this game or not.

I love torturing myself with scary games, and this series proved itself to be GROTESQUE mutant murder mayhem. I first tried out Episode 1 when it was on sale under $5. After deciding it was interesting enough and scoping out the positive reviews, I purchased the entire episode pack for around $20 on sale.

Visuals (art, graphics, character/map design) and sound are both great, as expected from the RE series. They do their job of paralyzing me with dread and occasionally getting me to scream my head off. The maps, although linear, are well designed and hold enough secrets (a.k.a achievement opportunities) in the nooks and crannies. 

Gameplay is also quite fun due to the dual layer of POV switching. First, each chapter has a Part A, in which you play as Claire and Moira, and Part B, in which you are Barry and Natalia. This introduces an interesting factor for storyline progression: The player must piece together parts of the story and how the main character’s actions relate to one another. Furthermore, it is interactive in the sense that what you do in Part A might affect exploration opportunities in Part B, and vice versa. 

The other function of POV switching is to give the player access to the wider variety of weapons that each character specializes in. This suits different play style preferences (stealth, melee, ranged, and environmental kills), although some situations will force you to adhere to one. For the boss fights, there is always a “creative” option (find and exploit its weakness to do large damage), but there is also the “Resident Evil” option: Empty enough bullets into it, and the thing will die. 

Second, you can POV switch to control different characters, i.e. you can choose to lead as Moira or Natalia rather than as Claire or Barry, and you can command them to wait or follow. Activating this mechanic is central to solving puzzles, and it is quite fun. It reminds me of Brothers - A Tale of Two Sons, except everything looks hideously terrifying and is trying to kill you. 

Leveling up for skills was relatively easy for me due to the fact that I loooted many gems for BP (skill points), and I replayed a few chapters if I didn't like the grade that I got after completing them. Scarcity of resources was also not an issue in normal mode--perhaps only in the very beginning when you are quite defenseless.

Controls can be buggy at times. For some reason, I found it significantly more difficult to pull off stealth kills as Claire than as Barry. Moira also let me down many times by failing to blind enemies with her flashlight when I set up what seemed like a opportunity. Not to mention, there was a handful of times in which the enemy pyramid head had seen me while I was crouched behind cover, far away! Lastly, I was forced to restart one time when I was controlling Moira, but Claire jumped next to me, got stuck on the ceiling, touched the floor, and promptly DIED.

The story ended up being somewhat stereotypical of the genre, and of what you expect for the Resident Evil series. It was decent, and the ending culminated in a satisfying boss fight for me. Furthermore, I think the writers did a good job of creating not only likeable characters, but also convincing rapport between them. I enjoyed the writing and found several interactions endearing. Unexpected sassiness also created some unintentionally funny moments for me.

Well anyway, On toward my opinion on this.

The gameplay is unique as playing each character, that Episode 1 has, only one character has guns, while the other either has a flashlight or points at things, mostly monsters, which makes an interesting twist since one character is (almost) completely harmless while the other one is armed to the teeth. Stealth Kills are quite useful too. When I played Raid mode, it had this arcade-ish feel to it to mix in with Revelations 2 gameplay. It also has the overused RPG Level element, as well as being able to see your health in that mode only. The other two modes, the Countdown clock and Invisible Enemies mode, give a small challenge to players who want to make it harder, especially the coundown clock one. Oh wait, I can't unless I spend MORE REAL money to get the next Episode, and since I bought weapons storage, I can't access Episode 2 on my brother's PC. That aside, as said before, the episode starts out with Clair and Moira for the first half, then fast forewards to Barry and Natalia for the second half. The Clair Half has you trying to escape, finding Items and weapons, etc., while the Barry half has you looking for Moira.... 6 months after the events of the Clair Half of all of the episodes. Between halves and episodes, you can use BP, which helps you out. Especially if you save enough for Clair/Barry to use their guns when you are not playing as them in the single player.

Raid Mode was fun, though they rehashed a lot of maps from Resident Evil 6. I dunno. I just liked this mode, it seemed fun when I first played it. In Raid Mode the main objective is to reach the goal. There are a group of zombies, and whatnot, to take down while heading there. After taking out a group of zombies..... and whatnot, you get a key to head to the next area. After that it's rinse and repeat until you finally reach the goal. Though there is exceptions, such as defending a crystal that you have to defend, I hate that one, as well as some of them requiring you to reach the goal under a set time limit. Before going on these "Missions" you are able to switch characters, mod your guns, buy and sell stuff, mostly guns and gun mods, etc. Eventually you gain the ability to merge same leveled weapon mods to make a better weapon mod...till you have to rank the toolbox up, which is just as impossible to do as unlocking Chris(?) Episodic stuff aside, the game is good, though I wish I had more for what I had to pay to even get this game. I just hope that, if there's a sequel, it doesn't go the episodic DLC model as this game did, that way I can enjoy more than just a demo's worth of content.

If you're looking for a game review you've come to the wrong place. But if youre looking for a fantastic ravioli recipe you've come to the right place.

Ingredients
- To Make the Dough
375 grams (3 cups) plain flour
1/2 teaspoon salt
2 eggs
1/4 cup (50 ml / 3½ tablespoons) olive oil
1/2 cup (120 ml / 8 tablespoons) water
Extra flour for dusting 


- To Make Cheese Filling
15 ounces (425 grams) container Ricotta cheese
5 ounces (142 g/about 1/2 cup plus 2 tablespoons) "3 Cheese Italian Blend" (Parmesan, Romano & Asiago)
Note: grate these cheeses yourself and create your own custom blend.
1/2 cup cheddar cheese
2 eggs, lightly beaten
1/2 teaspoon salt
1/2 teaspoon pepper


- Extras
Your favorite sauce for the ravioli (i.e. marinara/ marijuana)
Parmesan cheese
Basil
Fried vegetables
Shrimp
Fish slices
Chicken pieces 
Make the Ravioli filling.

- In a small mixing bowl, add the ricotta and mash with a fork.
- Add in the 3-cheese blend, Cheddar cheese, eggs, salt, and pepper.
- Mix all ingredients thoroughly until you have a smooth, paste-like consistency.
- Cover the bowl with plastic wrap and place it in the refrigerator for about 30 minutes. 

Make the Ravioli dough.

- Crack eggs into a large mixing bowl and beat them with a fork. Add water, oil, and salt. Mix.
- Add 1 cup flour to the bowl. Use a fork to mix the flour with the eggs, water, oil, and salt. Repeat with the rest of the flour. Mix until a smooth dough is formed.
- Clear and clean off a large work surface and dust it with flour. This is where you are going to roll out your dough.
- Take the dough out of the mixing bowl, shape it into a ball, and place it on your work surface. Knead for at least 10 minutes or until it becomes elastic.
- Dust a rolling pin with flour to prevent the dough from sticking. Roll out the dough until it is about 1/8 inch (1/3 cm) thick, or about the thickness of 2 stacked quarters.
- With a cookie cutter or upside-down water glass, cut out circles in the dough (will make about 15-20 dough circles).
- Ball up the unused dough and either roll it out and make a couple more raviolis, or wrap it and put in the freezer for another time. Dough can keep for weeks when frozen. Just make sure to wrap well so that it doesn’t suffer from freezer burn or absorb freezer odor. 

Fill the Ravioli shells.

- Take the ravioli filling out of the refrigerator and place a tablespoon of it in middle of a dough.
- Fill a small bowl with water, dip your fingers in, and moisten around the outer edge of the dough circle.
- Fold the dough in half over the filling, making a half-moon shape. Be sure all the filling stays inside. Pinch the edges together and then seal the edges of the ravioli with a fork. Make sure to press firmly and go all the way around. This will add a “homemade” touch as well.
- Repeat this process for all your dough circles.
- Dust the finished ravioli with flour to keep them from sticking together. 

Form the Shells and Fill Using a Ravioli maker.

- Roll the dough into two sheets.
- Place one sheet on the ravioli maker, and form the filling cups.
- Fill with the ravioli mixture.
- Lay the second sheet of dough on top, and roll it out. This will seal in the filling.
- Remove and separate the finished raviolis.

Cook the Ravioli.

- Fill a large pot with water and bring to a boil.
- Place the ravioli in boiling water for 5-6 minutes, or until they float. You can also test for doneness by nibbling on the edges to test.
- If you don't want to make all the ravioli at one time, you can freeze the rest.
- Take ravioli out of boiling water with large slotted spoon and place on warmed plates.

Serve it up.
Top with your favorite sauce, grate some fresh cheese over it, and enjoy!

[h1]Same old same old; interesting concept at the very least, but with a caveat[/h1]

Just as with Revelations 1, and any other recent Resident Evil title, Revelations 2 is a third person shooter that takes a more measured approach in its enemy placement. Rather than the horde-like COD inspired Chris Redfield campaign of RE6 you get something more akin to Ada's; fewer enemies, measured pace and scarcer ammo. Whereas Revelations 1, I felt, took this route out of necessity (you can't have giant hordes when you're making a game for the 3DS), this title had the opportunity to go the Chris Redfield route and it renegged. Capcom knows how to keep continuity, at least-wise choice.

As this game was developed for current-gen systems it is, graphically, a massive step up from Revelations 1. But the environments still feel scaled down; there is certainly an impression of scale in some of the environments that was never achieved in the first title, but if console power isn't holding this title back its clear that the budget alloted was.

And that allotment is perhaps what led to one of my disappointments here: the plot. I can't delve too deep into it, as there's spoilers inherent in discussing it. But I'll speak broadly: what we have here is a storyline that was certainly interesting with a narrative that leaves some mystery. I love mystery. But what I don't like is questions left unsolved towards the end. You have a basic, "we beat the bad guy" in the end with everything ending fine. What is lacking is a lot of the finer questions being answered: you surmize various facets of Natalia's story but Jesus Christ I was confused as to why *so much* is left unanswered. You get around 7 or so memos at the end of the game that explain a few things but it's as if they ran out of money when they got to the portion of the game that was supposed to tell us what happened. 

It's so irritating to have mystery built around the title only to completely forego actual explanations on matters. This isn't a spoiler but....how the hell did the big bad become so mutated....exactly. I mean, you don't make the bad guy a monster that was human and not explain how in the hell they....this is such *bad* writing. It's so infuriating I was close to not recommending it.

But I understand that story-telling and complex narratives in video games rarely deliver in any coherent manner. My expectations are too high; sensible requests like "explanations" are too much for this medium. Ugh....

I will say that the stand-out character here is Moira Burton. I don't know why I've taken a liking to her, but her personality is very....realistic. Whereas most characters feel like 'characters' in a medium, Moira feels like a real person. Her reactions and dialogue is realistic; its what the player would do if he was in the scenario. She casually curses, makes sarcastic remarks to situations that are somewhat preposterous if they were in the real world, and has her own issues that are fairly common in the real world. As an example, you hear the final boss talking with eloquence, to which her response is (paraphrasing): "♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ poetry?". It's as if a 20-something gamer wrote her dialogue, which is why it resonates. She doesn't really fall into any sort of character archetype I've seen in most Japanese medium; I'm sure there's one but I've yet to see it. Kudos for making a realistic character that most 20-something American gamers can relate to (more or less). Break out character here, boys. Maybe it's just me and my own biases.

Ultimately loved the ride; completely and utterly disappointed with its ending, but it's still a decent third person shooter with interesting enemies. Some require you to shoot particular points of the enemy to defeat them, whilst others will not allow you to get close to them lest you wish to risk an instant death. There's some creativity with the enemies here, albeit there's not too much variety in them. The budget rears its head once more. 

I mildly recommend this one. I don't think it's anything amazing, but the storyline is certainly more interesting than Revelations 1. It's just such a damn shame that for a franchise that has so much invested into its lore and universe it just....didn't even try towards the end here. Then again, RE writing has never been good to begin with, so perhaps I need to stop thinking this franchise will reach Deus Ex levels of coherence. Yes, I said coherence. Such a damn shame.

Revelations 2 copies a copious amount of elements from other games, ending up with a predictable and linear, yet enjoyable third-person horror shooter, where the replay value comes from the grinding requirements in both the campaign and the looter side game.

Long version:
Resident Evil: Revelations 2 tells a new side story to expand upon the franchise’s universe, this time bringing back two old-time protagonists, Claire Redfield and Barry Burton. They share a unique setting, where all four separately purchased episodes divide into a Claire chapter and a Barry chapter, with different enemy compositions, but often sharing stages.
Old-time RE gamers will probably recognise that both stories are copy-pasted: Claire’s is from Code Veronica (she ends up with a sassy teenage sidekick on a prison island run by a crazy Umbrella employee), and Barry’s is from Gaiden (he escorts a little girl with psychic powers that allow her to sense enemies).

Luckily, the game mechanics show more innovation. The campaign uses co-op mechanics, where only one player gets guns, whereas the other can stun enemies, open locks, and find consumables. This all falls apart in single-player though, since the non-controlled character usually just stands idly, turning fights into frantic character switches for sheer survival.

Grinding is an integral part of RER2, even in the campaign, where unlocking every possible skill and medal requires at least six full runs (although replaying the entire campaign takes less than 90 minutes).
It is even more prevalent in Raid mode, the looter side game returning from RER1, since all skills and all characters level separately, and weapon parts act more like consumables. It is a matter of taste if players prefer this or the more streamlined approach of RER1 Raid—especially if we consider that RER2 Raid levels are mostly tiny reused RE6 stages—but it is undeniable that this game mode feels rewarding and fun, even in the long run.

Revelations 1 was my first game in the Resident Evil series, and after completing Resident Evil 1, 4, 5 and 6 I finally decided to go back and finish Revelations 2 - and I was not disappointed.

The first half of the story revolves around Claire Redfield and Moira Burton who are kidnapped and sent to an island full of crazy people (and monsters) as part of a fear experiment, with a woman who calls herself The Overseer monitoring their every move.

In the second half Barry Burton arrives at the island six months later in search of his daughter Moira, teaming up with the mysterious, young girl Natalia who seems to have some sort of connection to the island and the monsters on it.

When playing as Claire or Barry the game plays out fairly similarly to the first game. You use your knife, guns and bombs (crafted using bottles and various supplies) to get to where you're going while fighting off the bad guys. In some parts you can choose to take a more stealthy approach, which lets you save your ammunition and herbs. As in most Resident Evil games managing your resources is very important, especially on the harder difficulties.

Unlike the first game the "partner characters" have their own role in this game. Moira is in charge of the flashlight and the crowbar, while Natalia has her "enemy detection" and brick. Yes, she uses a brick, and it's actually quite effective. They use their flashlight/senses to find hidden items all over the map, which can come in handy when you're running low on resources.

In addition to the standard story mode you have a countdown mode, invisible mode, DLC bonus stories and raid mode:
- [b]Countdown mode[/b]: In countdown mode you are on a timer, and have to finish the levels as fast as possible. You get extra time for breaking hourglasses across the map as well as killing enemies. For someone like me who usually kills everything and examines everything from top to bottom, having to rush through the levels as fast as I could was a nice change.
- [b]Invisible mode[/b]: All enemies are invisible. This mode was included in some of the other Resident Evil games as well, however in this game you can actually see the enemies briefly using Moira and Natalia, which makes it a bit easier to kill them when switching over to Claire or Barry.
-  [b]Little Miss[/b]/[b]The Struggle[/b]: The DLC bonus stories were nothing special, however they do give you more information on Moira and Natalia, so it's worth playing through them at least once.
- [b]Raid mode[/b]: After having gotten sick of raid mode in Revelations 1 I did not think I would enjoy raid mode in Revelations 2. I was wrong. The enemies keep coming, and you have to kill them all to gain gold/xp, upgrading your characters and weapons between stages. Many of the enemies and areas from the previous games such as Revelations 1, Resident Evil 5 and Resident Evil 6 also pop up, which was great.

My expectations for Revelations 2 were very high, and although I did enjoy the game a lot, there were some things that I felt could have been improved. The story, characters and atmosphere were not as good as in Revelations 1, and the game also felt a bit shorter. That said, Revelations 2 is still a great game, and raid mode as well as countdown mode and invisible mode were all great. As someone who cares about achievements, the game was far less grindy than some of the other Resident Evil games, which was also a plus.

All in all, I definitely recommend this game.

resident evil has always been increasingly silly in tone. it started out sober enough with the first game, where the most outrageous thing you could expect was the predictable mad science ubermensch final boss, and the 2nd game maintained that seriousness for most of its duration, only really going over the top towards the end, but little by little the series has shed its adventure game roots and become more action-oriented. we all know this, of course -- it was one of the big reasons they went the direction they did with RE7.

the revelations series are an obvious attempt at bringing back a bit of the old survival horror vibe from the early days while combining them with the more fluid controls of the later games, and on some level they succeed. but where they differ from each other is that revelations 2 is the vastly superior offering. revelations 1 had an amazingly silly yet convoluted plot and was quite easy due to its roots as a 3DS game (meaning mouse controls made combat trivial.) it also looked very dated, graphically (again, due to it originally being a 3DS game.) revelations 2, in contrast, not only manages to more closely hew to the old survival horror vibe (albeit in a very different fashion, set mostly in and around a former soviet closed city, giving it a run-down slavic vibe made classic by the likes of stalker and half-life 2) but is also perhaps the best-written game in the series in a very long time, mostly avoiding plot holes and having a much better english script than the average RE game, feeling far more natural than capcom translations usually are.

like revelations before it, the story is told from multiple perspectives, in this case each lengthy episode (of four) is split into two segments, with about six months' time in between. what's more is that each segment is focused on two series favorites. the first is claire, making a return to the series after having been relegated to flashbacks of RE2 and code veronica, and in violation of resident evil's habit of never aging characters, most definitely looks about 15 years older than she was in RE2. also rejoining the series is barry, who has not been seen in a canonical RE game since a single-screen cameo in RE3 and marks his first canonical appearance as a playable character -- and yes, he's still making dad jokes.

making things interesting is that claire's storyline feels very classically RE-like, with the occasional twists and turns and an explosive finale; barry's, meanwhile, comes off feeling like an homage to the last of us, not least because the gruff beard dad with a gun has a young girl in tow, natalia, that he has to protect. conversely, claire's companion is moira, a teenage girl who drops F bombs like they're punctuation, and her youthful pottymouth is refreshing compared to the stilted but otherwise mostly clean dialogue the series has always had. besides, there's something delightfully juvenile about phrases like "moist barrel of ♥♥♥♥♥."

gameplay wise you can expect the same OTS fun that's been a series staple since RE4, though things are a bit more sedate than 4, 5 or 6, with mostly smaller groups of enemies. they're more varied than the shapeless blobs of rev 1, too; claire and moira will face off "the afflicted," residents of the island turned into violent mutants through viral infection and torture. if you've played RE4 or 5 you know how this goes -- they're smarter than zombies and will try to surround you. barry and natalia, meanwhile, must deal with the much more zombie-like "rotten," the re-animated, nearly-skeletal corpses of all the afflicted claire killed. they're slow and stupid. this particular wrinkle helps keep the gameplay fresh, as you're never facing the same type of enemy throughout the whole game. other enemies appear as well, such as a terrifying invisible enemy that can one-shot you if it gets close.

moira and natalia are not gun users, one for personal reasons and the other for being literally like 10, but neither are above using melee when necessary (natalia can brick certain enemies if they're crawling.) what makes them useful is that moira carries a flashlight for claire's benefit, able to find items similar to the scanner in revelations 1 while also being able to use a high-beam that stuns enemies. natalia can also spot items lying around, but her most important skill is the ability sense enemies, even through walls, and as such is vital for dealing with the aforementioned invisible monsters. both characters can be switched to, as well, resurrecting a gameplay element from resident evil 0.

like revelations before it, over time you'll find upgrades for your weaponry; these upgrades can be added or removed at a bench, allowing you to make increasingly powerful weapons. in many cases, your actions in claire's story will have ramifications for things barry might face or find, such as an AK-47 in a sewer provided claire opens the right gate.

resident evil is a long-lived series, having been in the public consciousness for 21 years now, with a whopping 11 main series games and several spinoffs and assorted media. there are some who say the series has lost its way, and in some way that's true, having strayed very far away from its roots as an alone in the dark clone. but revelations 2 is a breath of fresh air, managing to create an atmosphere very removed from the comic book silliness that the series has indulged in over the years, with very little in the way of over-the-top huge monsters (even the final boss isn't that big.) having played most of the series, including the spinoffs, i can safely say this is up there with 4 or the original playstation trilogy in terms of quality and fun. the naturalistic script is a huge plus, and the little touches such as one campaign affecting the other are obvious throwbacks to the series' glory days.

it's not a return to the ancient method of survival horror, but it's as close to the last of us as the series is going to get. this is definitely highly recommendable to long-time RE fans.
